}

But reality is often harsh. When logical branches or nested functions appear in the code, and the object's lifecycle is transferred, manually controlling its delete becomes difficult:

```c++void Func() { Object* object = new Object; if (...) { // Do something delete object; return; } else if (...) { // Do something delete object; return; } else if (...) { // Do something delete object; return; } } 

For this reason, we often need an automatic object lifecycle management strategy. Currently, there are two main approaches:

- Smart pointers
- Garbage collection

### Smart Pointers

Various C++ libraries often provide the concept of shared pointers. Their core idea is:

- Wrap the actual object pointer with an external object. By monitoring the construction, destruction, and copying of the external object, use a piece of public memory to record the pointer's reference count. When the reference count reaches 0, destroy the object.

A simple imitation is as follows:

```c++
struct SharedPtrRefData {
    uint refCount = 0; 
};

template<typename _Ty>
class SharedPtr {
public:
    SharedPtr(_Ty* rawPtr)                      // Constructor
        : mRawPtr(rawPtr)
        , mRefData(new SharedPtrRefData)        // Create public memory
    {
        mRefData->refCount++;                   // Increment reference count
    }

    SharedPtr(const SharedPtr<_Ty>& other) {        // Copy constructor
        mRefData = other.mRefData;              // Transfer public memory
        mRefData->refCount++;                   // Increment reference count
    }

    ~SharedPtr() {                              // Destructor
        mRefData->refCount--;                   // Decrement reference count
        if (mRefData->refCount == 0) {  
            delete mRawPtr;                     // Destroy the object
            delete mRefData;                    // Destroy public memory
        }
    }
private:
    _Ty* mRawPtr;
    SharedPtrRefData* mRefData;
};

This structure is implemented in the following frameworks:

  • C++ standard library: std::shared_ptr
  • Unreal Engine: TSharedPtr
  • Qt: QSharedPointer

Using SharedPtr ensures that the pointer object is not released when accessed. However, sometimes we may want a "shared pointer" not to extend the object's lifecycle but to check if the object has been destroyed later. Frameworks generally call this structure a WeakPtr, which corresponds to:

  • C++ standard library: std::weak_ptr
  • Unreal Engine: TWeakPtr
  • Qt: QWeakPointer

Taking std as an example:

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::shared_ptr<int> sptr(new int);
    std::weak_ptr<int> wptr(sptr);
    if (const std::shared_ptr<int>& lock = wptr.lock()) {
        std::cout << "exist!!!" << std::endl;
    }
    else {
        std::cout << "not exist" << std::endl;
    }
    sptr.reset();
    if (const std::shared_ptr<int>& lock = wptr.lock()) {
        std::cout << "exist!!!" << std::endl;
    }
    else {
        std::cout << "not exist!" << std::endl;
    }
    return 0;
}

/*
exist!!!
not exist!
*/

In the simple SharePtr code above, when refCount is 0, both the object and public memory are destroyed. In reality, SharedPtrRefData contains two counters: refCount and weakCount. When refCount is 0, only the object is destroyed, not the public memory. This allows WeakPtr to still access the shared memory to check if the object exists. The public memory is only destroyed when weakCount also reaches 0.

For raw pointers, delete only destroys the object's memory, but the address pointed to by the pointer still exists. Improper management can lead to dangling pointers and memory leaks. WeakPtr solves this problem.

Another scenario: sometimes we want a new-created object to be destroyed when it goes out of scope, just like an ordinary object. For example:

class Example {
public:
    Example()
        : mObject(new Object)
    {}
    ~Example() {
        delete mObject;
    } 
private:
    Object* mObject;
};

In this case, we can use:

  • C++ standard library: std::unique_ptr
  • Unreal Engine: TUniquePtr
  • Qt: QScopedPointer

Qt's naming seems to better reflect its purpose.

The above code can be rewritten using UniquePtr as:

class Example {
public: Example()
    : mObject(new Object)
    {}
private:
    std::unique_ptr<Object> mObject;
};

Smart pointers can solve most problems in development, but they are not perfect. Here are some notes:

  • When using smart pointers, try to new objects in constructors or reset functions. Avoid manipulating raw pointers outside smart pointers.

  • Do not use std::shared<int> sptr(this). If you want to create a shared pointer using this, the class of this must inherit from the template enable_shared_from_this.

  • Excessive use of unnecessary SharedPtr can lead to waste. The original intention of using SharedPtr is to maintain the object's lifecycle; if you do not need the interface to transfer the object's lifecycle, you should not expose SharedPtr—instead, use WeakPtr or RawPtr.

  • When using in a multi-threaded environment, ensure that the SharedPtr used is thread-safe to ensure the reference count works correctly.

Additionally, there are some hidden dangers:

  • When using shared pointers, it is easy to overlook the lifecycle of captured parameters. If there are shared pointers internally, it can lead to memory leaks:
#include <iostream>
#include <functional>

class Example {
public:
    Example() {
        std::cout << "Create" << std::endl;
    }
    ~Example() {
        std::cout << "Destroy" << std::endl;
    }
};

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
    {
        std::function<void()> func0;
        {
            std::shared_ptr<Example> sptr(new Example);
            std::function<void()> func1 = [sptr]() {};    // Capture the shared pointer as a parameter
            std::cout << "---------0" << std::endl;
            // func0 = func1;     // Uncomment this line, and Example will be released between 1 and 2
        }
        std::cout << "---------1" << std::endl;
    }
    std::cout << "---------2" << std::endl;
    return 0;
}
/*
The captured parameters of a lambda are released only when they go out of scope and are not referenced by any function.
If the function is not destroyed or reset in time, the captured parameters will persist, leading to memory leaks.
*/
  • SharedPtr has a circular reference problem:
#include <iostream>

struct B;

struct A {
    ~A() {
        std::cout << "destruct A" << std::endl;
    }
    std::shared_ptr<B> mB;
};

struct B {
    ~B() {
        std::cout << "destruct B" << std::endl;
    }
    std::shared_ptr<A> mA;
};

int main() {
    {
        std::shared_ptr<A> a(new A);
        std::shared_ptr<B> b(new B); 
        a->mB = b;
        b->mA = a;
    }
    return 0; // Objects cannot be released
}
  • The destruction of SharedPtr is immediate. Destroying a large number of objects at once in a large-scale system can cause lag.

For more in-depth information on shared pointers, refer to this article:

  • https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/532215950

docs.title: Garbage Collection
docs.text:
To address the flaws of shared pointers, some high-level languages and large frameworks provide a Garbage Collection (GC) mechanism, aiming to solve circular reference problems and implement delayed destruction.

Due to C++'s features (historical reasons), introducing a poor GC mechanism into the C++ standard would only make it more chaotic. Therefore, GC in C++ is usually customized by frameworks, such as UE and Qt, which have deviated from the C++ standard. Netizens jokingly call them U++ and Q++.

Currently, the GC mechanisms the author is more familiar with include:

  • Unreal Engine
  • Qt, FBX SDK
  • Lua

For developers, there are two main points to understand about GC:

  • How to mark reference relationships between objects
  • How to perform garbage collection

For some high-level languages like Java, C#, Python, and Lua, it is easy to monitor reference relationships between objects due to the virtual machine. In C++, reference relationships between objects can only be set manually or analyzed through reflection.

Qt uses QObject as the base class, and its memory collection is very simple:

class QObject {
public:
    QObject(QObject * parent = nullptr);
private:
    QVector<QObject*> children;
    QObject *parent;
};
  • QObject has a parent pointer and a children list. Destroying a QObject will also destroy its children.
  • QObject also provides a deleteLater() function, which adds the object to an array. The object is destroyed after the event processing loop ends.

FBX SDK uses FbxObject as the base class, and a parent object must be specified when creating an instance:

FbxManager* lManager = FbxManager::Create();
FbxIOSettings* lIOSettings = FbxIOSettings::Create(lManager, "");
FbxScene* scene = FbxScene::Create(lManager,"");
FbxSkeleton* skeletonNode = FbxSkeleton::Create(scene,"SkeletonRoot");
FbxCluster* rootCluster = FbxCluster::Create(skeletonNode, "");
  • When the parent object is released, the child objects are also released.

The main memory collection structures of the above two frameworks are very simple. For loop problems, they detect when specifying parent and directly report an error if a loop occurs.

In contrast, UE's GC mechanism is much more complex. In UE, references are mainly built in two ways:

  • UProperty (reflection): UE determines the reference relationship between two objects by analyzing the Property of UObject.
  • FGCObject: An interface class for manually building reference relationships. Most frameworks in UE, such as UMG, Editor, Niagara, etc., derive from FGCObject to implement a set of GC reference management mechanisms. This allows developers to implicitly build reference relationships between objects when calling certain interfaces.

UE's collection method is relatively complex and will not be expanded here. Generally, it is only necessary to understand that it performs collection periodically and quantitatively.

Here is a simple mark-and-sweep algorithm. Its core is:

  • Store all recyclable objects in an array.
  • Store reference relationships between objects.
  • Have a global root node. If other nodes have a reference relationship to reach this node, it means the node is reachable.
  • During garbage collection, the game thread needs to be suspended to ensure no objects are in use.
  • Traverse from the root node, mark all reachable nodes.
  • Traverse the object array, destroy unreachable nodes.

A simple implementation is as follows (for more details, see: Mark-and-Sweep: Garbage Collection Algorithm):

class ObjectBase {
public:
    typedef short ID;
public:
    ObjectBase();
    virtual ~ObjectBase();
    void addRefrence(ObjectBase * ref);     // Add object reference
    void removeRefrence(ObjectBase* ref);   // Remove object reference
private:
    friend class ObjectManagement;
    ID id;                      // Assign a unique ID to this object
    std::list<ID> refrence;     // List of referenced object IDs
};

short is used here because it is only 2 bytes and can represent 2^15 (32767) numbers, which is sufficient for IDs.

To manage all ObjectBase objects, a global management object GObjectManagement is created. Objects are added to it during construction and removed during destruction:

ObjectBase::ObjectBase() {
    GObjectManagement.AddObject(this);
}

ObjectBase::~ObjectBase() {
    GObjectManagement.RemoveObject(this);
}

The definition of ObjectManagement is as follows:

class ObjectManagement {
public:
    ObjectManagement() {
        for (int i = 0; i < mObjects.size(); i++) {     // Initialize the ID stack
            mObjects[i].object = nullptr;
            mIdStack[i] = i;
        }
    }
    void AddObject(ObjectBase* obj) {       // Add an object
        if (obj != nullptr) {
            obj->id = allocId();
            mObjects[obj->id].object = obj;
            ++mCurrentNumberOfObject;
            mMaxIdOfObject = std::max(mMaxIdOfObject, obj->id);
        }
    }
    void RemoveObject(ObjectBase* obj) {    // Remove an object
        if (obj != nullptr) {
            mObjects[obj->id].object = nullptr;
            freeId(obj->id);
            --mCurrentNumberOfObject;
        }
    }
    void GarbageCollection() {              // Garbage collection
        MarkObjects(0);        // Assume node 0 is the global root node of the game; start traversal from it to mark reachable objects
        for (int i = 0; i <= mMaxIdOfObject; i++) {     // Simply traverse all objects and destroy unreachable ones
            if (!mObjects[i].reachable) {
                delete mObjects[i].object;
            }
            else {      // Restore state for the next reachability traversal
                mObjects[i].reachable = false;
            }
        }
    }

    void MarkObjects(const ObjectBase::ID& Id) {                // Depth-first traversal of all nodes
        ObjectBase* obj = mObjects[Id].object;
        if (obj != nullptr && !mObjects[Id].reachable) {        // Require the node to be unreachable to avoid loops
            mObjects[Id].reachable = true;
            for (auto& subId : obj->refrence) {
                MarkObjects(subId);
            }
        }
    }

private:
    ObjectBase::ID allocId() {                  // Allocate an ID from the top of the stack
        assert(mIdStackTop < mIdStack.size());
        return mIdStack[mIdStackTop++];
    }

    void freeId(ObjectBase::ID id) {            // Recycle an ID
        assert(mIdStackTop > 0);
        mIdStack[--mIdStackTop] = id;
    }

public:
    struct ObjectItem {
        ObjectBase* object;
        bool reachable = false;
    };

    static const int MAX_NUMBER_OF_OBJECT = std::numeric_limits<ObjectBase::ID>().max();

    std::array<ObjectItem, MAX_NUMBER_OF_OBJECT> mObjects;      // Create a fixed-size array of 32767 to store all objects

    std::array<ObjectBase::ID, MAX_NUMBER_OF_OBJECT> mIdStack;  // This fixed-size array simulates a stack to allocate and recycle IDs, ensuring IDs do not expand rapidly
    ObjectBase::ID mIdStackTop = 0;                             // Top index of the stack

    ObjectBase::ID mCurrentNumberOfObject = 0;                  // Current number of objects
    ObjectBase::ID mMaxIdOfObject = 0;                          // Maximum ID used in the program to reduce traversal count
};

// Global static object
static ObjectManagement GObjectManagement;

The following code is written for simple testing:

class Object : public ObjectBase {
public:
    Object(std::string name) : mName(name) {
        std::cout << "construct object : " << mName << std::endl;
    }
    virtual ~Object() {
        std::cout << "destruct object : " << mName << std::endl;
    }
private:
    std::string mName;
protected:
};

int main() {
    Object* root = new Object("Root");                      // By default, the first node is the game root node
    Object* a = new Object("A");
    Object* b = new Object("B");
    Object* c = new Object("C");                            
    Object* d = new Object("D");
    Object* e = new Object("E");
    Object* f = new Object("F");

    root->addRefrence(a);                                   //    root
    root->addRefrence(b);                                   //    /  \ 
    b->addRefrence(c);                                      //   A    B
    b->addRefrence(d);                                      //       / \ 
    c->addRefrence(e);                                      //      C   D
    c->addRefrence(f);                                      //     / \ 
    e->addRefrence(f);                                      //    E - F

    std::cout << "Garbage Collection : 0" << std::endl;      // No objects are recycled
    GarbageCollection();
    std::cout << "-----------------------" << std::endl;

    b->removeRefrence(c);                                   // Remove B's reference to C; C, E, F will be destroyed
    std::cout << "Garbage Collection : 1" << std::endl;
    GarbageCollection();
    std::cout << "-----------------------" << std::endl;
}

construct object : Root
construct object : A
construct object : B
construct object : C
construct object : D
construct object : E
construct object : F
Garbage Collection : 0
-----------------------
Garbage Collection : 1
destruct object : C
destruct object : E
destruct object : F
-----------------------

docs.title: Memory Scheduling Frameworks
docs.text: The open-source community has produced many memory scheduling frameworks aimed at reducing memory fragmentation and increasing cache hit rates. Some well-known ones include:

docs.title: mimalloc
docs.text:
mimalloc is a general-purpose allocator with excellent performance characteristics. It was originally developed by Daan Leijen for the runtime systems of the Koka and Lean languages.

  • Small and consistent: The library uses simple and consistent data structures, with approximately 8k LOC. This makes it very suitable for integration and adaptation to other projects. For runtime systems, it provides hooks for monotonic heartbeats and delayed release (for bounded worst-case time with reference counting).
  • Free list sharding: Instead of a single large free list (per size class), each "mimalloc page" has many smaller lists, which reduces fragmentation and increases locality—things allocated in time are allocated close together in memory. (A mimalloc page contains blocks of a single size class, typically 64KiB on 64-bit systems.)
  • Free list multi-sharding: A great idea! We not only shard the free lists per mimalloc page but also have multiple free lists per page. In particular, there is a list for thread-local free operations and another for concurrent free operations. Freeing from another thread can now be a single CAS without complex coordination between threads. Since there will be thousands of individual free lists, contention is naturally distributed across the heap, and the chance of contention at a single location will be low—much like randomized algorithms such as skip lists, where adding a random oracle eliminates the need for more complex algorithms.
  • Eager page reset: When a "page" becomes empty (more likely due to free list sharding), the memory is marked as unused by the operating system ("reset" or "purged") to reduce (real) memory pressure and fragmentation, especially in long-running programs.
  • Security: mimalloc can be built in secure mode, adding guard pages, random allocation, encrypted free lists, etc., to prevent various heap vulnerabilities. The performance penalty is usually around 10% higher on average in our benchmarks.
  • First-class heaps: Efficiently create and use multiple heaps for allocation across different regions. Heaps can be destroyed at once instead of freeing each object individually.
  • Bounded: It does not suffer from bloat, has bounded worst-case allocation time ( wcat ), bounded space overhead (about 0.2% metadata, up to 12.5% waste in allocation size), and no internal points of contention using only atomic operations.
  • Fast: In our benchmarks, mimalloc outperforms other leading allocators ( jemalloc , tcmalloc , Hoard , etc.) and usually uses less memory. A nice feature is that it consistently performs well across a wide range of benchmarks. There is also good huge OS page support for larger server programs.

docs.title: oneTBB
docs.text:
Intel® oneAPI Threading Building Blocks (oneTBB) is a flexible performance library that simplifies adding parallelism to complex applications across accelerated architectures, even if you are not a threading expert.

  • Specify logical performance, not threads: The runtime library automatically maps logical parallelism to threads to most effectively utilize processor resources.
  • Target threads for better performance: Focus on specific goals for parallelizing compute-intensive work, providing higher-level, simpler solutions.
  • Coexist with other thread packages: It can seamlessly coexist with other threads, giving you the flexibility to keep legacy code unchanged and use oneTBB for new implementations.
  • Emphasize scalable data parallel programming: oneTBB emphasizes data parallel programming rather than decomposing the program into functional blocks and assigning a separate thread to each block, allowing multiple threads to work on different parts of a collection. This scales well to more processors. As you add processors and accelerators, program performance improves.

docs.title: jemalloc
docs.text: jemalloc is a general-purpose malloc(3) implementation that emphasizes avoiding fragmentation and scalable concurrency support. It is designed to be used as a system-provided memory allocator, such as in FreeBSD's libc library, and for linking to C/C++ applications. jemalloc provides many introspection, memory management, and tuning features beyond those of standard allocators.

docs.title: tcmalloc
docs.text:
TCMalloc is Google's custom implementation of C malloc() and C++ operator new for allocating memory in C and C++ code. This custom memory allocation framework is an alternative to the frameworks provided by the C standard library (usually via glibc on Linux) and the C++ standard library.

  • Performance scales with the degree of parallelism in the application.
  • Optimized for C++14 and C++17, with slight differences from the standard while ensuring performance advantages (these are noted in the TCMalloc Reference).

  • Allows extensions for better performance on certain architectures, as well as other behaviors such as metric collection.

  • Performs allocation from the operating system by managing memory blocks of specific sizes (called "pages").

  • Uses separate pages (or runs of pages called "spans" in TCMalloc) for specific object sizes. For example, all 16-byte objects are placed in "spans" allocated specifically for that size of object. Operations to acquire or release memory in this case are much simpler.
  • Keeps memory in caches to speed up access to commonly used objects. Retaining such caches even after release helps avoid costly system calls if the memory is reallocated later.

docs.title: Usage Methods
docs.text:
These frameworks are easy to use. They provide their own memory allocation and release interfaces, and we only need to override C++'s operator and use these memory interfaces to manipulate memory:

Taking mimalloc as an example, the following code can override C++'s new and delete:

#include <vcruntime_new.h>

_NODISCARD _Ret_notnull_ _Post_writable_byte_size_(_Size) _VCRT_ALLOCATOR
void* __CRTDECL operator new(size_t Size) { return mi_malloc(Size ? Size : 1); }

_NODISCARD _Ret_notnull_ _Post_writable_byte_size_(_Size) _VCRT_ALLOCATOR
void* __CRTDECL operator new[](size_t Size) { return mi_malloc(Size ? Size : 1); }

_NODISCARD _Ret_maybenull_ _Success_(return != NULL) _Post_writable_byte_size_(_Size) _VCRT_ALLOCATOR
void* __CRTDECL operator new(size_t Size, const std::nothrow_t&) { return mi_malloc(Size ? Size : 1); }

_NODISCARD _Ret_maybenull_ _Success_(return != NULL) _Post_writable_byte_size_(_Size) _VCRT_ALLOCATOR
void* __CRTDECL operator new[](size_t Size, const std::nothrow_t&) { return mi_malloc(Size ? Size : 1); }

void __CRTDECL operator delete(void* Ptr) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete[](void* Ptr) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete(void* Ptr, const std::nothrow_t&) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete[](void* Ptr, const std::nothrow_t&) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete(void* Ptr, size_t Size) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete[](void* Ptr, size_t Size) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete(void* Ptr, size_t Size, const std::nothrow_t&) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete[](void* Ptr, size_t Size, const std::nothrow_t&) { mi_free(Ptr); }

_NODISCARD _Ret_notnull_ _Post_writable_byte_size_(_Size) _VCRT_ALLOCATOR
void* __CRTDECL operator new(size_t Size, std::align_val_t Alignment) { return mi_malloc_aligned(Size ? Size : 1, (std::size_t)Alignment); }

_NODISCARD _Ret_notnull_ _Post_writable_byte_size_(_Size) _VCRT_ALLOCATOR
void* __CRTDECL operator new[](size_t Size, std::align_val_t Alignment) { return mi_malloc_aligned(Size ? Size : 1, (std::size_t)Alignment); }

_NODISCARD _Ret_maybenull_ _Success_(return != NULL) _Post_writable_byte_size_(_Size) _VCRT_ALLOCATOR
void* __CRTDECL operator new(size_t Size, std::align_val_t Alignment, const std::nothrow_t&) { return mi_malloc_aligned(Size ? Size : 1, (std::size_t)Alignment); }

_NODISCARD _Ret_maybenull_ _Success_(return != NULL) _Post_writable_byte_size_(_Size) _VCRT_ALLOCATOR
void* __CRTDECL operator new[](size_t Size, std::align_val_t Alignment, const std::nothrow_t&) { return mi_malloc_aligned(Size ? Size : 1, (std::size_t)Alignment); }

void __CRTDECL operator delete(void* Ptr, std::align_val_t Alignment) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete[](void* Ptr, std::align_val_t Alignment) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete(void* Ptr, std::align_val_t Alignment, const std::nothrow_t&) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete[](void* Ptr, std::align_val_t Alignment, const std::nothrow_t&) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete(void* Ptr, size_t Size, std::align_val_t Alignment) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete[](void* Ptr, size_t Size, std::align_val_t Alignment) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete(void* Ptr, size_t Size, std::align_val_t Alignment, const std::nothrow_t&) { mi_free(Ptr); }
void __CRTDECL operator delete[](void* Ptr, size_t Size, std::align_val_t Alignment, const std::nothrow_t&) { mi_free(Ptr); }

In Unreal Engine, it implements a memory allocator base class FMalloc and derives the following subclasses. It uses FMemory::Malloc/FMemory::Free to call the memory allocator's interface, allowing switching between different memory allocators:

  • Ansi: Standard C allocator, directly calling malloc, free, realloc.

  • Stomp: Helps track problems caused by reading/writing during allocation, such as dangling pointers and memory out-of-bounds.

  • TBB: Thread Building Blocks, a 64-bit scalable memory allocator provided by Intel.

  • Jemalloc: Mainly used for Unix memory allocators.

  • Binned: Binned memory allocator, mainly used for iOS.

  • Binned: The binned allocator divides a block of memory ( Pool ) into many slots of different sizes. For example, Binned divides 64KB into 41 different slots on PC and allocates free slots from the end forward.

  • Binned2: The Binned2 allocator supports thread-local memory allocation and does not need to lock every time. This can significantly improve performance during frequent small memory allocations and releases.

  • Binned3: Uses virtual memory addresses (logical memory addresses), which can be arranged to perform high-speed Pool Index searches, so that the target size Pool can be calculated from the memory pointer.

  • Mimalloc: A general-purpose memory allocator superior to tcmalloc and jemalloc.

The support for memory allocators across different platforms in Unreal Engine is as follows:

Ansi TBB ® Jemalloc ® Binned Binned2 Binned3 Mimalloc ® Stomp Android √ √ default √ (64bits) IOS √ default Windows √ default √ √ √ (64bits) √ √ Linux √ √ √ default √ Mac √ default √ √ √ HoloLens √ default

docs.title: Basic Library Optimization
docs.text:
At the application level of memory, there is much room for optimization in C++'s basic containers and algorithms, which brings us to the C++ STL library. It has many shortcomings:

  • Some STL implementations (especially Microsoft STL) have poor performance characteristics, making them unsuitable for game development.
  • STL is sometimes difficult to debug because most STL implementations use cryptic variable names and unusual data structures.
  • STL allocators are sometimes painful to use because they have many requirements and cannot be modified once bound to a container.
  • STL contains excessive functionality that may cause code to behave unexpectedly. It is not easy to tell programmers they should not use a certain feature.
  • STL is implemented through very deep function calls. This leads to unacceptable performance in non-optimized builds and sometimes in optimized builds as well.
  • STL does not support alignment of contained objects.
  • STL containers do not allow you to insert entries without providing an entry to copy from. This can be inefficient.
  • Useful STL extensions found in existing STL implementations such as STLPort (e.g., slist, hash_map, shared_ptr) are not portable because they do not exist in other STL versions or are inconsistent between STL versions.
  • STL lacks useful extensions that game programmers find useful (e.g., intrusive_list), but they can be optimally implemented in a portable STL environment.
  • The STL specification limits our ability to use it effectively. For example, an STL vector does not guarantee contiguous memory, so it cannot be safely used as an array.
  • STL emphasizes correctness over performance, and sometimes you can achieve significant performance gains by reducing academic purity.
  • STL containers have private implementations that do not allow you to manipulate their data in a portable way, but sometimes this is important (e.g., node pools).
  • All existing versions of STL allocate memory in the empty version of at least some of their containers. This is not ideal and prevents optimizations such as container memory reset, which can greatly improve performance in some cases.
  • STL compiles slowly because most modern STL implementations are very large.

Excerpted from https://github.com/electronicarts/EASTL/blob/master/doc/Design.md

Its biggest shortcoming is:

  • STL emphasizes correctness over performance. In pursuit of academic purity, it does not take risks or take unconventional paths for performance.

For example, many people know that when using std::vector, they should use reserve to pre-allocate memory to avoid memory reallocation due to expansion. For containers like set and map, it is also possible to pre-allocate node memory, which not only reduces the number of memory allocations but also ensures that container elements are contiguous in memory, greatly increasing cache hit rates during access.

If you compare STL and UE's memory allocators, you can find obvious differences:

  • STL uses Allocator to allocate memory for new elements in the container.
  • UE's Allocator reallocates memory for the entire container. UE's containers all support an expansion mechanism like std::vector.

To solve the above problems, many engines maintain their own basic libraries. Open-source solutions mainly include the following:

docs.title: EASTL
docs.text:
EASTL is a C++ template library containing containers, algorithms, and iterators that can be used for runtime and tool development across multiple platforms. Its implementation is quite extensive and robust, with an emphasis on performance above all other considerations.

  • EASTL has a simplified and more flexible custom allocation scheme.
  • EASTL's code is easier to read.
  • EASTL has extended containers and algorithms.
  • EASTL has optimizations designed for game development.

Among the above points, the only incompatible difference with STL is the memory allocation situation.

docs.title: foonathan
docs.text: foonathan also aims to solve the flaws of STL, but unlike EASTL, it does not attempt to change STL.

docs.title: STL C++17 polymorphic memory source
docs.text:
Before C++17, memory allocation for STL containers needed to be done using allocator, which had the following main flaws:

  • allocator is part of the template signature. Containers with different allocators cannot be mixed.
vector<int, allocator0> v0;
vector<int, allocator1> v1;
v0 = v1;  // Error

  • allocator memory alignment cannot be controlled and requires passing a custom allocator.

  • allocator has no internal state.

C++17 provides a new memory allocation method for containers ——<memory_resource>.

Its usage is as follows:

#include <memory_resource>
#include <vector>
#include <string>            
#include <iostream>

class CustomMemoryResource : public std::pmr::memory_resource {   // Custom memory_source
public:
    CustomMemoryResource() {}
private:
    virtual void* do_allocate(const size_t _Bytes, const size_t _Align) override {
        return ::operator new(_Bytes, std::align_val_t(_Align));
    }                                                                                                                                             
    virtual void do_deallocate(void* _Ptr, size_t _Bytes, size_t _Align) {
        ::operator delete(_Ptr, _Bytes, std::align_val_t(_Align));
    };
    virtual bool do_is_equal(const memory_resource& _That) const noexcept {
        return this == &_That;
    };
};
int main() {
    std::pmr::unsynchronized_pool_resource ms1; // Non-thread-safe pool allocator
    std::pmr::synchronized_pool_resource ms2;   // Synchronized pool allocator
    CustomMemoryResource custom_memory_source;  // Custom allocator
    char buffer[20];
    std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource mbr(std::data(buffer), std::size(buffer), &custom_memory_source);   // Monotonic buffer allocator, allocates memory from the buffer. Memory is released only when mbr.release() is called. If the buffer is exceeded, the upper-level allocator is used for allocation.
    {
        std::pmr::vector<std::pmr::string> vec{ &mbr };
        vec.push_back("Hello World");
        vec.push_back("One Two Three");
    }   // vec's memory is not released
    mbr.release();  // Memory in mbr is released at this point
}

From the above code, it can be seen that MemoryResource perfectly solves the problems of allocator. We only need to use containers from the namespace std::pmr.

How does it do this?

Taking std::pmr::vector as an example, find its definition:

namespace pmr {
    template <class _Ty>
    using vector = std::vector<_Ty, polymorphic_allocator<_Ty>>;
} // namespace pmr

It is very simple; it is just a std::vector using polymorphic_allocator. Finding its definition, you can see the following code:

template <class _Ty>
class polymorphic_allocator {
public:
    //...
    _NODISCARD __declspec(allocator) _Ty* allocate(_CRT_GUARDOVERFLOW const size_t _Count) {
        // Get space for _Count objects of type _Ty from _Resource
        void* const _Vp = _Resource->allocate(_Get_size_of_n<sizeof(_Ty)>(_Count), alignof(_Ty));
        return static_cast<_Ty*>(_Vp);
    }

    void deallocate(_Ty* const _Ptr, const size_t _Count) noexcept /* strengthened */ {
        // Return space for _Count objects of type _Ty to _Resource
        // No need to verify that size_t can represent the size of _Ty[_Count].
        _Resource->deallocate(_Ptr, _Count * sizeof(_Ty), alignof(_Ty));

private:
    memory_resource* _Resource = _STD pmr::get_default_resource();    
};

It is not difficult to find that it actually just calls the methods of memory_resource on the original Allocator interface.

docs.title: GUI
docs.text:
A Graphical User Interface (GUI), also known as a graphical user interface, refers to a computer operating user interface displayed in a graphical manner.

A graphical user interface is an interface display format for communication between humans and computers, allowing users to use input devices such as a mouse to manipulate icons or menu options on the screen to select commands, call files, launch programs, or perform other daily tasks. Compared with character interfaces that complete routine tasks by entering text or character commands via the keyboard, graphical user interfaces have many advantages. A graphical user interface consists of windows, drop-down menus, dialog boxes, and their corresponding control mechanisms, which are standardized in various new applications—meaning the same operation is always completed in the same way. In a graphical user interface, what users see and operate are all graphical objects, applying computer graphics technology.

——《Baidu Encyclopedia》

If you're tired of the days of battling with the console, this article might help.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
GUI is mainly divided into two categories:

  • Native UI: Traditional native app development mode, using interface on the system platform for development
  • Web UI: Website applications that run specifically in browsers

Here's a more detailed introduction:

  • Zhihu: What are Native, Web App, and Hybrid?

Hybrid refers to mixed development using Native UI and Web UI

For debates about them, you can check:

  • Zhihu: Web App vs. Native App—Which is the Trend?

Web UI dominates the internet market due to low cost and fast development, while the reasons for using Native UI are nothing more than high performance, customization, and hardware interaction.

Although Web GPU has now become stable, offering more room for improvement for Web programmers, for students in graphics and engine fields, the author recommends taking the Native direction as it provides more controllable space.

Native UI solutions, categorized by language, mainly include:

C/C++: Qt, WxWidget, GTK, FLTK, DearImGUI, Nuklear, duilib, C++ Builder, MFC, EasyX

Python: PyQt, WxPython, PyGTK, PyFLTK, DearPyGUI, Tkinter, PyGame

C#: WPF, WinForm

Java: Swing, JavaFx

Among the above frameworks, using C/C++ has natural advantages. Of course, if you're a Python or C# developer without mandatory work requirements, there's no need to go to great lengths to learn C++ just for GUI.

  • Zhihu: Which Language is Most Suitable for GUI?

How to choose among these C++ GUI frameworks?

The author has learned them in the following order: EasyX - Tkinter - PyGame - JavaFx - FLTK - Qt - ImGUI - UE Slate

After using them all, the author found that GUI is essentially about:

  • Handling system (keyboard and mouse) interaction events
  • Filling pixels on the screen to draw a few graphics

This is the minimum functionality provided by the operating system or each GUI framework. Imagine having these two functions—binding a callback function to keyboard and mouse operations, and using loops to fill RGB values in screen pixels—what kind of cool graphical interface can't be created? For example, a program like this:

#include <conio.h>        // Console IO
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    char currentChar = '\0';
    const int width = 20;
    const int height = 20;
    while (true) {
        if (kbhit()) {             // kbhit can determine if there is a key input currently
            currentChar = getch(); // getch is a non-echo input function; unlike getchar, the input key will not be displayed on the console
        }
        system("cls");             // Clear console screen
        std::cout << "Please enter key:" << std::endl;
        for (int y = 0; y < height; y++) {
            for (int x = 0; x < width; x++) {
                std::cout << currentChar;
            }
            std::cout << std::endl;
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

The console program will flicker frantically during operation; this issue will be resolved below.

Compared to the above console program, GUI essentially encapsulates keyboard and mouse input into an interface, where width and height are the window dimensions, and colors are filled in pixels at corresponding coordinates.

The key factor in choosing a framework is its ecosystem, specifically reflected in:

  • More users and teammates, making recruitment easier
  • Wide framework coverage, rich tool libraries, and complete documentation
  • Long-term official maintenance, high iteration frequency, and fewer bugs

Among the above frameworks, the best one without a doubt is Qt.

Most modules in Qt follow the LGPL license, which allows us to use modules in the form of dynamic linking and release commercial software. For the open-source license of each module, please refer to:

  • https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/licenses-used-in-qt.html

If you want to modify Qt source code or use some commercial modules, you need to purchase a commercial license for Qt. For details, please refer to:

  • https://www.qt.io/licensing/open-source-lgpl-obligations

Due to Qt's strict open-source license, independence from C++ standards, and large size, many teams may still choose frameworks like WxWidget, C++ Builder, duilib, or GTK. While MFC, FLTK, and EasyX may be good GUI frameworks, their development ecosystems are not optimistic. If you have a choice, the author recommends not using them.

Dear ImGUI and Nuklear are lightweight, portable GUI toolkits following the Immediate Mode. Essentially, they provide some control interfaces for developers to complete the drawing of a frame of graphics. Taking ImGUI as an example, using the following code:

ImGui::Text("Hello Dear ImGUI");
static bool CheckState;
ImGui::Checkbox("CheckBox ", &CheckState);

Can generate such an interface:

Immediate Mode is mainly reflected in passing the pointer of the variable CheckState into the "control", while in traditional Retained Mode, such as in Qt, the code might look like this:

static bool CheckState;
QCheckBox* CheckBox = new QCheckBox;
CheckBox->setCheckState(CheckState ? Qt::Checked : Qt::Unchecked);        // Initialization
QObject::connect(CheckBox, &QCheckBox::stateChanged, [&](int state) {     // Bind signal-slot
    CheckState = (state == Qt::Checked);
});

It can be seen that QCheckBox does not use the pointer of CheckState; instead, it sets the initial state of the control through CheckState. When the control's stateChanged event occurs, it then sets the value of CheckState. That is, the control itself holds its own State, while Immediate Mode emphasizes statelessness by embedding the state into the control.

During development, storing too many local states requires writing a lot of code to keep them synchronized, which may accidentally introduce bugs—for example, easily causing certain events to execute multiple times or even enter an infinite loop.

For example, adjusting a color:

Using a color palette, dragging or entering channel values, hexadecimal input, screen color picking, etc., can all adjust the same color value. If using Retained Mode, after modifying the color through one method, other controls must be manually adjusted to ensure color synchronization. Although following some design patterns can solve this problem, Immediate Mode has natural advantages in such application scenarios. For debates about their differences, please refer to:

  • Zhihu: What are the Connections and Differences Between Retained and IMGUI?

Does this mean Dear ImGUI is better than Qt? Not necessarily. The author's views are as follows:

  • Immediate Mode is more suitable for game engines, but Dear ImGUI is still insufficient. It is just a small GUI toolkit. Although it is indeed easy to get started and can produce good interface effects, the development of large-scale software systems is an engineering art. A lower threshold will bring more problems. Unless there are enough people and energy for continuous iteration, developing with native Dear ImGUI is simply a disaster...

Here's an answer that, although not about Dear ImGUI, well exposes the problems of such frameworks: https://www.zhihu.com/question/66934513/answer/248036488

  • Retained Mode is just a way of control architecture; Qt != Retained Mode. Although the official controls of most Native UI frameworks use Retained Mode, you can also use Immediate Mode on these frameworks if you want.

Why Qt and not IMGUI?

Does this mean Qt is better? Not necessarily. Using Qt means introducing its entire Core and Widget modules along with moc, and since we cannot modify its source code due to open-source licensing, it is mostly used as an editor in game engines, such as:

  • O3DE: https://github.com/o3de/o3de

Currently, it is not suitable for in-game UI solutions:

  • Yunfeng's BLOG—Choice of Game UI Modules: https://blog.codingnow.com/2020/07/game_ui.html

Slate in UE is an excellent underlying UI framework:

  • https://docs.unrealengine.com/5.1/en-US/understanding-the-slate-ui-architecture-in-unreal-engine/

However, in the subsequent graphics-related tutorials of this series, Qt will be used as the main editor with ImGUI embedded for scene editing, mainly for the following reasons:

  • Qt has cross-platform Window encapsulation, allowing access to Handles for special processing using Native APIs
  • Qt has an elegant reflection system, facilitating editor construction. Using Signal-Slot can well decouple logic and improve readability
  • Qt has an independent container library, allowing us to avoid the torture of STL
  • Qt has many extended libraries with unified interface styles, such as basic math libraries, image codec libraries, and multimedia libraries, which can make learning outcomes more easily applicable
  • Qt 6.0 and later introduced RHI (Render Hardware Interface) supporting OpenGL, DX11, Vulkan, and Metal. It is much easier to use than OpenGL, and its architecture uses Vulkan-style glsl and modern graphics APIs without modification like bgfx. Most importantly, using Qt's RHI can well compatible with Native APIs, facilitating the use of advanced features provided by graphics APIs or hardware

Many architectural structures in Qt can be mapped to Unreal Engine. If your goal is Unreal Engine, Qt is definitely the best springboard because Qt's official code is highly readable and has a large number of documents, demos, and tutorials.

docs.title: Platform Basics
docs.text:
A GUI program will be displayed on the screen. To systematically manage the pixels on the screen, the operating system provides a structure called Window. On Windows 10, a standard Window is as follows, with a title bar (icon, title text, minimize button, maximize button, close button):

You can create a Window in the following way:

  • Create a new CMakeLists.txt and main.cpp file

  • Fill CMakeLists.txt with:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.12)
project(Window)
add_executable(Window WIN32 main.cpp)

Win32 indicates that the executable is a Win32 window, corresponding to Project Settings - Linker - System - Subsystem - Windows in Visual Studio

  • Fill main.cpp with:
#ifndef UNICODE
#define UNICODE
#endif 

#include <windows.h>

LRESULT CALLBACK WindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT uMsg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam);

int WINAPI wWinMain(HINSTANCE hInstance, HINSTANCE hPrevInstance, PWSTR pCmdLine, int nCmdShow)
{
    // Register the window class.
    const wchar_t CLASS_NAME[]  = L"Sample Window Class";

    WNDCLASS wc = { };

    wc.lpfnWndProc   = WindowProc;
    wc.hInstance     = hInstance;
    wc.lpszClassName = CLASS_NAME;

    RegisterClass(&wc);

    // Create the window.

    HWND hwnd = CreateWindowEx(
        0,                              // Optional window styles.
        CLASS_NAME,                     // Window class
        L"Learn to Program Windows",    // Window text
        WS_OVERLAPPEDWINDOW,            // Window style

        // Size and position
        CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT, CW_USEDEFAULT,

        NULL,       // Parent window    
        NULL,       // Menu
        hInstance,  // Instance handle
        NULL        // Additional application data
        );

    if (hwnd == NULL)
    {
        return 0;
    }

    ShowWindow(hwnd, nCmdShow);

    // Run the message loop.

    MSG msg = { };
    while (GetMessage(&msg, NULL, 0, 0) > 0)
    {
        TranslateMessage(&msg);
        DispatchMessage(&msg);
    }

    return 0;
}

LRESULT CALLBACK WindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT uMsg, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam)
{
    switch (uMsg)
    {
    case WM_DESTROY:
        PostQuitMessage(0);
        return 0;

    case WM_PAINT:
        {
            PAINTSTRUCT ps;
            HDC hdc = BeginPaint(hwnd, &ps);

            // All painting occurs here, between BeginPaint and EndPaint.

            FillRect(hdc, &ps.rcPaint, (HBRUSH) (COLOR_WINDOW+1));

            EndPaint(hwnd, &ps);
        }
        return 0;

    }
    return DefWindowProc(hwnd, uMsg, wParam, lParam);
}
  • Use CMake command line or CMake GUI to generate Visual Studio project files. In the Solution Explorer, right-click the Window project - Set as StartUp Project, and execute to see:

The above code comes from Microsoft's official tutorial. Interested readers can go through it themselves:

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/learnwin32/your-first-windows-program

docs.title: Spy++
docs.text:
After seeing this, do you think a Window is a box with maximize, minimize, and close buttons?

Not exactly. In Visual Studio, you can find Spy++: Menu Bar—Tools—Spy++

Using it, you can view all Windows in the system:

Spy++ displays all windows hierarchically from bottom to top, meaning everything you see on the monitor can be traced—for example, the bottom layer is the desktop (wallpaper).

Using its window search tool (Menu Bar—Search—Find Window—Drag the crosshair below to any window), you can locate the specific Item in Spy++, which is somewhat similar to the widget reflector in UE.

Through the above tool, you can find that windows are hierarchical and may not have a close button or even a border.

On Windows, the border and title bar are controlled by the system and do not belong to the program itself. We call this the Non-Client Area.

The area inside the border can be freely drawn by the program, which is called the Client Area.

  • What is windows client and non-client area?

Microsoft may have realized that its title bar limits UI beautification, so windows also support setting borderless and transparent background properties. Many software use this method to draw shaped windows, such as QQ Music's player:

System interaction events are passed to the currently Activated window, while windows in the Unactivated state are generally displayed in gray by the system:

Generally, there will only be one activated window, which means only one window can receive input events from the computer at present. However, some methods can break this rule, such as hooks.

docs.title: Multiple Buffering
docs.text:
In the previous console program, the page flickers frantically because we are adding things to a buffer little by little, and the console window is previewing this process. Due to the fast refresh speed, flickering occurs. To solve this type of problem, the concept of Multiple Buffering was proposed in computer science:

  • The buffer used for console preview is called the front buffer. The core of multiple buffering is that we do not directly operate the front buffer; instead, after processing the back buffer, we submit it uniformly to the front buffer. This can effectively avoid flickering and tearing.

When mentioning uniform submission, do you think of for copy and memcpy from the previous section?

To put all oranges from one basket to another, is it faster to put them one by one or lift the basket and pour them directly? Obviously the latter.

Hardware and interface providers clearly understand this principle. In most cases, they support operations like Map and Blit.

An example of using double buffering in the console is as follows:

#include <conio.h>        // Console IO
#include <iostream>
#include <Windows.h>

const int width = 20;
const int height = 20;
const int MaxBufferSize = width * height * 10;

void UseSingleBuffer() {
    char currentChar = '*';
    while (true) {
        if (kbhit()) {             // kbhit can determine if there is a key input currently
            currentChar = getch(); // getch is a non-echo input function; unlike getchar, the input key will not be displayed on the console
        }
        system("cls");             // Clear console screen
        for (int y = 0; y < height; y++) {
            for (int x = 0; x < width; x++) {
                std::cout << currentChar;
            }
            std::cout << std::endl;
        }
    }
}

void UseDoubleBuffer() {
    HANDLE frontendBuffer = GetStdHandle(STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE);     // Get the default buffer

    HANDLE backendBuffer = CreateConsoleScreenBuffer(            // Create a new buffer as the back buffer
        GENERIC_READ | GENERIC_WRITE,
        FILE_SHARE_READ | FILE_SHARE_WRITE,
        NULL,
        CONSOLE_TEXTMODE_BUFFER,
        NULL
    );

    // Hide the cursors of both buffers
    CONSOLE_CURSOR_INFO cci;
    cci.bVisible = FALSE;
    cci.dwSize = 1;
    SetConsoleCursorInfo(frontendBuffer, &cci);
    SetConsoleCursorInfo(backendBuffer, &cci);


    char bufferData[MaxBufferSize];     // Buffer data temporary storage area
    DWORD bufferLength = 0;
    COORD zeroCoord = { 0, 0 };
    char currentChar = '*';

    while (true) {
        if (kbhit()) {
            currentChar = getch();
        }
        bufferLength = 0;

        CONSOLE_SCREEN_BUFFER_INFO backendBufferInfo;          // Get the number of characters per line in backendBuffer
        GetConsoleScreenBufferInfo(backendBuffer, &backendBufferInfo);
        int lineWidth = backendBufferInfo.srWindow.Right - backendBufferInfo.srWindow.Left + 1;

        for (int y = 0; y < height; y++) {
            for (int x = 0; x < width; x++) {
                bufferData[bufferLength++] = currentChar;
            }
            while (bufferLength % lineWidth != 0) {             // Fill characters to achieve line break effect
                bufferData[bufferLength++] = ' ';
            }
        }

        // Write bufferData of length bufferLength starting from zeroCoord in backendBuffer
        WriteConsoleOutputCharacterA(backendBuffer, bufferData, bufferLength, zeroCoord, &bufferLength);
        SetConsoleActiveScreenBuffer(backendBuffer);            // Display backendBuffer
        std::swap(backendBuffer, frontendBuffer);               // Swap front and back buffer operation handles; frontendBuffer will be the backendBuffer for the next loop
    }
}

int main() {
    // UseSingleBuffer();
    UseDoubleBuffer();
    return 0;
}

Most GUI frameworks use double buffering, while games even use triple buffering. Generally, we call this structure a swap chain.

For details about multiple buffering, you can refer to:

  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_buffering

docs.title: DPI
docs.text:
The number of pixels per inch length of an image.

DPI (Dots Per Inch) is a unit of measurement used for dot-matrix digital images, referring to the number of sampling, displayable, or output points per inch length.

On Windows, the system DPI is adjusted by setting Scale and Layout.

The operating system will adjust the window size and content according to a certain configurable mechanism based on DPI changes. For details about DPI awareness, please refer to:

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/zh-cn/windows/win32/hidpi/high-dpi-desktop-application-development-on-windows
  • https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/highdpi.html
  • https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dots_per_inch

During GUI development, supporting multi-DPI preview has always been a headache because it is difficult to adjust the effect and layout of the entire interface through a few parameters.

A major pitfall in graphics development is:

  • Window Size != Buffer Size. Many friends create Frame Buffers using Window Size, which works normally on computers with 100% scaling but has problems in other cases.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
https://courses.qt.io/how-to-install-qt/index.html#/lessons/WDj_gIccDJa6gmhH_-3P7uC2QDaZHbYA

If you want to continue learning the subsequent graphics chapters, please select Custom installation during installation and ensure the following modules are installed:

  • Any version above Qt 6, preferably the latest (e.g., 6.5.2 beta), including:
  • MSVC 2019 64-bit: Supports Qt development using Visual Studio
  • Sources: Qt source code
  • Qt 5 Compatibility Module: Coexistence module for Qt 5
  • Qt Shader Tools: Qt's shader tool for converting glsl to hlsl, msl
  • Qt Debug Information Files: Optional, large size, used for debugging Qt source code
  • Developers and Designer Tools
  • Debugging Tools For Windows: Windows debugging tools
  • CMake: Build tool; no need to install if already present
  • Qt Installer Framework: Optional, used to package Qt programs into installation packages

In addition, the author also recommends not using Designer (*.ui) and Design Studio in the early stages of learning, as they will be the biggest resistance to your early improvement.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
• Create a new CMakeLists.txt and main.cpp file

  • Fill CMakeLists.txt with:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.12)
project(QtExample)

add_executable(QtExample main.cpp)

find_package(Qt6 COMPONENTS Core Widgets REQUIRED)      # Find Qt6 modules

target_link_libraries(QtExample                         # Link Core and Widget to QtExample
    PRIVATE 
        Qt6::Core                     
        Qt6::Widgets
)
  • Fill main.cpp with:
#include <QApplication>
#include <QWindow>

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    QApplication a(argc, argv);
    QWindow window;
    window.setTitle("Hello Qt!");
    window.show();
    return a.exec();
}

  • Use Cmake command line or CMake GUI to generate a Visual Studio project

  • Select QtExample as the startup project, compile and run to see:

QApplication is Qt's scheduling and control center for the entire program. Through it, you can:

  • Parse program input parameters (i.e., argument count and argument value above)
  • Manage event communication between objects
  • Handle the program's event loop
  • Access all Windows and Widgets
  • Provide various operations related to program processes
  • ...

Corresponds to GenericApplication and SlateApplication in UE

You can operate it anywhere in the program through QApplication::instance() or the macro qApp. Check the official documentation to know what it can do:

  • https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qapplication.html

QApplication inherits from QGuiApplication and comes from the Widgets module. If you need a console program instead of a window, using QCoreApplication from the Core module is sufficient.

In actual application development, you can derive QApplication and add some global management operations to it.

QApplication::exec() will start Qt's event loop, which is equivalent to:

#include <QApplication>
#include <QWindow>

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    QApplication a(argc, argv);
    Q_ASSERT(QApplication::instance() == &a);

    QWindow window;
    window.setTitle("Hello Qt!");
    window.show();
    while (true) {                        // QApplication has an internal exit signal, but it is private, so it can only be a dead loop here
        QApplication::processEvents();    // Comment it out, and you will find the window can no longer respond to interaction events
    }
}

During development, you may often perform some slow operations that cause the interface to freeze. At this time, you can manually call QApplication::processEvents() in the middle of these operations to allow the interface to refresh.

docs.title: Object
docs.text:
Most classes in Qt are derived from QObject, which facilitates managing all its child objects and provides mechanisms such as reflection, Signal-Slot, garbage collection, and events. An example of a QObject subclass definition is as follows:

class QExmapleClass : public QObject {
    Q_OBJECT            // Q_OBJECT is the entry point for Qt reflection data; it can be omitted if reflection functionality is not needed
};

docs.title: Meta Object System
docs.text:
Qt's meta-object system provides mechanisms such as Signal-Slot, runtime type information, and dynamic property systems.

To enable the reflection function of QObject in a project using CMake as the build system, you need to enable AUTOMOC before add_executable in CMakeLists.txt:

set(CMAKE_AUTOMOC ON)

AUTOMOC will automatically detect whether macros like Q_OBJECT exist in the header file. If they exist, Qt's reflection compiler moc will scan the file, and after scanning, a *.moc file will be generated, which contains the definition of Qt reflection data.

You can find Qt's moc in a path similar to the following. Open cmd in the current directory and execute moc -h to see its help documentation.

The source code of moc is located in the following path:

UE's reflection compiler is UHT (Unreal Header Tool)

For Q_OBJECT written in *.cpp, you need to manually include *.moc at the end to trigger the execution of moc. For example:

/* main.cpp
*/

#include <QApplication>
#include <QMetaType>
#include <QMetaProperty>

class QExmapleClass : public QObject {
    Q_OBJECT
    Q_PROPERTY(int Var READ getVar WRITE setVar)                // Declare MetaProperty through Getter and Setter
public:
    int getVar() {
        return mVar;
    }
    void setVar(int inVar) {
        mVar = inVar;
    }

    Q_INVOKABLE void sayHello(const QString& inName) {         // Declare MetaMethod
        qDebug() << "Hello " << inName.toLatin1().data();
    }

    enum Number {
        Zero, One, Two, Three
    };
    Q_ENUM(Number)                                             // Declare MetaEnum
protected:
    int mVar= 5;
};

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    QApplication a(argc, argv);

    QExmapleClass obj;

    // Get MetaObject
    const QMetaObject* metaObjectFromStatic = &QExmapleClass::staticMetaObject;
    const QMetaObject* metaObjectFromVirtual = obj.metaObject();

    // Read and write properties
    obj.setProperty("Var", QVariant::fromValue<int>(10));
    QVariant var = obj.property("Var");
    qDebug() << "Property : " << var.value<int>();

    // Call function
    qDebug() << "Invoke Method Begin:";
    metaObjectFromStatic->invokeMethod(&obj, "sayHello", Q_ARG(QString, "Boy"));
    qDebug() << "Invoke Method End";

    // MetaType operation
    QMetaType metaType = var.metaType();
    qDebug() << "Meta Type : " << metaType.name() << " ID: " << metaType.id();

    // Traverse and read/write properties in MetaObject, and print property types
    for (int i = metaObjectFromStatic->propertyOffset(); i < metaObjectFromStatic->propertyCount(); i++) {
        const QMetaProperty& metaProperty = metaObjectFromStatic->property(i);
        metaProperty.write(&obj, QVariant::fromValue<int>(15));
        QVariant varFromMetaObject = metaProperty.read(&obj);
        qDebug() << "Meta Property : " << metaProperty.name() << varFromMetaObject;
    }

    // Traverse functions in MetaObject and print parameter information
    for (int i = metaObjectFromStatic->methodOffset(); i < metaObjectFromStatic->methodCount(); i++) {
        const QMetaMethod& metaMethod = metaObjectFromStatic->method(i);
        QByteArrayList paramNames = metaMethod.parameterNames();
        QStringList paramsDefineList;
        for (int j = 0; j < metaMethod.parameterCount(); j++) {
            paramsDefineList << metaMethod.parameterTypeName(j) + " " + paramNames[j];
        }
        qDebug() << QString("Meta Method : %1 %2(%3)")
            .arg(metaMethod.typeName())
            .arg(metaMethod.name())
            .arg(paramsDefineList.join(',')).toLatin1().data();
    }

    // Traverse enums in MetaObject and print enum information
    for (int i = metaObjectFromStatic->enumeratorOffset(); i < metaObjectFromStatic->enumeratorCount(); i++) {
        const QMetaEnum& metaEnum = metaObjectFromStatic->enumerator(i);
        qDebug() << "Meta Enum : " << metaEnum.name();
        for (int j = 0; j < metaEnum.keyCount(); j++) {
            qDebug() << "-- " << metaEnum.key(j) << " : " << metaEnum.value(j);
        }
    }
    return a.exec();
}

#include "main.moc"        // Must include main.moc to trigger moc compilation

The above code is a good example of Qt reflection. For more detailed content, please refer to:

  • Qt Meta Object System: https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/metaobjects.html
  • QMetaObject: https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qmetaobject.html
  • Qt Property System: https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/properties.html

docs.title: Signal-Slot
docs.text:
The signal-slot mechanism is used for communication between objects and is a core feature of Qt. A pseudocode example of its function is as follows:

class Student{
    Signal nameChanged(string OldName, string NewName);
public:
    void setName(string inName){
        nameChanged.Emit(mName, inName);
        mName = inName;
    }
private:
    string mName;
};

class Teacher{
public:
    void OnStudentNameChanged(string OldName, string NewName){
        // do something
    }
};

class Class{
protected:
    void connectEveryone(){
         for(auto Student:mStudents){
             Student.nameChanged.Connect(mTeacher, &Teacher::OnStudentNameChanged);
         }
    }
private:
    Teacher mTeacher;
    TArray<Student> mStudents;
};

Through the connectEveryone function, it can be seen as: "The teacher tells the students in the class that if they change their names, please notify me."

There is no direct modification to the structures of Teacher and Student; instead, the relationship between the two is bound in a third-party collection (the class), thus achieving good decoupling.

This mechanism corresponds to delegates in UE, which are more detailed than Qt's signal-slot. However, the translation has some flaws. If it were also called Signal, it would be easier to evoke developers' associations and adopt the correct usage.

For more detailed explanations, please refer to:

  • https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/signalsandslots.html

docs.title: Event System
docs.text:
In Qt, an event refers to an instance object of a subclass of the abstract class QEvent, which is used to describe the result of internal or external activities of the application. In function, it can be regarded as a heavyweight Single-Slot. The interaction mechanism in QWidget is implemented through events.

When an event occurs, Qt represents it by constructing an appropriate QEvent subclass instance and calls:

  • static bool QCoreApplication::sendEvent(QObject* receiver, QEvent event)

To send the event to the corresponding QObject, and QObject has a virtual function:

  • virtual bool QObject::event( QEvent* e )

By overriding event, you can handle events or further distribute them to other functions.

In addition, Qt also supports an event listener mechanism. You can override QObject's virtual function:

  • bool QObject:: eventFilter ( QObject * watched , QEvent* event )

To make it a filterObj, then call:

  • void QObject:: installEventFilter ( QObject* filterObj )

Thus allowing this object to act as an event listener for other objects.

For details about the event system, please refer to:

  • https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/eventsandfilters.html

docs.title: Garbage Collection
docs.text:
As mentioned in the previous section on memory management, Qt's GC is very simple: a QObject can specify a unique parent, and when the parent is released, the children will also be released. In addition, you can use QObject::deleteLater to delay the release of a QObject.

In QWidget, adding child controls will implicitly set the parent. In most cases, there is no need to manually delete them, but you need to pay attention to controlling the parent's lifecycle. If a node in the object tree has a flaw, the entire subtree of objects cannot be released.

docs.title: Window
docs.text:
Earlier, we used the Win API to simply create a window. That code is not at all "modern"—a large number of macros and strange naming conventions.

QPlatformWindow is the underlying cross-platform Window encapsulation detail of Qt. Qt wraps it to provide an interface, which is QWindow.

This corresponds to GenericWindow and SWindow in UE.

I definitely don't believe there's no "affair" between them 0.0

In the client area of a Window, there are often many small widgets, such as the following window:

It has many buttons and controls. If we simply use a window's click event (which can get the mouse coordinates) to determine which part of the window was clicked and then handle the drawing little by little, when the window's complexity increases, the entire code will become extremely chaotic and difficult to manage. Although Windows provides a SubWindow mechanism, due to the high cost of maintaining a Window, many frameworks have proposed the concept of Widget.

Corresponds to QWidget in Qt and SWidget in UE.

A Widget can be regarded as a lightweight Window, with the following characteristics:

  • In display, a Widget can be regarded as a block, which essentially divides the client area of the Window. This area is drawn by the Widget itself.
  • In logic, Widgets have a tree-like hierarchy, and events are often passed from top to bottom.

docs.title: Widget
docs.text:
QWidget is the core of Qt GUI. Most visual widgets in Qt are derived from it.

It is also very simple to create:

#include <QApplication>
#include <QWidget>

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    QApplication a(argc, argv);
    QWidget widget;
    widget.setWindowTitle("Hello QWidget!");
    widget.show();
    return a.exec();
}

In the development of a single widget, it mainly involves setting the Properties of QWidget:

And overriding Events:

To achieve various complex interface effects and interaction logic.

docs.title: WindowOption
docs.text:
In general, developers may not even come into contact with QWindow because the outermost (or top-level) QWidget will automatically generate a QWindow. We can make some settings on this QWidget to affect the generation of the Window:

  • WindowFlag: Adjust the Window's flags, such as pop-up windows, dialog boxes, tooltips, borderless...

  • WindowModality: Set a modal window. A modal window will block input to other windows, generally used to force the user to select certain options before continuing execution.

  • WindowState: The states of a Window include: default, minimized, maximized, fullscreen (borderless), activated. You can call setWindowState, and Qt also provides some convenient APIs, such as activateWindow().

For example, code like this:

QWidget widget;
widget.setWindowFlags(Qt::FramelessWindowHint|Qt::Tool);
widget.resize(200,200);
widget.show();

You can see a 200*200 gray square on the screen, and its icon is also hidden in the taskbar below.

It should be noted that a Window is not created when creating a Widget. Most of the time, our settings for the Widget are just adjusting its parameter state machine. Only when the event is executed will the actual operation be performed according to these states. For example, you can only get the Window's handle after calling show.

docs.title: Attribute
docs.text:
In the Qt namespace, there is a set of enumeration values starting with WA_ that can be used to set WidgetAttribute. You can set many useful properties for QWidget, among which the commonly used ones are:

  • Qt::WA_DeleteOnClose: Destroy the object when the window is closed
  • Qt::WA_TranslucentBackground: Make the window's background transparent

docs.title: Event
docs.text:
The display of a GUI lies in QWidget's paintEvent. We can override it and use QPainter to draw any graphics we want.

The essence of GUI is nothing more than using various interaction events to adjust the property state machine and switch the drawing results of paintEvent.

This is a good example:

#include <QApplication>
#include <QWidget>
#include <QMouseEvent>
#include <QPainter>

class QExmapleWidget:public QWidget {
    Q_OBJECT
private:
    QPoint mMousePressPos;
    bool bIsHovered = false;
protected:
    void mousePressEvent(QMouseEvent* event) override {
        if (event->button() == Qt::LeftButton)        // Record the position when the left mouse button is pressed
            mMousePressPos = event->pos();
    }
    void mouseMoveEvent(QMouseEvent* event) override {
        if (event->buttons() & Qt::LeftButton)        // Adjust the Widget's position when dragging with the left mouse button pressed
            move(event->pos() + this->pos() - mMousePressPos);
    }

    void enterEvent(QEnterEvent* event) override {
        bIsHovered = true;                             // Mouse enters the Widget
        setCursor(Qt::ClosedHandCursor);               // Set the shape of the mouse cursor
        update();                                      // Request to refresh the interface
    }

    void leaveEvent(QEvent* event) override {
        bIsHovered = false;                            // Mouse leaves the Widget
        setCursor(Qt::ArrowCursor);                    // Set the shape of the mouse cursor
        update();                                      // Request to refresh the interface
    }

    void paintEvent(QPaintEvent* event) override {
        QPainter painter(this);

        painter.fillRect(this->rect(), bIsHovered ? Qt::green : QColor(0, 100, 200));    // Fill color in the area

        painter.setPen(QPen(Qt::white));
        painter.setFont(QFont("", 20, 90));                                             // Use the default font and set the font size and weight
        painter.drawText(this->rect(), Qt::AlignCenter, "Hello Qt");                    // Draw text
    }
};

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    QApplication a(argc, argv);
    QExmapleWidget widget;
    widget.setWindowFlags(Qt::FramelessWindowHint);         // Borderless
    widget.setAttribute(Qt::WA_TranslucentBackground);      // Transparent background
    widget.setAttribute(Qt::WA_AlwaysStackOnTop);           // Stay on top
    widget.resize(200, 200);
    widget.show();
    return a.exec();
}

#include "main.moc"

Running it, you can see the following effect:

Using QWidget, you can achieve any effect we want.

Qt officially provides many basic controls for developers to use:

  • https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/widget-classes.html

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
In a program, there is often more than one QWidget, so we also need to organize the layout of these Widgets. The commonly used layout in Qt is BoxLayout. Here is a simple example:

#include <QApplication>
#include <QWidget>
#include <QHBoxLayout>
#include <QPushButton>

class QMainWidget :public QWidget {
    Q_OBJECT
public:
    QMainWidget() {
        createUI();
    }
private:
    void createUI() {
        QHBoxLayout* hLayout = new QHBoxLayout(this);
        // QHBoxLayout* hLayout = new QHBoxLayout();         // Equivalent
        // setLayout(hLayout);

        hLayout->setContentsMargins(5, 5, 5, 5);             // Set margins
        hLayout->setSpacing(10);                              // Set spacing between internal elements
        hLayout->setAlignment(Qt::AlignLeft|Qt::AlignVCenter);    // Set left alignment and vertical center
        hLayout->addWidget(new QPushButton("A"));
        hLayout->addSpacing(20);                              // Add blank filling
        hLayout->addWidget(new QPushButton("B"));
        hLayout->addWidget(new QPushButton("C"));
    }
};

int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
    QApplication a(argc, argv);
    QMainWidget widget;
    widget.resize(300, 300);
    widget.show();
    return a.exec();
}

#include "main.moc"

For a complete introduction to layouts, please refer to:

  • https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/layout.html

For:

  • The outermost Widget
  • Widgets without a layout but with a hierarchical relationship

You can adjust the following properties through coordinates relative to the top-left corner of the parent:

  • pos: https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qwidget.html#pos-prop
  • geometry: https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qwidget.html#geometry-prop

For Widgets at the same level, you can call the following interfaces to adjust the Z Order:

  • raise(): Bring to front
  • lower(): Send to back

docs.title: Graphics API Overview
docs.text:
Before starting to learn, you need to clearly recognize that C/C++ is just a tool for materializing practical theories in computers, and you must be proficient in using it. Otherwise, you should continue to study in depth. The author believes that without building a complete basic knowledge system and good code literacy, you are not capable or even qualified to further your learning.

Defining this is quite difficult. You can think of it like playing Spider Solitaire. It's best to ask for a new deal only when you feel there's no way out, because entering a new field will provide some entry points but also face greater challenges, or even lead you into a dead end.

In addition, you need to consider whether it is necessary to learn it. If your future career direction is:

  • Game engines, graphics
  • VR, AR, XR
  • 3D industrial software
