docs.title: Code Reference
docs.text:
UE provides a Widget Reflector that can quickly locate the creation code of the corresponding UI. Its launch point is located in the editor's main panel: Top Menu Bar - Tools - Debug - Widget Reflector:

In addition, the official engine source code also provides a SlateViewer project that demonstrates the basic use of most Slate widgets:

With the help of the IDE's code search tool, you can find parameter examples of corresponding widgets in the engine. In Visual Studio, you can also view the class inheritance relationship in the Solution Explorer to overview all widgets:

docs.title: Advanced Customization
docs.text:
The above skills can meet most needs of UI development, but when it comes to some complex interaction mechanisms and rendering logic, you need to customize SLeafWidget.

Here is a good example that implements a draggable and movable widget:

The code is as follows:

#pragma once
#include "Styling/StyleColors.h"
#include "Brushes/SlateColorBrush.h"

class SCustomSlateWidget : public SLeafWidget {
    SLATE_DECLARE_WIDGET(SCustomSlateWidget, SLeafWidget)   // Declare the Slate widget using the macro SLATE_DECLARE_WIDGET
public:
    SLATE_BEGIN_ARGS(SCustomSlateWidget) {}
    SLATE_END_ARGS()
    void Construct(const SCustomSlateWidget::FArguments InArgs) {
        SetCursor(EMouseCursor::GrabHand);                  // Set the mouse style when entering the widget area
    }
protected:
    FReply OnMouseButtonDown(const FGeometry& MyGeometry, const FPointerEvent& MouseEvent) override {
        if (MouseEvent.IsMouseButtonDown(EKeys::LeftMouseButton)) {
            LastMouseDownPosition = MyGeometry.AbsoluteToLocal(MouseEvent.GetScreenSpacePosition());// Convert the mouse position from screen space to the widget's local space
            return FReply::Handled().CaptureMouse(SharedThis(this));                                // Start high-frequency capture of global mouse movement
        }
        return FReply::Handled();
    }
    FReply OnMouseMove(const FGeometry& MyGeometry, const FPointerEvent& MouseEvent) override {
        if (MouseEvent.IsMouseButtonDown(EKeys::LeftMouseButton)) {
            auto Window = FSlateApplication::Get().FindWidgetWindow(SharedThis(this));                  // Get the window of this widget
            auto CurrentMousePosition = MyGeometry.AbsoluteToLocal(MouseEvent.GetScreenSpacePosition());
            auto CurrWindowPosition = Window->GetPositionInScreen();
            auto TargetPosition = CurrentMousePosition + CurrWindowPosition - LastMouseDownPosition;    // Calculate position movement
            Window->MoveWindowTo(TargetPosition);
        }
        return FReply::Handled();
    }
    FReply OnMouseButtonUp(const FGeometry& MyGeometry, const FPointerEvent& MouseEvent) override {
        LastMouseDownPosition = FVector2D::ZeroVector;
        return FReply::Handled().ReleaseMouseCapture();                                         // Release mouse capture
    }
    int32 OnPaint(const FPaintArgs& Args, const FGeometry& AllottedGeometry, const FSlateRect& MyCullingRect, FSlateWindowElementList& OutDrawElements, int32 LayerId, const FWidgetStyle& InWidgetStyle, bool bParentEnabled) const override {
        static FSlateFontInfo FontInfo = FCoreStyle::GetDefaultFontStyle("Bold", 30);
        static const FSlateBrush* Brush = FAppStyle::GetBrush("WhiteBrush");
        FLinearColor BackgroundColor = IsHovered() ? FLinearColor(0.6f, 0.5f, 0.9f) : FLinearColor(0.1f, 0.5f, 0.9f);
        FSlateDrawElement::MakeBox(OutDrawElements, LayerId, AllottedGeometry.ToPaintGeometry(), Brush, ESlateDrawEffect::None, BackgroundColor);       // Draw background
        FSlateDrawElement::MakeText(OutDrawElements, LayerId, AllottedGeometry.ToPaintGeometry(), FText::FromString("Hello Slate"), FontInfo);          // Draw text
        return LayerId;
    }
    FVector2D ComputeDesiredSize(float LayoutScaleMultiplier) const override {
        return FVector2D::ZeroVector;                                                           // Using zero vector will fill the parent widget's content
    }
private:
    FVector2D LastMouseDownPosition = FVector2D::ZeroVector;
};

// The following code needs to be placed in cpp
SLATE_IMPLEMENT_WIDGET(SCustomSlateWidget)                          // Generate code implementation using the macro SLATE_IMPLEMENT_WIDGET
void SCustomSlateWidget::PrivateRegisterAttributes(FSlateAttributeInitializer& AttributeInitializer)    // This function must be implemented
{
}

FSlateApplication::Get().AddWindow(
    SNew(SWindow)
    .ClientSize(FVector2D(200, 200))                    // Set window size to 200*200
    .SizingRule(ESizingRule::FixedSize)             // Fixed window size
    .SupportsMaximize(false)                        // Disable maximize
    .SupportsMinimize(false)                        // Disable minimize
    .CreateTitleBar(false)                          // Do not create a title bar
    .AutoCenter(EAutoCenter::PreferredWorkArea)     // Display centered
    .IsTopmostWindow(true)                          // Keep on top
    [
        SNew(SCustomSlateWidget)
    ]
);

The workflow for customizing SLeafWidget is:

  • Declare the widget using the macro SLATE_DECLARE_WIDGET(WidgetType, ParentType)
  • Define the code implementation in cpp using the macro SLATE_IMPLEMENT_WIDGET(WidgetType), and implement the function:
  • void WidgetType::PrivateRegisterAttributes(FSlateAttributeInitializer& AttributeInitializer)
  • Override the function for widget size calculation:
  • virtual FVector2D SWidget::ComputeDesiredSize(float LayoutScaleMultiplier) const = 0
  • Override various interaction events.
  • Adjust the widget's attribute state machine
  • Add drawing elements in the drawing function (OnPaint) according to the attribute state machine

docs.title: Interaction Events
docs.text:
SWidget provides a large number of interaction events (virtual functions starting with On) for developers to override:

  • OnFocusReceived: Gain focus
  • OnFocusLost: Lose focus
  • OnFocusChanging: Focus changes
  • OnKeyChar: When keyboard input occurs
  • OnKeyDown: Keyboard key pressed
  • OnKeyUp: Keyboard key released
  • OnMouseButtonDown: Mouse button pressed
  • OnMouseButtonUp: Mouse button released
  • OnMouseMove: Mouse moves
  • OnMouseEnter: The moment the mouse enters the Widget area
  • OnMouseLeave: The moment the mouse leaves the Widget area
  • OnMouseButtonDoubleClick: Mouse double-click
  • OnMouseWheel: Mouse wheel scrolls
  • OnDragEnter: The moment something is dragged into the Widget area
  • OnDragLeave: The moment something is dragged out of the Widget area
  • OnDragOver: When something is dragged over the Widget area
  • OnDrop: Release the dragged item on the Widget
  • ...

For detailed descriptions, see the definition of SWidget, which has explanations and trigger timings for each event. For usage, you can search for corresponding use cases in the UE source code.

Usage instructions:

  • These events are called by FSlateApplication. Their function parameters generally contain all the information carried by the event. We only need to override them and implement our own logic based on the event data.

  • The return type of the event is FReply, which is used to define the subsequent processing of the event. Its constructor is private, so you must use the following static functions to create an instance:

    • FReply::Handled(): Indicates that the event has been processed, and the event will not continue to be passed down.
    • FReply::Unhandled(): Indicates that the widget does not handle the event, and the event will continue to be passed down.

    FReply provides a series of operations for processing after the event ends:

docs.title: Drawing Events
docs.text:
The actual drawing function of SWidget is Paint, but since there are some fixed steps in the drawing process, Slate exposes the drawing event OnPaint for us to customize the drawing logic. Its definition is as follows:

virtual int32 OnPaint(const FPaintArgs& Args, 
                      const FGeometry& AllottedGeometry,
                      const FSlateRect& MyCullingRect, 
                      FSlateWindowElementList& OutDrawElements, 
                      int32 LayerId,
                      const FWidgetStyle& InWidgetStyle,
                      bool bParentEnabled) const = 0;

Parameter description:

  • const FPaintArgs& Args: Parameters of the drawing event, which can get the current time, interval, parent window...
  • const FGeometry& AllottedGeometry: The geometric size allocated to the SWidget (relative to the parent window)
  • const FSlateRect& MyCullingRect: The culling rectangle of the SWidget, which can be used to discard drawing elements during drawing
  • FSlateWindowElementList& OutDrawElements: This is the drawing element list of the entire SWindow. Our drawing is to modify this object.
  • int32 LayerId: The LayerID for drawing, generally used to layer the UI for unified processing of drawing elements at the same level.
  • const FWidgetStyle& InWidgetStyle: The Style passed from the parent window
  • bool bParentEnabled: Whether the parent window is in the enabled state.

In the OnPaint function, we mainly create drawing elements through many static functions named starting with Make in FSlateDrawElement, including:

static void MakeBox( // Draw a box; by setting the Brush, it can be a color block or an image
    FSlateWindowElementList& ElementList,
    uint32 InLayer,
    const FPaintGeometry& PaintGeometry,
    const FSlateBrush* InBrush,
    ESlateDrawEffect InDrawEffects = ESlateDrawEffect::None,
    const FLinearColor& InTint = FLinearColor::White );

static void MakeRotatedBox(...);        // Draw a rotated box
static void MakeGradient(...);          // Draw a gradient box
static void MakeText(...);              // Draw text
static void MakeShapedText(...);        // Draw shaped text
static void MakeLines(...);             // Draw lines
static void MakeSpline(...)             // Draw a curve
static void MakeDrawSpaceSpline(...);    // Draw a curve in the drawing space
static void MakeCubicBezierSpline(...);  // Draw a cubic Bezier curve
static void MakeViewport(...)           // Draw FSlateViewport
static void MakeCustom(...);            // Draw a custom element; you can implement the element's Render function yourself
static void MakeCustomVerts(...);       // Draw according to vertices
static void MakePostProcessPass(...);   // Draw post-processing filters (blur)

These functions are used very frequently in UE, and you can search for related code for reference.

For details: Runtime\SlateCore\Public\Rendering\DrawElements.h

docs.title: FSlateBrush
docs.text:
FSlateBrush is used to control the filling area and is frequently used in the interface. Therefore, Slate also provides some convenient extensions for it:

  • FSlateBorderBrush: Fill border
  • FSlateBoxBrush: Box brush
  • FSlateRoundedBoxBrush: Rounded rectangle brush
  • FSlateColorBrush: Color brush
  • FSlateImageBrush: Image
    • FSlateVectorImageBrush: Vector image
  • FSlateDynamicImageBrush: Brush that can dynamically switch images
  • FSlateNoResource: Brush without any resources

Some of the above brushes are essentially constructed by some specific parameters to FSlateBrush. If the above brushes need to be combined, you can combine them according to their construction parameters.

UE provides some built-in FSlateBrush, which can be found by searching for ::Get().GetBrush in the source code:

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
If you want to fill the entire SWidget with red, you can use code like this:

int32 SCustomSlateWidget::OnPaint(const FPaintArgs& Args,
                                  const FGeometry& AllottedGeometry,
                                  const FSlateRect& MyCullingRect,
                                  FSlateWindowElementList& OutDrawElements,
                                  int32 LayerId,
                                  const FWidgetStyle& InWidgetStyle,
                                  bool bParentEnabled) const {
    static FSlateColorBrush ColorBrush(FColor(255, 0, 0));
    FSlateDrawElement::MakeBox(OutDrawElements,
                               LayerId, 
                               AllottedGeometry.ToPaintGeometry(),
                               &ColorBrush,
                               ESlateDrawEffect::None, 
                               ColorBrush.TintColor.GetColor(InWidgetStyle));
    return LayerId;
}

docs.title: ESlateDrawEffect
docs.text:
ESlateDrawEffect provides some effects for Slate, which can be the following values:

enum class ESlateDrawEffect : uint8
{
    None                    = 0,            // No effect
    NoBlending          = 1 << 0,           // No blending
    PreMultipliedAlpha  = 1 << 1,           // Premultiplied Alpha
    NoGamma             = 1 << 2,           // No Gamma correction
    InvertAlpha         = 1 << 3,           // Invert transparency
    // ^^ These Match ESlateBatchDrawFlag ^^

    NoPixelSnapping     = 1 << 4,           // Disable pixel alignment
    DisabledEffect      = 1 << 5,           // Effect in disabled state
    IgnoreTextureAlpha  = 1 << 6,           // Ignore transparency in the texture

    ReverseGamma            = 1 << 7        // Reverse Gamma
};

docs.title: FSlateFontInfo
docs.text:
FSlateFontInfo is used to specify font information, corresponding to font assets in UE. Part of its definition is as follows:

struct SLATECORE_API FSlateFontInfo
{
    /**The font object (valid when used from UMG or a Slate widget style asset) */
    TObjectPtr<const UObject> FontObject;

    /**The material to use when rendering this font */
    TObjectPtr<UObject> FontMaterial;

    /**Settings for applying an outline to a font */
    FFontOutlineSettings OutlineSettings;

    /**The composite font data to use (valid when used with a Slate style set in C++) */
    TSharedPtr<const FCompositeFont> CompositeFont;

    /**The name of the font to use from the default typeface (None will use the first entry) */
    FName TypefaceFontName;

    /**
     * The font size is a measure in point values. The conversion of points to Slate Units is done at 96 dpi.  So if 
     * you're using a tool like Photoshop to prototype layouts and UI mock ups, be sure to change the default dpi 
     * measurements from 72 dpi to 96 dpi.
     */
    int32 Size;

    /**The uniform spacing (or tracking) between all characters in the text. */
    int32 LetterSpacing = 0;

    /**The font fallback level. Runtime only, don't set on shared FSlateFontInfo, as it may change the font elsewhere (make a copy). */
    EFontFallback FontFallback;
};

UE has a dedicated font editor, and it is cumbersome to construct it directly in C++. However, UE also provides some built-in FSlateFontInfo, such as:

  • FCoreStyle::Get().GetFontStyle("NormalFont")
  • FCoreStyle::Get().GetFontStyle("SmallFont")
  • FCoreStyle::GetDefaultFontStyle("Regular", FontSize);
  • FCoreStyle::GetDefaultFontStyle("Bold", FontSize)
  • FCoreStyle::GetDefaultFontStyle("Italic", FontSize);
  • FCoreStyle::GetDefaultFontStyle("Mono", FontSize);

docs.title: FontMeasure
docs.text:
Most GUI frameworks have the concept of FontMeasure: measuring the drawing width and height of a certain text in a specific font format.

In UE, you can measure it in the following way (pseudocode):

FSlateApplication::Get().GetRenderer()->GetFontMeasureService()->Measure(
    const FText& Text,                      // Text
    const FSlateFontInfo& InFontInfo,       // Font
    float FontScale                         // Font scale
) -> FVector2D                              // Returns width (X) and height (Y)

docs.title: Performance Optimization
docs.text:
To optimize the Paint and Tick performance of the UI, Slate provides an SInvalidationPanel widget, which allows caching of high-consumption operations in child widgets. Only when some specific operations cause cache invalidation (Invalidate), will they be re-executed.

For details: Understanding the Slate UI Architecture in Unreal Engine - Polling Data Flows and Delegates | Unreal Engine 5.2 Documentation

We can manually call the Invalidate() function of the child widget to invalidate the cache:

void SWidget::Invalidate(EInvalidateWidgetReason InvalidateReason);

The values of EInvalidateWidgetReason can be:

enum class EInvalidateWidgetReason : uint8
{
    None = 0,
    Layout = 1 << 0,        // If you need to change the size required by the Widget, invalidate the layout. This is an expensive invalidation operation, so don't use it if you only need to repaint a widget
    Paint = 1 << 1,             // Invalidate painting
    Volatility = 1 << 2,        // Triggered when Volatility changes
    ChildOrder = 1 << 3,        // Triggered when adding or removing child widgets; invalidating it will rebuild the order of Children
    RenderTransform = 1 << 4,   // Triggered when RenderTransform changes
    Visibility = 1 << 5,        // Triggered when visibility changes
    AttributeRegistration = 1 << 6,     // Triggered when binding attributes
    Prepass = 1 << 7,                   // Invalidate Prepass

    /**
     * Use Paint invalidation if you're changing a normal property involving painting or sizing.
     * Additionally if the property that was changed affects Volatility in anyway, it's important
     * that you invalidate volatility so that it can be recalculated and cached.
     */
    PaintAndVolatility = Paint | Volatility,
    /**
     * Use Layout invalidation if you're changing a normal property involving painting or sizing.
     * Additionally if the property that was changed affects Volatility in anyway, it's important
     * that you invalidate volatility so that it can be recalculated and cached.
     */
    LayoutAndVolatility = Layout | Volatility,
};

Slate provides a method based on attributes (SlateAttribute): linking changes in attributes to cache reconstruction.

The specific approach is:

  • Wrap the attribute with TSlateAttribute (different from the purpose of TAttribute). The attribute wrapped by TSlateAttribute needs to pass the parameter (*this) during construction initialization.

  • In the function void WidgetType::PrivateRegisterAttributes(...), use the macro SLATE_ADD_MEMBER_ATTRIBUTE_DEFINITION(_Initializer, _Property, _Reason) to register the attribute.

Here is a brief example:

class SCustomSlateWidget : public SLeafWidget {
    SLATE_DECLARE_WIDGET(SCustomSlateWidget, SLeafWidget)
public:
    SLATE_BEGIN_ARGS(SCustomSlateWidget) {}
    SLATE_END_ARGS()
    void Construct(const SCustomSlateWidget::FArguments InArgs) {           
    }
protected:
    SCustomSlateWidget()
        : ClickedCounter(*this) {   // Initialize SlateAttribute
    }
    FReply OnMouseButtonDown(const FGeometry& MyGeometry, const FPointerEvent& MouseEvent) override {
        if (MouseEvent.IsMouseButtonDown(EKeys::LeftMouseButton)) {
            ClickedCounter.Set(*this, ClickedCounter.Get() + 1);        // Increment the counter; here, mouse down is treated as a click
            return FReply::Handled();
        }
        return FReply::Handled();
    }
    int32 OnPaint(const FPaintArgs& Args, const FGeometry& AllottedGeometry, const FSlateRect& MyCullingRect, FSlateWindowElementList& OutDrawElements, int32 LayerId, const FWidgetStyle& InWidgetStyle, bool bParentEnabled) const override {
        static FSlateFontInfo FontInfo = FCoreStyle::GetDefaultFontStyle("Bold", 30);
        FSlateDrawElement::MakeText(OutDrawElements, LayerId, AllottedGeometry.ToPaintGeometry(), FText::FromString(FString::FromInt(ClickedCounter.Get())), FontInfo);                 // Draw the current number of mouse clicks
        return LayerId;
    }
    FVector2D ComputeDesiredSize(float LayoutScaleMultiplier) const override {
        return FVector2D::ZeroVector;                                                           
    }
private:
    TSlateAttribute<int> ClickedCounter;        // Counter for mouse clicks
};

SLATE_IMPLEMENT_WIDGET(SCustomSlateWidget)
void SCustomSlateWidget::PrivateRegisterAttributes(FSlateAttributeInitializer& AttributeInitializer) {
    // Link changes in ClickedCounter to repaint events
    //SLATE_ADD_MEMBER_ATTRIBUTE_DEFINITION(AttributeInitializer, ClickedCounter, EInvalidateWidgetReason::Paint);
}

FSlateApplication::Get().AddWindow(
    SNew(SWindow)
    .SupportsMaximize(false)
    .SupportsMinimize(false)
    .IsTopmostWindow(true)
    .ClientSize(FVector2D(200,200))
    .SizingRule(ESizingRule::FixedSize)
    .CreateTitleBar(false)
    .AutoCenter(EAutoCenter::PreferredWorkArea)
    [
        SNew(SInvalidationPanel)            // Wrap with SInvalidationPanel
        [
            SNew(SCustomSlateWidget)
        ]
    ]
);

This code creates a clickable square:

Clicking the square increments ClickedCounter by 1, but the screen doesn't change. When you uncomment the code in PrivateRegisterAttributes:

void SCustomSlateWidget::PrivateRegisterAttributes(FSlateAttributeInitializer& AttributeInitializer) {
    // Link ClickedCounter changes to redraw events
    SLATE_ADD_MEMBER_ATTRIBUTE_DEFINITION(AttributeInitializer, ClickedCounter, EInvalidateWidgetReason::Paint);
}

Restart the program, and you'll see that the UI redraws when ClickedCounter changes:

docs.title: From Slate to UMG
docs.text:
UE's logic programming is built on UObject, but Slate doesn't use the heavy UObject mechanism to manage UI objects in pursuit of extreme performance.

In Slate, Shared Pointers are used to manage the lifecycle of UI objects.

To improve UI development efficiency for game developers, UE wraps Slate widgets with UObject, exposes some properties and functions of Slate widgets through reflection, and supports visual UI design. This layer of interface is what we know as UMG.

For details about UMG, refer to the official documentation:

  • https://docs.unrealengine.com/5.2/zh-CN/umg-ui-designer-for-unreal-engine/

The following short code snippet well illustrates the relationship between Slate and UMG:

#pragma once

#include "UObject/ObjectMacros.h"
#include "Widgets/Text/STextBlock.h"
#include "Components/Widget.h"
#include "CustomUWidget.generated.h"

UCLASS(meta = (DisplayName = "CustomWidget"))                   // DisplayName is the widget name
class UMGEXTENDUTILITIES_API UCustomWidget : public UWidget
{
    GENERATED_BODY()
protected:
    virtual TSharedRef<SWidget> RebuildWidget() override {                      // Rebuild the widget and assign it to the member variable
        return SAssignNew(MyTextBlock, STextBlock);
    }
    virtual void SynchronizeProperties() override {                             // Synchronize UObject properties to the Slate widget
        MyTextBlock->SetText(Text);
        Super::SynchronizeProperties();
    }
    virtual void ReleaseSlateResources(bool bReleaseChildren) override {        // Release Slate resources
        MyTextBlock.Reset();
    }

#if WITH_EDITOR
    virtual const FText GetPaletteCategory() override {                         // Widget category in the editor
        return FText::FromString("CustomCategory");
    }
#endif

public:
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)        // Expose the function to Blueprints
    FText GetText() const {
        return Text;
    }
    UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
    void SetText(FText InText) {
        Text = InText;
        if (MyTextBlock) {              // Set the property; if the widget is already created, directly pass the value to the widget
            MyTextBlock->SetText(Text);
        }
    }
protected:
    UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintGetter = "GetText", BlueprintSetter = "SetText")
    FText Text;                         // Expose the property to the editor

    TSharedPtr<STextBlock> MyTextBlock; // Actual Slate widget
};

In C++, the way to use UMG is:

UWidget* UMGWidget = LoadObject<UWidget>(nullptr, TEXT("{AssetPath}"));                // Load from asset, or use NewObject
TSharedPtr<SWidget> SlateWidget = UMGWidget->TakeWidget();                             // This creates a new SWidget
TSharedPtr<SWidget> CachedSlateWidget = UMGWidget->GetCachedWidget();                  // Get the previously created SWidget
// Then use the Slate usage method

docs.title: Lifecycle Management
docs.text:
UWidget uses UObject's garbage collection. It holds a shared pointer to the SWidget. To ensure that the UWidget isn't garbage-collected while the widget is displayed (when the TSharedPtr<SWidget> still exists), UMG uses a widget SObjectWidget that inherits from FGCObject to add a reference to the UWidget.

Going back to the example code above, we can see that the widget obtained by calling UWidget::TakeWidget() isn't the one created in UWidget::RebuildWidget(), but is wrapped an extra layer with SObjectWidget. Their hierarchical relationship during creation is as follows:

During destruction, their release order is as follows:

  • SObjectWidget inherits from FGCObject and adds a reference to the UWidget, ensuring the UWidget isn't GC'd while the SObjectWidget exists.
  • When the widget starts to be destroyed, the SObjectWidget's reference count becomes 0 and it's destroyed, which then releases the reference to the UWidget.
  • When the UWidget's reference count becomes 0, it's released in the next garbage collection, and only then is the shared pointer to the SWidget it holds released.

docs.title: An Incomplete Guide to LOD
docs.text:
The invention of electronic computers originated during World War II, when artillery and ballistic calculations became increasingly complex, and existing computing tools could no longer meet the demands. To solve these problems, scientists and engineers began developing electronic computers.

With the advent of electronic computers, video games also emerged.

In the development of video games, there are always some creative ideas and technologies that continuously break through the limitations of hardware developers' thinking, maximize the performance of hardware, and drive computers to develop in an amazing direction:

  • Zhihu | The Past, Present and Future of Video Games - Maipian

And LOD (Level of Detail), is a technology that emerged during this development process and has been used to this day. Its purpose is:

  • Adopt different precision strategies in scenarios of different Significance to minimize resource waste and increase the upper limit of the entire system.

This ideological strategy is reflected in all aspects of game production.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
In terms of models, the application of LOD mainly involves creating multiple low-poly versions of the model with different precision levels. High-precision models are used at close distances, while low-precision models are used at long distances.

In large-scale 3D scenes used in real-time rendering, creating model LODs is usually an unavoidable challenge for development teams to ensure the program's frame rate.

High time and labor costs make it very difficult for many independent developers and small teams to build complex scenes.

This changed dramatically with the emergence of UE's virtual geometry technology—Nanite, which significantly lowered the threshold for scene production.

Nanite analyzes the importance information of model geometry and automatically generates high-quality LODs. It not only occupies less storage space but also can be rendered with very high performance. It is undoubtedly the future of geometric rendering.

However, currently, in some specific scenarios, we still cannot completely abandon LOD:

  • The GPU computing power of modern PCs is usually redundant. Most mid-range GPUs are sufficient to handle rendering of some common complex scenes. However, for other platforms such as mobile devices, Xbox, Switch..., their computing power is currently only barely sufficient for projects with high graphical requirements. To pursue better visual effects, it is often necessary to customize some relatively hacky rendering mechanisms for extreme optimization, and the remaining computing power allocated is difficult to support the operation of Nanite.
  • Nanite's model simplification algorithm still has much room for optimization in some special model types, such as vegetation. If it is a complex scene with high vegetation density and a wide range, using LOD can compress performance to a greater extent, which was mentioned in a previous article.

In most previous game projects, LODs were usually created by artists in DDC software. While providing the model source files, artists produced the corresponding LODs for the models according to certain specifications.

This approach has certain limitations currently:

  • The early model production process was relatively "pragmatic". Most of the time, models could only be created manually. However, many mesh processing SDKs have emerged now, which often provide some effective model simplification algorithms. High-quality LODs can be generated without re-modeling.
  • Manually creating LODs often requires high costs. It's okay if the team has sufficient manpower and resources. If it is outsourced to a third-party team, it will undoubtedly be a huge expense.
  • Any methodology has certain applicable conditions, and model production is no exception. Except for some established production companies, most teams should find it difficult to develop a perfect production specification at the beginning of game production. Often, many hidden problems gradually emerge as the development progress advances. Moreover, art production is the largest expense in the entire project. For LOD production, if the source model or specifications change, the previously produced "products" will be wasted. Therefore, we need to shift our focus from creating specific LODs to building an iterable LOD production pipeline.
  • Although the source models are created by artists, they are often not sensitive to performance and have a limited understanding of LOD. When facing models that are difficult to meet the specifications no matter how they are created, they will only feel helpless.

At this point, if someone has an in-depth understanding of geometric processing, graphics rendering, and the editor direction, and takes charge of these tasks in a procedural way, it can save the team a lot of production costs. Such professionals are generally defined as Pipeline TA / Engine Pipeline Engineer.

docs.title: Production Process
docs.text:
Before creating LODs, it is best to build a simple preview level and use a simple editor tool to automatically arrange assets to achieve the following goals:

  • Determine all assets to be previewed based on the asset list or asset path.
  • Arrange assets horizontally using the model's bounding sphere radius as the interval.
  • Convert the LOD's screen size to distance and arrange all LODs vertically.
  • Display some key information on the generated models, such as screen size, distance, vertex count, face count...

In this view, we can more intuitively view and manage the model specifications:

In the early LOD production process, we generally used the distance between the model and the camera as the criterion for LOD switching. A simplified model with a certain precision level is switched every certain distance. In this way, we might create an LOD chain like this:

However, it was soon discovered that using distance does not provide an intuitive way to establish the distance intervals between LODs. Because some models are large and some are small, different distance intervals must be evaluated for each model to ensure appropriate precision distribution. To solve this problem, we introduced another parameter—Screen Size: it comprehensively evaluates the camera distance, camera's perspective matrix, and the model's bounding sphere radius to obtain a value, which can be roughly regarded as the model's screen occupancy ratio. Here is its calculation formula:

float ConvertDistanceToScreenSize(float ObjectSphereRadius, float Distance)
{
    const float FOV = 90.0f;                                // Camera parameters can be confirmed uniformly
    const float FOVRad = FOV * (float)UE_PI / 360.0f;
    const FMatrix ProjectionMatrix = FPerspectiveMatrix(FOVRad, 1920, 1080, 0.01f);     
    const float ScreenMultiple = FMath::Max(0.5f * ProjectionMatrix.M[0][0], 0.5f * ProjectionMatrix.M[1][1]);
    return 2.0f * ScreenMultiple * ObjectSphereRadius / FMath::Max(1.0f, Distance);
}

We determine the intervals between LODs by reducing the screen size by a certain percentage each time, which is easier than using distance directly:

However, although using screen size does provide an intuitive way to set the intervals between LODs, if the distance intervals of the LOD chains generated for models of different sizes are not uniform, the visual artifacts will become more obvious.

If we generate LODs by decreasing the screen size by a fixed percentage, we can see that the distances of the LOD chains for different models are inconsistent (here, the LOD simplification amplitude is deliberately set very large to make the artifacts visible):

Compare this with generating LODs using a fixed distance gradient:

It can be seen that the​画面​ changes are smoother when using fixed distance gradient LODs:

Although using screen size does allow intuitive setting of LOD intervals, since the engine uses distance to limit certain visual effects (such as shadows, distance field lighting...), if we want visual effects to transition more smoothly, it is recommended to use the following strategy to generate LODs:

  • Use fixed LOD distance gradients
  • Determine the number of LODs based on the bounding sphere radius
  • Determine the simplification amplitude based on screen size, vertex density, and model features

The above key parameters will change with project iteration, increasing complexity, and platform performance requirements. Therefore, we should not generate LODs manually but build an iterable LOD production pipeline, which can be continuously iterated and optimized.

Common strategies for generating simplified models include three types:

  • Reduce: Delete vertex data from the original model according to importance and a certain simplification amplitude to generate simplified models.
  • Remesh: Use voxelization model algorithms to approximate the source model with a certain voxel precision to obtain simplified models.
  • Impostor: A clever way to maintain the model's visual effect, which usually breaks the original geometric structure of the model.

Currently, most teams build this pipeline between DDC and the engine. However, Unreal Engine currently provides very excellent model processing interfaces. If we build the pipeline directly on the engine side, we can better combine the actual game scene environment to generate better results.

For example, the Octahedron Impostor mentioned in the previous vegetation chapter:

  • https://shaderbits.com/blog/octahedral-impostors

Although UE engine natively provides some model simplification algorithms, there are some geometric processing SDKs that can reduce the rendering overhead of models to a greater extent while ensuring visual effects:

  • Simplygon - Setting the Standard for 3D Game Content Optimization
  • InstaLOD - Everything You Need to Produce and Automatically Optimize 3D Content

Using the interfaces provided by these SDKs, an LOD chain generation pipeline can be easily built.

Here are some reference documents for LOD production:

  • Does Polygon Count Matter in 3D Modeling for Game Assets? – 3D-Ace Studio
  • What to Consider When It Comes to LOD Transitions? - Simplygon Blog

docs.title: Creating Custom Meshes
docs.text:
UPackage* NewPackage = CreatePackage(TEXT("/Game/NewStaticMesh"));                                              // Create a new package
UStaticMesh* NewStaticMesh = NewObject<UStaticMesh>(NewPackage, "NewStaticMesh",  RF_Public | RF_Standalone);   // Create a new mesh, specify Outer as the new package so that when saving the new package, this object will be serialized and stored

{   // LOD0
    FStaticMeshSourceModel& NewSourceModel = NewStaticMesh->AddSourceModel();                                   // Create a new source model    
    FMeshDescription& NewMeshDescription = *NewStaticMesh->CreateMeshDescription(0);                            // Create a mesh description for this source model
    FStaticMeshAttributes AttributeGetter = FStaticMeshAttributes(NewMeshDescription);                          // Create an attribute getter for the mesh description
    AttributeGetter.Register();

    TPolygonGroupAttributesRef<FName> PolygonGroupNames = AttributeGetter.GetPolygonGroupMaterialSlotNames();   // List of polygon group names, corresponding to the respective MeshSections
    TVertexAttributesRef<FVector3f> VertexPositions = AttributeGetter.GetVertexPositions();                     // Vertex array
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<FVector3f> Normals = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceNormals();               // Normal array
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<FVector3f> Tangents = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceTangents();             // Tangent array
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<float> BinormalSigns = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceBinormalSigns();       
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<FVector4f> Colors = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceColors();                 // Vertex color array
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<FVector2f> UVs = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceUVs();                       // Texture coordinate array

    int32 VertexCount = 4;
    int32 VertexInstanceCount = 6;
    int32 PolygonCount = 2;
    NewMeshDescription.ReserveNewVertices(VertexCount);                                                         // Preallocate memory
    NewMeshDescription.ReserveNewVertexInstances(VertexInstanceCount);
    NewMeshDescription.ReserveNewPolygons(PolygonCount);
    NewMeshDescription.ReserveNewEdges(PolygonCount * 2);
    UVs.SetNumChannels(PolygonCount);
    {
        const FVertexID VertexID0 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertex();
        const FVertexID VertexID1 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertex();
        const FVertexID VertexID2 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertex();
        const FVertexID VertexID3 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertex();

        VertexPositions[VertexID0] = FVector3f(0.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f);
        VertexPositions[VertexID1] = FVector3f(100.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f);
        VertexPositions[VertexID2] = FVector3f(100.0f, 0.0f, 100.0f);
        VertexPositions[VertexID3] = FVector3f(0.0f, 0.0f, 100.0f);

        const FVertexInstanceID VertexInstanceID0 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertexInstance(VertexID0);
        const FVertexInstanceID VertexInstanceID1 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertexInstance(VertexID1);
        const FVertexInstanceID VertexInstanceID2 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertexInstance(VertexID2);

        const FVertexInstanceID VertexInstanceID3 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertexInstance(VertexID0);
        const FVertexInstanceID VertexInstanceID4 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertexInstance(VertexID2);
        const FVertexInstanceID VertexInstanceID5 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertexInstance(VertexID3);

        UVs[VertexInstanceID0] = FVector2f(0.0f, 0.0f);
        UVs[VertexInstanceID1] = FVector2f(1.0f, 0.0f);
        UVs[VertexInstanceID2] = FVector2f(1.0f, 1.0f);
        UVs[VertexInstanceID3] = FVector2f(0.0f, 0.0f);
        UVs[VertexInstanceID4] = FVector2f(1.0f, 1.0f);
        UVs[VertexInstanceID5] = FVector2f(0.0f, 1.0f);

        Normals[VertexInstanceID0] 
            = Normals[VertexInstanceID1] 
            = Normals[VertexInstanceID2] 
            = Normals[VertexInstanceID3] 
            = Normals[VertexInstanceID4] 
            = Normals[VertexInstanceID5] 
            = FVector3f(0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f);

        UMaterialInterface* Material = UMaterial::GetDefaultMaterial(MD_Surface);

        {   // Mesh Section 0
            FPolygonGroupID PolygonGroup0 = NewMeshDescription.CreatePolygonGroup();
            PolygonGroupNames[PolygonGroup0] = "LOD0_Section0";
            NewMeshDescription.CreatePolygon(PolygonGroup0,
                {
                    VertexInstanceID0,
                    VertexInstanceID1,
                    VertexInstanceID2,
                });
            NewStaticMesh->GetStaticMaterials().Add(FStaticMaterial(Material));
        }

        {   // Mesh Section 1
            FPolygonGroupID PolygonGroup1 = NewMeshDescription.CreatePolygonGroup();
            PolygonGroupNames[PolygonGroup1] = "LOD0_Section1";
            NewMeshDescription.CreatePolygon(PolygonGroup1,
                {
                    VertexInstanceID3,
                    VertexInstanceID4,
                    VertexInstanceID5
                });
            NewStaticMesh->GetStaticMaterials().Add(FStaticMaterial(Material));
        }
    }
    NewSourceModel.ScreenSize = 1;                                                      // Set screen size
    NewStaticMesh->CommitMeshDescription(0);                                            // Commit mesh description
}

{
    FStaticMeshSourceModel& NewSourceModel = NewStaticMesh->AddSourceModel();
    FMeshDescription& NewMeshDescription = *NewStaticMesh->CreateMeshDescription(1);
    FStaticMeshAttributes AttributeGetter = FStaticMeshAttributes(NewMeshDescription);
    AttributeGetter.Register();

    TPolygonGroupAttributesRef<FName> PolygonGroupNames = AttributeGetter.GetPolygonGroupMaterialSlotNames();
    TVertexAttributesRef<FVector3f> VertexPositions = AttributeGetter.GetVertexPositions();
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<FVector3f> Tangents = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceTangents();
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<float> BinormalSigns = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceBinormalSigns();
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<FVector3f> Normals = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceNormals();
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<FVector4f> Colors = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceColors();
    TVertexInstanceAttributesRef<FVector2f> UVs = AttributeGetter.GetVertexInstanceUVs();

    int32 VertexCount = 3;
    int32 VertexInstanceCount = 3;
    int32 PolygonCount = 1;
    NewMeshDescription.ReserveNewVertices(VertexCount);
    NewMeshDescription.ReserveNewVertexInstances(VertexInstanceCount);
    NewMeshDescription.ReserveNewPolygons(PolygonCount);
    NewMeshDescription.ReserveNewEdges(PolygonCount * 2);
    UVs.SetNumChannels(1);
    {
        const FVertexID VertexID0 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertex();
        const FVertexID VertexID1 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertex();
        const FVertexID VertexID2 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertex();

        VertexPositions[VertexID0] = FVector3f(0.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f);
        VertexPositions[VertexID1] = FVector3f(100.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f);
        VertexPositions[VertexID2] = FVector3f(50.0f, 0.0f, 100.0f);

        const FVertexInstanceID VertexInstanceID0 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertexInstance(VertexID0);
        const FVertexInstanceID VertexInstanceID1 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertexInstance(VertexID1);
        const FVertexInstanceID VertexInstanceID2 = NewMeshDescription.CreateVertexInstance(VertexID2);

        UVs[VertexInstanceID0] = FVector2f(0.0f, 0.0f);
        UVs[VertexInstanceID1] = FVector2f(1.0f, 0.0f);
        UVs[VertexInstanceID2] = FVector2f(0.5f, 1.0f);

        Normals[VertexInstanceID0]
            = Normals[VertexInstanceID1]
            = Normals[VertexInstanceID2]
            = FVector3f(0.0f, 1.0f, 0.0f);

        UMaterialInterface* Material = UMaterial::GetDefaultMaterial(MD_Surface);

        {
            FPolygonGroupID PolygonGroup0 = NewMeshDescription.CreatePolygonGroup();
            PolygonGroupNames[PolygonGroup0] = "LOD1_Section0";
            NewMeshDescription.CreatePolygon(PolygonGroup0,
                {
                    VertexInstanceID0,
                    VertexInstanceID1,
                    VertexInstanceID2,
                });
            NewStaticMesh->GetStaticMaterials().Add(FStaticMaterial(Material));
        }
    }
    NewSourceModel.ScreenSize = 0.5f;
    NewStaticMesh->CommitMeshDescription(1);
}

NewStaticMesh->ImportVersion = EImportStaticMeshVersion::LastVersion;           // Declare that this build uses the latest version of data to prevent automatically generated LODs from replacing our filled model data
NewStaticMesh->Build();                                                         // Build the mesh
NewStaticMesh->PostEditChange();
NewStaticMesh->WaitForPendingInitOrStreaming(true, true);

FStaticMeshCompilingManager::Get().FinishAllCompilation();
FAssetRegistryModule::AssetCreated(NewStaticMesh);                              

FPackagePath PackagePath = FPackagePath::FromPackageNameChecked(NewPackage->GetName());
FString PackageLocalPath = PackagePath.GetLocalFullPath();
UPackage::SavePackage(NewPackage, NewStaticMesh, RF_Public | RF_Standalone, *PackageLocalPath, GError, nullptr, false, true, SAVE_NoError);         // Save the new package

docs.title: Material Textures
docs.text:
For materials, in some early projects, LODs were also generated for the corresponding materials when generating model LODs. Although simplifying material logic can theoretically reduce performance overhead, material LODs will undoubtedly increase the size of the material set, and the performance improvement is not particularly obvious. The more complex management method also makes this approach difficult to promote in actual projects.

Currently, more attention is focused on textures, and the application of LOD mainly involves generating Mipmaps for textures.

Most people's understanding of Mipmaps (Multilevel Mipmaps) is that they solve the moiré pattern phenomenon:

  • Zhihu | Computer Graphics VII: Texture Mapping and Mipmap Technology - Sun Xiaolei

In addition to solving moiré patterns, Mipmaps currently have other uses in UE:

  • Texture Streaming: To alleviate the pressure of video memory usage, UE will allocate a texture streaming pool of a certain size by default (configured using r.Streaming.PoolSize). It streams in a certain MipLevel of the texture according to the texture's importance (camera distance and texture group priority) to minimize overall video memory usage. Here are some very valuable articles about texture streaming:
    • Zhihu | UE4 Texture Streaming - mike
    • Zhihu | Summary of Unreal Engine (UE4) Extreme Compression Processing for Mobile Texture Resources (ASTC) - Sparrowfc
  • UI Adaptation: Since games may run in environments with different resolutions, when UI textures are scaled down, the excessive span of Downsampling texels will cause jagged edges in the textures. For UI with dynamically adjusted positions, obvious flickering will also occur. At this time, Mipmaps can be generated for UI textures because the engine will determine which MipLevel of the UI texture to use based on DDX(UV) and DDY(UV).

We can specifically customize the Mipmaps of a certain texture here:

However, the best way is to classify textures into different TextureLODGroups and adopt unified configurations for each texture group. This will be much more convenient when performing performance tuning across multiple platforms.

In UE 5, you can uniformly set the configuration of texture groups for different platforms here:

docs.title: Terrain
docs.text:
The terrain operation mechanism of UE5 is very complete. Terrain LOD is achieved by adjusting the precision of tessellation. Currently, 8 levels of LOD are used by default. To modify the LOD, you only need to adjust these parameters:

UE5.1 and later versions support Nanite terrain. Since the terrain uses very standardized model data, enabling Nanite will undoubtedly result in more reasonable geometric organization. Compared with LOD, it usually has fewer triangles and more realistic visual effects:

Although Nanite's scheduling algorithm is more complex than tessellation and requires an additional copy of mesh data, when the camera is stationary, Nanite's rendering consumption is significantly lower than LOD. Moreover, Nanite is friendly to virtual shadows. If there are no platform restrictions, Nanite terrain will be a better choice.

Currently, some projects use static meshes as terrain. With the streaming and HLOD of world partition, a better balance of performance can be achieved without the limitations of terrain editing. However, the main advantage of terrain is that it can tile a large area using several high-resolution Tile textures (the resolution of the texture is much smaller than the terrain resolution). The disk space it occupies is much smaller than that of using models to tile a terrain with the same visual precision.

docs.title: HLOD
docs.text:
The several types of LOD mentioned above mainly target individual assets, while HLOD involves creating LODs after batching assets.

Currently, there are two ways to use HLOD in UE:

  • For ordinary maps, you can use tools to merge meshes and generate HLOD according to this document:
    • Epic Games | Building HLOD
  • For open-world maps, it is necessary to classify scene objects and set HLODLayer to automatically generate HLOD for the Grid Cell of the world partition:
    • Epic Games | Building HLOD for World Partition

Let's elaborate on the latter method.

Because World Partition divides the scene meshes into many cells and only loads a key part of the area (such as around the player) through Streaming, which can effectively reduce the pressure on program execution:

However, for cells that have been unloaded, we still want them to be displayed but do not want to increase the performance overhead too much. Therefore, we generate HLODs for the objects in the cells, which can further reduce the loading range of streaming because HLOD can:

  • Reduce Draw Calls
  • Reduce the number of primitive components and improve culling efficiency
  • Reduce the precision of geometry and textures in the distance, improve rendering efficiency and reduce memory pressure

But it also has problems:

  • Can only expand the display range to a certain extent
  • Will increase the size of disk space

Currently, UE provides four basic HLOD generation strategies, which are only for static mesh assets:

  • Instancing: Merge the objects in the cell into ISM
  • Merging: Merge the objects in the cell into a single mesh
  • Simplification: Merge the objects in the cell and then simplify the mesh
  • Approximation: Merge the objects in the cell and then approximate the mesh

They are suitable for different mesh categories. Suppose we use the following partitioned meshes:

GirdName Cell Size Loading Range Priority BlockOnSlowStreaming MainGrid（Default） 12800 25600 0 false DeferGrid 25600 25600 -9 true AdvanceGrid 51200 51200 9 true SmallGrid 6400 19200 -9 false

They can be divided into the following categories:

  • Terrain patches: Mainly some static mesh patches used to supplement the ground surface (non-terrain components), distributed in AdvanceGrid. The size of terrain blocks can generally be 25600. For terrain patches, they are placed in cells of 51200, and geometry is merged to generate HLOD to reduce DrawCalls and the number of primitive components.
  • Ordinary models: Distributed in MainGrid, placed in cells of 12800. The HLOD generation method is to eliminate small objects, merge them, and then simplify or approximate to generate HLOD simplified models, which can have multiple HLOD levels.
  • Vegetation: Distributed in AdvanceGrid, using HISM of 25600 to organize Partition, placed in cells of 51200. The HLOD strategy is to merge HISM and degenerate it into ISM of size 51200.
  • Others: Some custom or dynamic rendering components (such as particles, water bodies...). It is best to avoid displaying them in the distance. Usually, such objects need to expand the loading distance and have good LODs, or customize exclusive HLOD generation strategies.

docs.title: Effects
docs.text:
Effects (Niagara) are very special rendering components. GPU particles use Compute Shader to simulate particle movement, and the simulated data is handed over to the particle renderer for Indirect Rendering.

Particle optimization mainly involves reducing the complexity of simulation logic, reducing emitters, clipping, optimizing materials, and reducing OverDraw.

The main application of LOD lies in the fact that Niagara provides some engine-built-in variables:

Usually, we dynamically adjust the number of particles and their life cycles according to the LOD distance to optimize the performance consumption of particles.

docs.title: Unreal Engine 5 Development - Texture Graph
docs.text:
Texture Graph is an experimental plugin introduced in UE 5.4, primarily used for procedural texture generation.

There are many comprehensive resources available for the usage and introduction of Texture Graph:

  • [Chinese Live Stream] Episode 51 | UE5.4 New Feature: TextureGraph | Zhu Changsheng (Tianzhichuan)
  • UE5.4 Texture Graph Introduction - CG World
  • UE5.4 New Feature - Texture Graph Getting Started Brief | CSDN | Electronic Cloud and Long-Range Entanglement
  • UE5.4TextureGraph | GALAXIX Anime Continent

Many friends may feel that it seems useful after watching the plugin introduction, but doesn't really relate to them. However, it is actually a very powerful plugin!

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
If you are a graphics developer, you should know that we use many Graphics Rendering Pipelines to draw geometric shapes (Primitives) onto a Render Target (which can be understood as a texture or image). This process is generally called the Base Pass (or Mesh Pass, Primitives Pass):

For the final​画面​ presented to the audience, we often need to add additional effects (such as global illumination, post-processing...) based on the image output from the Base Pass:

Such effects are usually generated using a series of Render Passes. A Render Pass typically requires some texture inputs and ultimately generates some RTs. These generated RTs can then serve as texture inputs for another Render Pass. Treating these Render Passes as nodes and connecting their inputs and outputs with lines, we eventually get a graph-like structure:

We usually call this a Render Graph / Frame Graph.

The Texture Graph we use follows a similar process. The difference is that Render Graph is used to complete the rendering of a frame of game​画面​, while Texture Graph usually is used to generate texture assets during the editor phase.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
Although Texture Graph is essentially for procedural textures, its feature set is far less comprehensive than mature procedural texture tools (such as Substance Designer). It is more suitable for people like the author who have neither in-depth knowledge of procedural textures nor proficiency in using PS, but know how to write code and have a basic foundation in image processing knowledge.

The author uses it for these things:

  1. Drag nodes to quickly write logic for simple image processing. For developers, when the input and output are clear, writing code is often more intuitive and efficient than operating the editor.
  2. Build reusable texture generation pipelines, i.e., templating. This is very useful when there are a large number of source (input) textures or when source textures are frequently iterated over time cycles.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Here are a few examples to briefly introduce what the author has done with it.

docs.title: Image Processing Widget
docs.text:
Some time ago, I watched Ashes of Time again, and there was a super cool shot in it 0.0

I wanted to take it down as a background, but the style was a bit greasy. Maybe turning it black and white would look better, so I did a grayscale conversion:

It looked pretty good, but the gloss on the nose felt weird. So I opened PS: - Tried the eraser pen, but it got blurry. - Used the lasso tool to frame the bright area and adjust the brightness range. Oh no, the edges couldn't be smoothed after adjustment.

It was clearly a simple logic—I just wanted the nose area not to be so bright—but I struggled for a long time without success. Finally, I opened Qt, wrote a rendering pipeline, and solved it with a few lines of code. The fragment shader code was roughly like this (values are not accurate):

void main(){
    vec4 TextureColor = texture(Texture, UV);
    float Gray = (TextureColor.r + TextureColor.g + TextureColor.b) / 3;        // Grayscale conversion
    if( UV.x > 0.53 && UV.x < 0.56 && UV.y > 0.45 && UV.y < 0.51)                   // Area selection
    {
        if(Gray > 0.2)                                                          // Select parts with grayscale value greater than 0.2
        {
            Gray = 0.2 + (Gray - 0.2) * 0.1;                                    // Scale the grayscale of parts exceeding 0.2 to 0.1 times the original.
        }
    }
    OutFragColor = vec4(Gray, Gray, Gray, 1);
}

The final effect was pretty good:

Of course, this can also be quickly implemented with Python and CV, but many friends who know UE can't write code or use those complex software (learning UE clearly is already hard enough). However, they usually know how to write materials, so the significance of Texture Graph is that it allows friends who know UE to do some simple image processing without having to spend a lot of effort learning a certain software for a relatively simple requirement.

It's also very simple to modify it to use Texture Graph to achieve the same function:

Unreal Engine 5 Development — Procedural Content Management
docs.text:
There is no denying that content has always been the core of the gaming experience, which is very similar to the film and television industry. However, there are significant differences in the production processes between the gaming and film/television industries. Although games offer excellent interactive feedback that allows players to deeply engage, the strict constraint of computing power, like the Sword of Damocles hanging overhead, greatly restricts content production in the gaming industry.

When creating content, the film and television industry can, to some extent, rely on massive investments of manpower, material resources, and time, adopting a "brute force" approach—pouring in huge resources and achieving high-quality content output through resource accumulation and intensive production.

However, the gaming industry finds it difficult to follow this path. Due to computing power limitations, games cannot endlessly pile up content elements; otherwise, issues like game lag and unstable operation will occur, severely impacting the player experience.

Therefore, before engaging in content production in the gaming industry, solving engineering problems becomes particularly crucial. Only by optimizing engineering processes, rationally applying technical means, and improving resource utilization efficiency can we achieve high-quality, efficient output of game content under limited computing power conditions, meeting players' ever-growing demands.

docs.title: Procedural Technology
docs.text:
In the past, procedural techniques were primarily a concept focused on by developers. But in recent years, with the acceleration of game industrialization, they have quietly permeated every link of game content production, like precision gears embedded in a large machine, driving the overall operation efficiently. There is no doubt that procedural technology has become a key driving force for enhancing game content production capacity, injecting a steady stream of vitality into the development of the gaming industry.

The essence of Procedural applications is to store the problem-solving process as data assets, ensuring that subsequent development can rely on these operational data for reuse, iteration, etc. (Conceptually, it is a program, just a program within a program).

Current applications of procedural technology in the gaming industry mainly include:

  • Procedural Content Generation
  • Procedural Modeling
  • Procedural Textures
  • Procedural Animation
  • Procedural Audio

These technologies have gradually permeated the daily work of art asset production, with a notable feature: creating assets through programming rather than just parameter tuning.

Unreal Engine provides excellent support for procedural techniques:

docs.title: Procedural Content Generation
docs.text:
Procedural Content Generation is a toolset for PCG in Unreal Engine. It provides technical artists, designers, and programmers with the ability to build fast, iterative tools and content of any complexity, ranging from assets (such as building or biome generation) to entire worlds.

docs.title: Meta Sounds
docs.text:
Meta Sounds supports user customization, third-party extensibility, graph reuse, and provides powerful tools for sound design within the editor.

docs.title: Geometry Script
docs.text:
Geometry Script provides a set of APIs for generating and editing mesh geometry using Blueprints and Python. It can write Geometry Scripting and Asset Actions in Editor Utility Widgets to create custom mesh analysis function libraries, processing and editing tools. It can also be used in Actor Blueprints to create procedural objects and implement complex geometric queries.

Related References:

  • Introduction to Geometry Scripting in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.5 Documentation | Epic Developer Community

docs.title: Animation Blueprints
docs.text:
Blueprints used to simulate or control skeletal meshes in games. They can mix animations, adjust skeletons, and create logic to define the final animation pose used each frame.

Related References:

  • Animation Blueprints in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.5 Documentation | Epic Developer Community

docs.title: Material Blueprint
docs.text:
Blueprints used to define the surface properties of scene objects. They can use various images (textures), node-based material expressions, and the inherent properties of materials themselves to define the final surface properties of scene objects.

Related References:

  • Unreal Engine Materials | Unreal Engine 5.5 Documentation | Epic Developer Community

docs.title: Texture Graph
docs.text:
Texture Graph provides artists with an interface to create or edit texture assets directly within Unreal Engine without the need for external image editing packages. Using a familiar node graph similar to the Material Editor, a series of nodes can be connected to the output texture.

You can combine texture graphs with Blueprints, materials, and material functions to achieve unique workflows that can only be implemented within Unreal Engine.

Texture Graph can be used for many interesting applications. For example, the author recently used it for:

  • Image Editing: For development, the freedom of writing code is much higher than editor operations.

  • UI Asset Production: Unreal's UI system does not support complex interface effects such as edge blur, drop shadows, neumorphism, etc. This is because UI is only a small part of the overall graphical content with a limited budget, and using these features requires complex rendering structures. However, with Texture Graph, we can generate the necessary asset maps for these effects. Combined with some simple editor extensions, this workflow becomes very smooth.

  • Stylized Reference Generation: You can extend Texture Graph with an AI call node, allowing Unreal Engine's native graphical content to easily achieve stylized references with AI. For example, the author used it to generate:
    • Splash screens and thumbnails for engine startup loading based on project content
    • Dynamically generate a stylized minimap for the scene using Scene Capture
    • Generate stylized loading pages for certain scenes
    • ...

Related References:

  • Getting Started with Texture Graph | Epic Developer Community
  • [Chinese Live Broadcast] Episode 51 | UE5.4 New Feature: TextureGraph | Zhu Changsheng (Tianzhichuan)
  • UE5.4 Texture Graph Introduction CG World

docs.title: Procedural Content Management
docs.text:
The application of the procedural technologies mentioned above has endowed us with unprecedented creative efficiency. Compared to the past, we can now produce richer game content in a shorter time and with a lower budget. This not only significantly improves development efficiency but also expands the boundaries of game content, bringing more diverse experiences to players.

However, every coin has two sides. The production of more content also means that management costs will grow exponentially. From asset management and version control to testing and update iteration, each link requires more investment of manpower, material resources, and time costs to ensure that the​庞大​ content system can operate in an orderly manner without any chaos or errors.

Previously, the author highly recommended using PCG technology for scene construction because integrating a generation pipeline is definitely easier for iteration and optimization.

But in reality, the industry's application of PCG is still relatively idealistic, and there are not many practical application scenarios that can be truly implemented.

A major reason for this is that PCG is not "grounded". Currently, the job responsibilities for scene design in most game production teams are generally divided as follows:

  • Game Planner: Responsible for planning the overall framework of the game scene, including the scene's functions, story background, style positioning, player experience flow in the scene, etc., providing clear directions and requirement documents for scene design.
  • Concept Designer: Based on the planner's requirements, conduct concept design of the scene, drawing concept sketches of the overall style, atmosphere, general form of main buildings and terrain through hand-drawing or digital painting, providing visual references for subsequent detailed design.
  • Scene Concept Artist: On the basis of concept design, conduct detailed concept art design of specific elements in the scene, including the structure of buildings, decorative details, undulating changes of terrain, styles of vegetation and props, etc., presenting the shape, color, material and other details of each element in the form of precise paintings, providing accurate production blueprints for modelers.
  • 3D Modeler: Use 3D modeling software to construct the designed scene elements into 3D models based on scene concept art, including building the basic framework of buildings, terrain, props, etc., endowing them with volume and spatial sense, and performing preliminary UV unwrapping to prepare for subsequent texture painting.
  • Material and Lighting Artist: Add materials and textures to 3D models to simulate the real texture of objects, such as wood texture, metal luster, stone roughness, etc. At the same time, responsible for setting the lighting effects in the scene, creating different atmospheres and light and shadow effects, enhancing the realism and visual impact of the scene.
  • Scene Sound Designer: Responsible for creating, selecting, and adding appropriate sound effects for the scene, conducting sound effect design according to the theme, emotion, atmosphere of the scene, and through collection, editing, mixing and other operations, making the sound effects perfectly integrate with the scene, enhancing the immersion of the scene.
  • VFX Artist: According to the needs of the scene, design and produce various special effects, such as fire, smoke, water flow, magic effects, etc., adding vividness and interest to the scene, and improving the player's immersion.
  • Level Designer: Mainly responsible for the layout and planning of the scene, reasonably arranging the positions of monsters, props, task points, obstacles and other elements in the scene according to gameplay and planner requirements, designing the player's movement route and level difficulty curve, ensuring that players can obtain a good gaming experience in the scene.
  • Scene Optimizer: Perform performance optimization on the completed scene, reducing the resource occupation of the scene on hardware by reducing the number of model faces, compressing textures, reasonably setting light baking, etc., improving the running efficiency of the game, and ensuring smooth operation on different devices.

In the process of scene design, close communication and frequent iteration between the above positions are usually required to complete the final delivery.

The reason for using PCG is that after game teams significantly improve the production capacity of content raw materials (models, materials, VFX, sound effects...), they also need an efficient means to complete scene construction while considering performance optimization issues.

However, due to the complexity of PCG pipeline design, multi-person collaboration is very, very difficult. Specifically in actual projects, it may require a high-level TA to be responsible for writing PCG logic. This person must not only be proficient in the art production process, supervise the standardization of raw materials, but also take into account the game planner's requirements, respond to changes in a timely manner, and understand the underlying engine to formulate performance optimization strategies.

According to related information, during the development of Unreal Engine's The Matrix: Awakens demo, approximately 20-30 people were responsible for handling assets, and the entire team had 50-70 staff members. This is undoubtedly an absolute feat.

In this demo, we can see the huge potential of PCG: it "easily" built such a magnificent city.

The reason why PCG is difficult to implement can be directly attributed to the fact that many teams can hardly have the same team quality as Epic.

Secondly, the goal of PCG is to summarize and conclude a sustainable iterative production pipeline. But for game products, what attracts players is always content and creativity, which are inevitably unconstrained.

Specifically in project teams, PCG can centralize the responsibilities of multiple positions. It has advantages such as quickly responding to iterations, but also has disadvantages such as limiting the creative play of various personnel, thereby affecting content quality and production capacity.

Unlike PCG, procedural content management is more like a post-processing:

  • It aims to use procedural means to make content organization convergent.

Therefore, this article does not focus on introducing those profound cutting-edge technologies, but focuses on sorting out and integrating a series of common procedural means to manage Objects, Assets, and Worlds in Unreal Engine during the current game content production process.

The reason for using procedural means to manage content, simply put, is:

  • Some operations that seem very "intuitive" are just difficult to do at the editor level.

This dilemma can be illustrated by a short dialogue:

A: Do you know elephants?

B: Of course I do.

A: I'm very curious about what it looks like. Can you draw it?

B: Sorry, I can't draw, so I can't~

The purpose of procedural technology is that we do not directly process specific targets, but describe what we want to do through features, so that the input and process of the operation can have a certain degree of flexibility. It is equivalent to giving such a response:

B: Sorry, although I can't draw an elephant, I can tell you that elephants are very tall, with gray bodies, four thick and strong legs, big ears like palm-leaf fans, long trunks that can roll up things, and two sharp and long teeth. You will definitely recognize it at a glance when you see it later~

For game projects, some heavyweight editors related to content production usually need to be developed and commissioned by professional personnel. But besides that, there are also a large number of trivial micro-requirements in the process of game content production. Although it is unnecessary to arrange professional personnel to develop editor tools for these requirements, without the assistance of editor tools, these tasks will be very difficult to complete. For example:

  • Select all Actors in the coordinate area [X0,Y0 - X1,Y1] and export them as a sub-level for local testing
  • Filter out all light sources with shadows enabled in the scene and check the rationality of their shadows
  • Overview all mesh components, and batch apply certain lighting and culling LOD strategies to components based on the size of the bounding box and other features
  • Overview the bounding box sizes of all scene effects and retrieve whether there are abnormal items in the effect bounding boxes
  • Batch adjust properties of specific components, such as displacement transformation, light switch, physics strategy, rendering properties...
  • Batch modify the switch status of certain properties of assets
  • Batch filter out Actors with specific features and highlight them
  • Collect all static models SM_BigTree0001 in the scene and batch replace them with encapsulated Blueprints BP_BigTree0001, which additionally provides particle effect components for falling leaves and sound effect components for leaf friction for the tree model
  • Batch send rays to a certain area to sample the scene, and save the scene data obtained from ray detection for making special effects
  • Batch preview, sort, search, and edit the Disallow Nanite property of StaticMeshComponent of all StaticMeshActors in the scene
  • Automatically merge static meshes in a certain area into a hierarchical instanced static mesh component
  • ...

These requirements usually appear frequently in the processes of map editing, scene management, asset management, and performance optimization. In small-scale game projects, since content is accumulated gradually, and people usually have the mentality of "cutting it if it doesn't work", there are generally no major problems. But in large-scale game projects, the relationships between contents are intricate. Although PCG technology can alleviate some pressure, if these micro-requirements are not properly solved in a timely manner, content management is also very easy to get out of control:

  • The Witcher 3 - Open World Content Optimization Pipeline: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p8CMYD_5gE8

docs.title: Procedural Content Processing Plugin
docs.text:
There is no doubt that Unreal Engine is currently the most powerful and versatile game engine, which largely benefits from its excellent core structure design. Since our goal is to efficiently manage content in Unreal Engine using procedural means, it is particularly necessary and significant to deeply understand its architecture.

Since expanding this part of the content will take up a lot of space, the author has updated part of the content in the previous basic system document according to the current focus. If you are interested in more details, there are many excellent analysis articles online:

  • Core Architecture: InsideUE - Dazhao
  • Rendering System: Blog Park - Yearning | Analyzing Unreal Rendering System
  • Asset Management: Zhihu - UE4 Resource Management

In addition, it should be reminded that without proper project specifications, even God would shake his head:

  • Unreal Engine Specification Guide: https://github.com/thejinchao/ue5-style-guide

Procedural content processing can usually be summarized into three basic steps:

graph TD
    A(Collection: Collect the objects and data we need by describing features)
    B(Review [Optional]: Review and filter the collected data)
    C(Processing [Optional]: Execute the corresponding operation logic___________)
    A --> B
    B --> C

Based on the above process, the author has built a simple and compact editor framework (ProceduralContentProcessor) to complete these steps. As a toolbox, it can easily derive and extend editor tools with a unified structure. The plugin's Github repository is:

  • https://github.com/Italink/ProceduralContentProcessor

The following text will elaborate on the specific processing steps of each stage based on this plugin.

After placing the plugin in the project's Plugins directory, you can find the Procedural Content Processor Mode in the editor mode of the level editor:

Procedural Content Processor provides three available Blueprint assets, and you can derive Blueprints to extend your own editor modes:

  • ProceduralAssetProcessor: Used to write editor tools related to Asset operations
  • ProceduralWorldProcessor: Used to write editor tools related to World processing
  • ProceduralActorColorationProcessor: Used to write Actor debugging coloring strategies.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
Procedural Content Processor itself does not provide many complex mechanisms; it mostly relies on the engine's native functions.

A key point is:

  • Blueprint functions with CallInEditor (Call in Editor) checked (or C++ functions with the CallInEditor identifier in UFUNCTION) will generate corresponding buttons on the object's details panel. Clicking this button will execute the corresponding function logic:

Taking this as an opportunity, we can easily write a large number of editor tools.

Some options in the Blueprint Class Settings of the procedural content processor will affect the display of the editor outline:

  • Sort Priority: Sort priority, affecting the sorting of the drop-down box in the editor outline.
  • Document Hyperlink: The document link of the processor. Clicking the 【? button】 on the editor outline will open the corresponding URL.
  • Override UMGClass: Use a UMG widget to replace the default details panel, generally used for customizing the editor's UI.
  • Blueprint Display Name: The actual display name of the processor in the editor outline.
  • Blueprint Description: The prompt information of the processor in the editor outline.
  • Blueprint Namespace: The category of the processor in the editor outline. Multi-level categories are separated by ..

Some configurations in the Blueprint properties will affect the details panel:

  • Editable Instance: Only properties with Editable Instance checked can be edited on the object's details panel; otherwise, only the default values can be modified in the Blueprint editor.
  • Read Only Blueprint: When checked, the property will become uneditable but will be previewed.
  • Config Variable: When checked, the value of the property will be stored in the configuration file, and the previous configuration will be read when the processor is started next time.

During editor production, some property identifiers and metadata are very useful, but they are not exposed to the Blueprint editor. Here is a recommended plugin: https://github.com/DoubleDeez/MDMetaDataEditor

The procedural content processor has four basic event functions that can be overridden:

  • void Activate(): Called when the processor is activated.
  • void Tick(DeltaTime): Called every frame after the processor is activated.
  • void Deactivate(): Called when the processor exits.
  • void PostEditChangeProperty(PropertyName): Called when the processor's properties change.

For C++, the following function can be overridden to deeply customize the editor:

  • virtual TSharedPtr<SWidget> BuildWidget()

UE's details panel is very powerful. We can quickly build simple and easy-to-use editors just through properties + functions:
