docs.title: Object Property Matrix
docs.text:
In Unreal Engine, the official provides a Property Matrix function for batch changing certain properties of assets:

Based on this, Procedural Content Processor supports building a property editing matrix for any object (UObject) in a procedural way.

We only need to add a member variable of type Procedural Object Matrix in the Blueprint:

Call the following interfaces in the editor function to construct the object property matrix, which will be displayed on the object's details panel:

  • void ClearObjectMaterix(): Clear the object matrix
  • void AddTextField(Owner, FieldName, FieldValue): Add a simple preview text, meaning that the row {Owner} and column {FieldName} will be filled with {FieldValue}
  • void AddPropertyField(Owner, PropertyName): Add a property editor, meaning that the row {Owner} and column {PropertyName} will be filled with the editor of the 【Owner object's PropertyName property】.
  • void AddPropertyFieldBySecondaryObject(Owner, SecondaryObject, SecondaryObjectPropertyName): Add a property editor, meaning that the row {Owner} and column {SecondaryObjectPropertyName} will be filled with the editor of the 【SecondaryObject's SecondaryObjectPropertyName property】.

Here is an example of its use in the engine:

docs.title: Object Details View
docs.text:
Unreal's details panel can easily edit the properties of any UObject:

But it usually requires explicitly selecting the object. The plugin provides a Blueprint function to display the property panel of any object:

This makes it easy to adjust the properties of some objects, such as UI, runtime sub-objects, temporary objects, etc.

docs.title: Geometry Processing
docs.text:
Recently, I was invited by a friend to team up for the 5th National Artificial Intelligence Competition held in Shenzhen, where we won the third prize. During the competition, I interacted with students from academic backgrounds and learned a lot of knowledge and experience that I wouldn't have encountered in my daily work. The only regret is that I could only participate as a competitor—since I couldn't see the processes and strategies of other teams, it was hard to learn and communicate with other students. Darn it, I originally planned to hand out my resume directly if I met any experts T.T

Getting back to the point, the competition task was:

  • Input a set of images, select specific objects, and reconstruct a high-quality model.

In the early stages, we conducted extensive solution testing for this task. After finalizing our strategy, we divided it into two main phases:

  1. Select specific objects from the images and convert them into models.
  2. Optimize the models to meet industrial production requirements.

Phase 1 was handled by another classmate, and since it involves his research direction, details cannot be disclosed 0.0.

As for the geometry optimization part, which I was responsible for, my initial plan was to use some geometry processing SDKs, such as the ones I've mentioned before:

  • Simplygon - Setting the Standard for 3D Game Content Optimization
  • InstaLOD - Everything You Need to Produce and Automate 3D Content Optimization

However, these SDKs are commercial and environment-bound. Since the competition program needed to be submitted to a virtual environment, these SDKs couldn't be used. While there are some open-source geometry algorithms and libraries, they are often not comprehensive. So I turned my attention to Unreal Engine 0.0. After completing the work, all I can say is:

  • It's amazing!

docs.title: Modeling Tools
docs.text:
I wonder if any of you have used Unreal Engine's Modeling Tools plugin:

It provides a very comprehensive set of geometry processing tools, so I thought: Could I extract these tools and use them independently?

When I actually tried it, I initially focused on the low-level mesh processing interfaces. I found that extracting them wasn't easy, as they essentially share the same underlying layer as another plugin called GeometryScript.

But when I shifted my focus to the Interactive Tools Framework, I discovered that it seemed to have been designed with offline operation in mind from the start, making it surprisingly easy~

Every operation visible on the panel is a UInteractiveTool, and the engine has numerous derived classes:

Among them, the ones related to mesh processing are these:

If we want to perform a Remesh operation on a mesh, we just need to write code like this:

void UMinimalEngineCommandlet::Remesh(UStaticMesh* StaticMesh, int TargetPercentage, float InSmoothingStrength, int MaxRemeshIterations, bool bSplitEdge)
{
    // Create editor tools
    FCommandletEditorModeTools CommandletTools;   

    // Create interactive tool context
    auto InteractiveToolsContext = NewObject<UEditorInteractiveToolsContext>();                  

    // Initialize context
    InteractiveToolsContext->InitializeContextWithEditorModeManager(&CommandletTools, nullptr);   

    // Register transform gizmo
    UE::TransformGizmoUtil::RegisterTransformGizmoContextObject(InteractiveToolsContext);         

    // Create RemeshTool builder
    auto ToolBuilder = NewObject<URemeshToolBuilder>();                                           

    // Register tool type in context with name "MyTool"
    InteractiveToolsContext->ToolManager->RegisterToolType("MyTool", ToolBuilder);  

    // Add target selection factory to context
    InteractiveToolsContext->TargetManager->AddTargetFactory(NewObject<UStaticMeshComponentToolTargetFactory>());  

    // Select MyTool in context
    InteractiveToolsContext->ToolManager->SelectActiveToolType(EToolSide::Left, "MyTool");

    // Create temporary StaticMeshComponent and set its asset to the StaticMesh to modify
    UStaticMeshComponent* StaticMeshComp = NewObject<UStaticMeshComponent>();
    StaticMeshComp->SetStaticMesh(StaticMesh);

    // Select temporary component in editor tools
    CommandletTools.SelectComponents({ StaticMeshComp });

    // Activate left tool (corresponds to MyTool)
    InteractiveToolsContext->ToolManager->ActivateTool(EToolSide::Left);

    // Get activated tool
    if (auto Tool = Cast<URemeshTool>(InteractiveToolsContext->ToolManager->ActiveLeftTool)) {

        // Pass tool runtime parameter configurations
        Tool->SetSettings(TargetPercentage, InSmoothingStrength, MaxRemeshIterations, bSplitEdge);

        // Simulate a render loop
        InteractiveToolsContext->ToolManager->Render(nullptr);

        // Simulate tool task execution loop
        while (!Tool->CanAccept()) {
            Tool->Tick(0.01f);
        }

        // Simulate tool result acceptance request
        Tool->Shutdown(EToolShutdownType::Accept);
    }
}

FCommandletEditorModeTools is a custom-derived class because the editor panel tools use a global singleton:

// UnrealEngine\Engine\Source\Editor\UnrealEd\Private\UnrealEdGlobals.cpp
FEditorModeTools& GLevelEditorModeTools()
{
    checkf(!IsRunningCommandlet(), TEXT("The global mode manager should not be created or accessed in a commandlet environment. Check that your mode or module is not accessing the global mode tools or that scriptable features of modes have been moved to subsystems."));
    if (!ensureMsgf(Internal::EditorModeToolsSingleton.IsValid(), TEXT("The level editor is not started up yet. If you need to access the global mode manager early in the startup phase, please use FLevelEditorModule::OnLevelEditorCreated to gate the access.")))
    {
        Internal::EditorModeToolsSingleton = MakeShared<FEditorModeTools>();
    }
    return *Internal::EditorModeToolsSingleton.Get();
}

For some reasons, it's not allowed to be used in commandlets. So we just need to create a simple derived class—FEditorModeTools essentially only handles selection:

#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "EditorModeManager.h"

class FPreviewScene;
class UWorld;

class FCommandletEditorModeTools : public FEditorModeTools
{
public:
    FCommandletEditorModeTools();
    virtual ~FCommandletEditorModeTools() override;

    // FEditorModeTools interface
    virtual USelection* GetSelectedActors() const override;
    virtual USelection* GetSelectedObjects() const override;
    virtual USelection* GetSelectedComponents() const override;
    virtual UWorld* GetWorld() const override;
    void SelectActors(TArray<AActor*> Actors);
    void SelectComponents(TArray<USceneComponent*> Components);
protected:
    UWorld* CommandletWorld = nullptr;
    USelection* ActorSet = nullptr;
    USelection* ObjectSet = nullptr;
    USelection* ComponentSet = nullptr;
    FPreviewScene* PreviewScene = nullptr;
};

#include "CommandletEditorModeTools.h"
#include "Engine/Selection.h"
#include "PreviewScene.h"
#include "Elements/Framework/TypedElementSelectionSet.h"

FCommandletEditorModeTools::FCommandletEditorModeTools()
{
    CommandletWorld = UWorld::CreateWorld(EWorldType::Editor, true);
    CommandletWorld->AddToRoot();

    UTypedElementSelectionSet* ActorAndComponentsSelectionSet = NewObject<UTypedElementSelectionSet>(GetTransientPackage(), NAME_None, RF_Transactional);
    ActorSet = USelection::CreateActorSelection(GetTransientPackage(), NAME_None, RF_Transactional);
    ActorSet->SetElementSelectionSet(ActorAndComponentsSelectionSet);
    ActorSet->AddToRoot();

    ComponentSet = USelection::CreateComponentSelection(GetTransientPackage(), NAME_None, RF_Transactional);
    ComponentSet->SetElementSelectionSet(ActorAndComponentsSelectionSet);
    ComponentSet->AddToRoot();

    ObjectSet = USelection::CreateObjectSelection(GetTransientPackage(), NAME_None, RF_Transactional);
    ObjectSet->SetElementSelectionSet(NewObject<UTypedElementSelectionSet>(ObjectSet, NAME_None, RF_Transactional));
    ObjectSet->AddToRoot();
}

FCommandletEditorModeTools::~FCommandletEditorModeTools()
{
    if (UObjectInitialized()){
        CommandletWorld->RemoveFromRoot();
        ActorSet->RemoveFromRoot();
        ComponentSet->RemoveFromRoot();
        ObjectSet->RemoveFromRoot();
    }
}

USelection* FCommandletEditorModeTools::GetSelectedActors() const
{
    return ActorSet;
}

USelection* FCommandletEditorModeTools::GetSelectedObjects() const
{
    return ObjectSet;
}

USelection* FCommandletEditorModeTools::GetSelectedComponents() const
{
    return ComponentSet;
}

UWorld* FCommandletEditorModeTools::GetWorld() const
{
    return CommandletWorld;
}

void FCommandletEditorModeTools::SelectActors(TArray<AActor*> Actors)
{
    ActorSet->DeselectAll();
    for (auto Actor : Actors) {
        ActorSet->Select(Actor);
    }
}

void FCommandletEditorModeTools::SelectComponents(TArray<USceneComponent*> Components)
{
    ComponentSet->DeselectAll();
    for (auto Component : Components) {
        ComponentSet->Select(Component);
    }
}

URemeshToolBuilder is not an engine-provided type either—it's a simple derivation of URemeshMeshToolBuilder. Since most variables and functions of URemeshMeshTool are protected, derivation is needed to access them:

UCLASS()
class URemeshToolBuilder : public URemeshMeshToolBuilder
{
    GENERATED_BODY()
public:
    virtual UMultiSelectionMeshEditingTool* CreateNewTool(const FToolBuilderState& SceneState) const override{
        return NewObject<URemeshTool>(SceneState.ToolManager);
    }
};

UCLASS()
class URemeshTool : public URemeshMeshTool
{
    GENERATED_BODY()
public:
    void SetSettings(int TargetPercentage, float InSmoothingStrength = 0.25f, int MaxRemeshIterations = 20, bool bSplitEdge = true){
        this->BasicProperties->SmoothingStrength = InSmoothingStrength;
        this->BasicProperties->MaxRemeshIterations = MaxRemeshIterations;
        this->BasicProperties->TargetTriangleCount *= TargetPercentage / 100.0f;
        this->BasicProperties->bSplits = bSplitEdge;
        this->Preview->InvalidateResult();          // Invalidate current tool result, which reactivates tool task execution
    }
};

The basic usage is similar for other tools, but there are minor considerations when simulating Tick. For example, we manually simulated a render loop above:

InteractiveToolsContext->ToolManager->Render(nullptr);

For some tools, the lack of an actual preview scene may cause crashes. You can remove this line—it usually doesn't affect the result. If it does, you need to complete the tool's input environment. For example, UHoleFillTool requires selecting which holes to fill. You can manually call this before configuring settings:

void UHoleFillTool::SelectAll()

For complex tasks involving asynchronous state updates, besides simulating the tool's Tick, you may need to simulate the engine's Tick. In such cases, you can call the following function:

while (!Tool->CanAccept()) {
    Tool->Tick(0.01f);
    FakeEngineTick(CommandletTools.GetWorld(), 0.01f, 1); 
}

void FakeEngineTick(UWorld* InWorld, float InDelta /*= 0.03f*/, int InCount /*= 1*/)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < InCount; i++) {
        if (IsRunningCommandlet()) {
            GEngine->EmitDynamicResolutionEvent(EDynamicResolutionStateEvent::EndFrame);
            CommandletHelpers::TickEngine(InWorld);
            GEngine->EmitDynamicResolutionEvent(EDynamicResolutionStateEvent::EndFrame);
        }
        else if (FSlateApplication::IsInitialized()) {
            FApp::SetDeltaTime(InDelta);
            bool bIsTicking = FSlateApplication::Get().IsTicking();
            GEngine->EmitDynamicResolutionEvent(EDynamicResolutionStateEvent::EndFrame);
            GEngine->Tick(FApp::GetDeltaTime(), false);
            FSlateApplication::Get().PumpMessages();
            FSlateApplication::Get().Tick();
            GFrameCounter++;

            if (!bIsTicking && GIsRHIInitialized) {
                if (FSceneInterface* Scene = InWorld->Scene) {
                    ENQUEUE_RENDER_COMMAND(BeginFrame)([](FRHICommandListImmediate& RHICmdList) {
                        GFrameNumberRenderThread++;
                        GFrameCounterRenderThread++;
                        FCoreDelegates::OnBeginFrameRT.Broadcast();
                        });

                    ENQUEUE_RENDER_COMMAND(EndFrame)([](FRHICommandListImmediate& RHICmdList) {
                        FCoreDelegates::OnEndFrameRT.Broadcast();
                        RHICmdList.EndFrame();
                        });
                    FlushRenderingCommands();
                }
                ENQUEUE_RENDER_COMMAND(VirtualTextureScalability_Release)([](FRHICommandList& RHICmdList) {
                    GetRendererModule().ReleaseVirtualTexturePendingResources();
                    });
            }

            FTaskGraphInterface::Get().ProcessThreadUntilIdle(ENamedThreads::GameThread);

            FSlateApplication::Get().GetRenderer()->Sync();

            FThreadManager::Get().Tick();

            FTSTicker::GetCoreTicker().Tick(FApp::GetDeltaTime());

            GEngine->TickDeferredCommands();

            GEngine->EmitDynamicResolutionEvent(EDynamicResolutionStateEvent::EndFrame);

            FAssetCompilingManager::Get().FinishAllCompilation();
        }
    }
}

After figuring this out, Unreal Engine becomes a true​神器​ (godsend)!

We can adjust parameters in the editor to visually see the results of each step, quickly refining an optimal strategy. Finally, we encapsulate the refined strategy into a standalone command-line program for the algorithm side to call.

A quick complaint about Unreal's editor module: Since we needed to build a command-line program including (Modeling Plugin -> Interactive Tools Framework -> Editor Module), we created a new engine startup loop and adjusted UBT configurations. However, the default built package had many strange dependencies. Even after some trimming, the final package size was still over 1GB+.

Upon checking, over 400 modules were loaded when entering the engine loop. Looking at the code made me tear up T.T:

  • For example, DmgType is loaded during AWorldSettings construction

  • Also, when registering blueprint types, an entire Sequencer Editor (with huge dependencies) is loaded chain-style:

Some thoughts:

In my work experience, I often encounter tricky performance optimization issues. A common one is:

  • Models from 3D reconstruction or even manual modeling often can't be used directly in the engine—they need to meet certain specifications, which change over time and project scale.

Both model creators and managers are tormented by this problem.

Earlier, I tried building a geometry processing pipeline to address this. While it supported parameterized input, good results often required subjective human judgment.

This was also a weakness in our competition strategy—lack of innovation. It was mostly based on existing algorithms and tools, with most issues being code and engineering-related.

Stepping back from frontline business development and participating in this competition exposed me to many cutting-edge technical directions. For example, 3D reconstruction technology is already very mature, and it feels like it's just one bridge away from real-time rendering. AI is very good at such quantifiable problems.

But—darn it, I don't know how to do it T.T. Interested friends can give it a try~

docs.title: 16.3DGaussianSplatting
docs.text: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a computer graphics technology for real-time radiance field rendering. It has been a hot topic in academic research in recent years and is widely used in the field of 3D reconstruction.

docs.title: 3D Reconstruction Technology
docs.text:
Most technical fields emerge from the combined effects of technological breakthroughs reducing costs, demand upgrades creating markets, academic research providing theories, and industrial transformations expanding scenarios.

Against the backdrop of the current explosion in computer technology, the development of the 3D reconstruction field stems from the urgent demand for 3D information across various industries:

  • Industrial Manufacturing: Upgrading from "Manufacturing" to "Intelligent Manufacturing"

    • Reverse Engineering: Acquire data of existing parts through 3D scanning to quickly reconstruct CAD models, shortening the R&D cycle of new products (e.g., mold design for automotive body panels);

    • Quality Inspection: Compare reconstructed models with design drawings to detect surface defects or assembly errors (e.g., high-precision inspection of aerospace components);

    • Digital Twins: Build 3D virtual models of production lines to monitor equipment status in real time and optimize processes, promoting the implementation of intelligent manufacturing.

  • Medical Health: Precision Medicine and Visualization Revolution

    • 3D Medical Imaging: Generate 3D models of organs and tumors from CT/MRI tomographic images to assist doctors in determining lesion locations and surgical paths (e.g., preoperative planning in neurosurgery);

    • Biomechanical Simulation: Simulate joint movements based on personalized bone models of patients to develop customized prosthetics or rehabilitation plans.

  • Cultural Heritage and Urban Management: Digital Preservation and Smart Governance

    • Cultural Relic Protection and Restoration: High-precision 3D reconstruction (e.g., the digitalization project of the Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang) permanently preserves the details of cultural heritage, providing a basis for virtual restoration of damaged cultural relics;

    • Smart City Modeling: Reconstruct urban building clusters through drone aerial surveys or vehicle-mounted LiDAR to support applications such as traffic planning and disaster simulation (e.g., flood inundation analysis).

  • Entertainment and Interaction: Technical​刚需​ for Immersive Experiences

    • Game and Film Industrialization: Efficient modeling, virtual production, photorealistic rendering, and collaborative production drive the transformation of game and film industrialization toward automated, high-quality, cross-platform collaborative digital production models;

    • VR/AR Interaction: Real-time 3D environment reconstruction is the core of SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping), supporting spatial perception and virtual-real fusion in head-mounted devices such as Meta Quest.

  • ...

For 3D reconstruction algorithms, the industry usually classifies them based on whether the sensor actively emits light to the object:

  • Active: Actively project structured light (e.g., laser, fringe light, coded light) or sound waves onto the object, use sensors to receive signals reflected from the object surface, and finally analyze the signals to obtain 3D information of the object. Common methods include laser scanning, Moiré fringe method, structured light method, ToF (Time of Flight), phase measurement profilometry, etc.
  • Passive: Based on visual geometry principles, collect 2D images of the object through monocular or multi-view cameras, then analyze the images to obtain 3D information of the object. Common methods include stereo vision, SfM+MVS, optical flow method, monocular depth estimation (e.g., deep learning methods), etc.

The main differences between them are as follows:

Dimension Active 3D Reconstruction Passive 3D Reconstruction Hardware Cost High (requires active light source, dedicated sensors) Low (only requires a camera) Precision High (sub-pixel level, suitable for high-precision requirements) Medium-low (depends on texture and viewing angle, suitable for macro scenes) Speed Fast (single frame or few images, suitable for real-time applications) Slow (multi-view matching, requires offline computation) Texture Dependence Low (actively projects texture) High (depends on the object's own texture) Dynamic Adaptability Poor (sensitive to motion) Good (some algorithms can handle dynamic objects in static scenes) Typical Scenarios Industrial inspection, high-precision modeling of cultural relics Consumer-grade scanning, drone surveying, large scene reconstruction

Among them, the development of passive methods is closely related to computer graphics:

  • The 1993 SIGGRAPH paper View interpolation for image synthesis first proposed the concept of multi-view interpolation for image synthesis, defining the view synthesis problem and leading the field of image-based rendering (IBR). At that time, computer graphics rendering was limited by the quality of geometric, lighting, and material input models. IBR provided an alternative method to create new images by combining photorealistic input images. Subsequently, work related to view synthesis and image-based rendering grew rapidly, with classic papers on light field rendering, light field maps, layered depth maps, etc.

  • The 2020 ECCV paper NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis proposed a neural network-based approach that can generate high-quality novel view images from a small number of 2D images, opening a new chapter in 3D reconstruction. NeRF uses a fully connected neural network (multi-layer perceptron, MLP) to represent 3D scenes. It queries 5D coordinates along camera rays and uses volume rendering techniques to project output colors and densities onto images to synthesize views. It also introduces positional encoding to enable the MLP to recover high-frequency functions and produce high-quality results.

  • The 2023 SIGGRAPH paper 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering proposed a scene representation method using 3D Gaussian distributions as graphical primitives. It is an important breakthrough after NeRF, combining rendering efficiency and reconstruction quality, and quickly became a hot topic in academic research.

In the film and game industry, Mesh is usually used as the mainstream rendering carrier for graphics, which has the following prominent features: Primitive (usually triangles) + Texture

This is because the structure of meshes is highly flexible and easy for iterative editing, which makes the development of modern graphics rendering pipelines inseparable from it. A large number of mature toolchains have been derived, forming standardized industry workflows.

However, although the expression method of separating geometric precision and material precision in meshes has many advantages, it also brings many complex problems. For example, meshes usually require manual or algorithmic pre-assumptions about the object's topological structure (e.g., vertex connection relationships, surface types, etc.).

The task of graphics rendering is to convert graphics into images, while 3D reconstruction is its inverse solution process (image -> graphics). Therefore, Point Cloud is used as the basis for data collection and processing. It is easier to record unbiased sampling data of the reconstructed scene and retain original geometric information (e.g., edges, holes, non-manifold structures).

The point cloud shown above is generated using the open-source tool Colmap with SFM (Structure from Motion) + MVS (Multi-View Stereo). We only need to input images from multiple perspectives:

The SFM process will execute the following steps in sequence:

  • Feature Extraction: Load input images and perform preprocessing to extract feature points contained in each image.

  • Feature Matching: Find the same feature points between different images and establish corresponding relationships.

  • Incremental Reconstruction (Mapper): Gradually recover camera poses and sparse point clouds based on matching relationships.

The MVS process further processes the Sparse Point Cloud obtained from SFM to get a Dense Point Cloud, which includes the following steps:

  • Depth Map Estimation (Stereo): Generate a pixel-wise depth map for each input image, i.e., estimate the distance from each pixel-corresponding scene point to the camera.

  • Depth Map Fusion: Merge depth maps from multiple images into a globally consistent dense point cloud, eliminating conflicts and filling holes.

However, for the same graphic structure, point clouds usually have a huge data volume. The original model of the above scene has 4,876 triangles, but after converting to a lower-precision point cloud, it still contains 429,113 points. Therefore, the 3D reconstruction field still needs to consider converting point clouds to meshes. Here are some common methods:

  • Poisson Reconstruction: Treat the point cloud as sampling points of a signed distance function (implicit surface), and extract the isosurface (i.e., mesh surface) by solving the Poisson equation.
  • Moving Least Squares (MLS): Fit the tangent plane of each point through local weighted least squares to generate an implicit surface, then extract the mesh using the Marching Cubes algorithm.
  • Delaunay Triangulation: Generate a triangular mesh in 2D or 3D space by maximizing the empty sphere criterion (Delaunay condition), corresponding to tetrahedral subdivision in 3D scenes.
  • Ball Pivoting Algorithm: Roll a ball of fixed radius on the point cloud surface. The intersection points of the ball and the point cloud form triangles. Adjust the ball radius to control mesh density and details.
  • Marching Cubes Algorithm: For each voxel unit (cube), find predefined isosurface patterns based on whether vertices are inside or outside the surface (determined by distance function or density function) to generate triangles. Common strategies include TSDF (Truncated Signed Distance Function).
  • Deep Learning Methods: Use neural networks to directly predict mesh vertices and topology from point clouds, suitable for automated processing or complex shape reconstruction. Examples include AtlasNet, PointToMesh, Mesh R-CNN, ConvONet, etc.

docs.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting
docs.text:
Academically, 3DGS can be regarded as a transformation and expansion of the traditional SFM + MVS process.

It can use SFM results as input, adopt 3D Gaussian distributions as graphical primitives, and use Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) to approximate the original scene, thereby obtaining high-quality graphic effects. The process looks like this:

A 3D Gaussian primitive takes a 3D spatial point as the center, and its probability density (or radiance intensity) decays exponentially with increasing distance from the center. This may sound abstract, but you can simply imagine a 3D Gaussian distribution as a colored semi-transparent ellipsoid.

Taking the above figure as an example, if the "ellipsoid" does not follow a 3D Gaussian distribution and is opaque, the graphic will look like this:

Then restore transparency and 3D Gaussian distribution in sequence:

This makes it easy to understand what a 3D Gaussian distribution is. Defining a 3D Gaussian point mainly uses the following parameters:

  • Center Position (X, Y, Z): The center position of the Gaussian point in 3D space.
  • Covariance Matrix (Mat3X3): Controls the morphological structure (fatness/thinness) of the Gaussian ellipsoid.
  • Color Parameters (R, G, B): Controls the color of the ellipsoid.
  • Opacity: Controls the opacity of the ellipsoid.

The training process of Gaussian Splatting ultimately generates a *.ply file that actually stores a bunch of such Gaussian points. The overall process can be briefly summarized as:

  • The input process uses a set of point clouds with basic morphological structures (e.g., sparse point clouds obtained from SFM) as the initial positions of Gaussian primitives.
  • During iteration, 3D Gaussian primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane, weights and losses are calculated, and all Gaussian parameters (position, color, covariance, opacity) are updated through backpropagation using stochastic gradient descent.
  • During iteration, the number of Gaussian points is dynamically adjusted, low-contribution primitives are eliminated, and densification is performed in high-error regions.

Considering parameter control and optimization during gradient descent, the covariance matrix and color parameters use alternative expressions. The covariance matrix is decomposed as follows:

  • S is a diagonal scaling matrix, represented by 3 scaling values. Note that during actual training, to keep the scale parameter always positive (since length cannot be negative) and facilitate network optimization, the scale is usually stored in logarithmic form, meaning:
    • The network output / stored in the Ply file is log(scale)
    • When used, the exponential exp(log(scale)) needs to be taken to restore the actual positive scale.
  • R is a rotation matrix, represented by a quaternion.

The color parameters use Spherical Harmonics (SH) instead of directly storing RGB, which allows the color of each Gaussian sphere to change with the viewing direction, showing richer surface reflections and lighting effects, making rendering more realistic.

If the viewing direction is not considered, converting SH to RGB is very simple:

C0 = 0.28209479177387814
def SH2RGB(sh):
    return sh * C0 + 0.5

In addition, for numerical stability, gradient calculation, etc., the opacity is usually not stored directly as normalized opacity but as logits:

  • The network output / stored in the Ply file is logit(opacity)
  • When used, 1.0f / (1.0f + exp(-opacity)) is needed to get the real opacity.

So far, we have understood the input, process, and output of 3D Gaussian Splatting. One reason why 3DGS is so popular is its high rendering efficiency.

Because the 3D Gaussian distribution is differentiable, we use a set of parameters to represent the "ellipsoid" in 3D space. When rendering, it is projected onto the screen space and becomes a 2D ellipse, which still follows a 2D Gaussian distribution. This means we can derive the shape structure of the ellipse in screen/image space based on 3D Gaussian parameters and camera parameters and perform rasterization directly, which can greatly reduce the computational load required for graphic rendering.

However, due to the semi-transparent nature of Gaussian primitives, it is essential to sort them semi-transparently according to the camera during data processing.

Currently, there are three main strategies for rendering 3DGS:

  • diff-gaussian-rasterization: The official 3DGS rasterization library using Cuda.
  • 3DGS.cpp: A 3DGS rasterization library implemented through the Vulkan compute pipeline, referencing the Cuda version.
  • Using the graphics rendering pipeline, the specific steps are: treat Gaussian primitives as planar quadrilaterals at the geometric level, and draw 2D Gaussian distributions in the shading stage. This approach has high versatility, with some open-source references:
    • fast-gaussian-rasterization: A version implemented using Python OpenGL with geometry shaders.
    • splat: A version implemented using C++ OpenGL through instanced rendering.
    • QEngineUtilities: Contains a version implemented using C++ QRhi through instanced rendering.

The above is all about 3DGS. If you are interested in mathematical details, here is a good resource:

  • Comprehensive Overview of Gaussian Splatting: https://medium.com/data-science/a-comprehensive-overview-of-gaussian-splatting-e7d570081362

docs.title: Applications in Unreal Engine
docs.text:
Regarding the application of 3DGS, there is a popular discussion on Zhihu:

  • How much impact will 3DGaussianSplatting technology have? - Zhihu

The UP first learned about 3DGS at the end of 2024 when watching a video on Bilibili:

  • "Reconstructing" a mountain takes only 10 minutes? How can the magical NeRF technology be used! - Film and Television Hurricane

Due to the misleading title, the UP reproduced the process in the video and, after seeing the actual effect, exclaimed that NeRF has great potential! After being slapped in the face, it was discovered that the technology used here was actually 3DGS, not NeRF.

Driven by a potential development requirement, the UP conducted in-depth research on 3DGS:

  • Because the open scene that actually enters the game needs to load a large amount of resources (tens of GB), most games use a Launch/Loading level to delay user operations and start loading in advance. To make this process more seamless, I hope the background of the Launch level is a dynamic bird's-eye view of the entire open scene, somewhat similar to this effect. When loading is complete, it can smoothly transition from the bird's-eye view to the player's view. Therefore, a lightweight visual proxy for the entire scene is needed. Because the actual scene in the engine has huge geometric data and complex material effects, it is difficult to complete using traditional mesh baking simplification, and common image synthesis methods often have some flaws. Therefore, I thought of using 3D reconstruction technology to make this visual proxy.

Compared with traditional graphical primitives, 3DGS has many disadvantages:

  • When expressing graphics with high precision and rich surface effects, the number of Gaussian primitives is similar to or even more than that of triangles.
  • Due to the semi-transparent nature of Gaussian primitives, some culling optimization methods become ineffective, and the primitives need to be sorted semi-transparently during rendering.
  • Gaussian point clouds are not aligned to the model surface and are discontinuous, containing only color features, which makes it difficult to achieve the lighting effects of graphics or only work in a high-loss way.

These disadvantages are essentially determined by the mathematical properties of Gaussian distribution and gradient descent optimization strategy. Although the academic community has conducted extensive exploration on these issues, many people still criticize 3DGS as only useful for writing papers.

Returning to the industry, computer graphics technology has undergone revolutionary evolution in recent decades, from early polygon modeling to today's next-generation rendering. Breakthroughs in precision, efficiency, and realism have directly shaped the evolution of gaming experiences:

This is not only due to the rapid development of hardware devices but also inseparable from the wide application of three core computer technologies in the gaming process:

  • LOD (Level of Detail): "Hierarchical Response, Dynamic Adaptation"
    • Dynamically adjust processing precision according to the Significance of the target object, finding the optimal balance between resource consumption and effect.
  • Culling: "Targeted Filtering, Precise Focus"
    • Quickly identify and exclude elements that do not need to be processed through preset rules, reducing system redundant overhead.
  • Streaming: "On-Demand Acquisition, Real-Time Scheduling"
    • Treat resources as continuous data streams, dynamically loading/unloading according to real-time needs, thereby breaking through physical resource limitations.

As developers pursue higher game graphics and complex logic, to break through the limitations of hardware devices and optimize existing software technology solutions, another technology has emerged — Imposter:

  • A general methodology to achieve system optimization through abstract substitution, whose core is using a sufficiently good simplified model to replace complex originals in a specific context.

This idea spans multiple fields such as graphics, distributed systems, and AI, becoming a key tool for building high-performance, elastic systems.

Imposter technology continues to find the optimal solution between "limited resources" and "unlimited experience", becoming an invisible accelerator for modern game development. It usually brings significant reductions in computational load and memory usage, which is very important for real-time graphics systems. Here are some applications of Imposter technology in the game industry:

  • LOD Optimization: Use Billboard, Flipbook, Mesh Cards, Octahedron, etc., to generate Imposters of static models, reducing the rendering overhead of distant objects.

  • Crowd Optimization: Degrade non-critical NPCs in the distance (e.g., distant passersby) into static instanced meshes, and bake skeletal animations into textures to achieve dense crowd effects.

  • Culling Optimization: Use low-polygon Imposters instead of bounding boxes to build a specialized GPU occlusion culling pipeline, improving occlusion culling efficiency.

  • Shadow Optimization: Pre-bake the self-shadow of graphic objects, use Imposters to generate the cast shadow of the instance, thereby greatly reducing the execution overhead of the shadow process.
  • ...

3DGS is likely another derivative of the Imposter scheme in LOD optimization.

In the traditional LOD production process, the industry generally uses simplification to generate model LODs:

Usually, a simplification rate of 50% can better balance performance and viewing quality, but this strategy does not yield ideal results for models with complex detail features and irregular geometric shapes.

For example, a model with one million triangles usually requires 14 levels of LOD if we follow a 50% simplification efficiency, which obviously generates a large amount of data and high LOD scheduling overhead. To limit the number of LODs to within 8, the simplification efficiency must be increased to 75%, like this:

To ensure smoother visual changes when switching LODs, the interval between LOD chains must be increased, which will significantly increase the operating overhead of the entire graphics system.

Therefore, introducing Imposter can solve this problem well. Common Imposter strategies include:

  • Billboard: Render the model from a specific angle onto a texture.
  • Flipbook: Render the model from multiple angles onto a texture, and finally switch the displayed texture according to the player's viewing angle in the material.
  • Billboard Cloud/ Mesh Card Cloud: Render the model on many mesh cards to stack a viewing effect similar to the source model.
  • Octahedron: Render the model with a certain viewing angle distribution onto a texture, and finally interpolate images from multiple angles in the material to present a reliable viewing angle transition effect.

For a comparison of these strategies, it was briefly mentioned in the previous article on vegetation optimization. See:

  • https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/713731229

These strategies have different advantages and disadvantages and are suitable for different usage requirements. Although they can significantly reduce performance overhead, they are usually only suitable for single models with relatively "symmetrical" structures. For complex combined models like this, the effect is somewhat unsatisfactory:

The 3DGS process itself approximates the original image through gradient descent. Although at high precision, the number of GS is easily more than the number of triangles in the original mesh, at low precision, compared with traditional optimization methods, the more complex the model, the better the fitting effect of 3DGS and the higher the cost performance:

Gaussian point clouds have another advantage over meshes:

  • Gaussian point clouds are discontinuous feature points, unlike triangles that require continuous topology.

Therefore, the LOD scheme for Gaussian point clouds is very easy to implement. You only need to sort the Gaussian points according to the importance of features, and dynamically scale the Gaussian points that need to be drawn in the current viewport through GPU scheduling when finally displaying.

With these theoretical supports, the UP made some engineering attempts. Although the process was a bit difficult, interested friends can download and try it:

  • https://github.com/Italink/Cosmos/releases/tag/v0.0.1
Project Scene Size Content Size 3DGS Size (Uncompressed) 3DGS Size (Compressed) Frame Rate/GPU Time (5090D 4K) Frame Rate/GPU Time (3060 Laptop 1K) Generation Time (7950X+5090D) City Sample 16 km² 64.8 GB 0.69GB 46.6 MB 326 FPS / 1.97 ms 112 FPS / 7.51ms 30+ hours Project Titan 64 km² 49.4 GB 1.78 GB 115.1 MB 294 FPS / 2.48 ms 104 FPS / 7.93 ms 80+ hours

Thanks to Unreal Engine's highly optimized rendering architecture, after implementing this Gaussian rendering mechanism, the rendering performance of the overall system is not as bad as imagined. More importantly, compared with traditional open scene construction schemes, 3DGS has very strong versatility, which is of great value for scene management.

In fact, the current implementation still has a lot of room for optimization:

  • 3DGS training requires a point cloud with basic geometric shapes as input, which currently comes from Colmap's SFM reconstruction. Since the graphics themselves are known to the engine, the Colmap stage can be bypassed to generate point clouds directly.

  • The LOD effect focuses more on the edges and corners of the graphics, which can be used to optimize the densification path of 3DGS.

  • Although the Niagara implementation has good versatility, state management, memory scheduling, and rendering paths are not optimal.

  • Currently, the open-source Spz compression algorithm is used on the CPU with a compression ratio of about 10x, but there are some compression schemes using Cuda in the academic community that can achieve a compression ratio close to 100x.

Due to limited personal energy, if you are interested in these functions, you can try them yourself. The plugin is now fully open source:

  • Github | Gaussian Splatting For Unreal Engine - Italink

Development is not easy. If this plugin helps you, please give it a Star 0.0:

The functions of the corresponding file structure in the plugin directory are as follows:

  • Content: UE assets related to 3DGS. The current asset version is 5.5.4.

  • Scripts: Auxiliary scripts for calling Colmap and 3DGS algorithms.

  • Source:

    • GaussianSplattingRuntime: Runtime module.

      • GaussianSplattingPointCloud: Custom UE asset containing the structure of 3DGS point clouds.
      • AGaussianSplattingPointCloudActor: Reserved GSActor base class.
      • GaussianSplattingPointCloudDataInterface: Niagara data interface for submitting GaussianSplattingPointCloud data to the GPU for use by the particle system.
      • Spz: 3D GS compression algorithm, derived from https://github.com/nianticlabs/spz

    • GaussianSplattingEditor: Editor module, not involved in final packaging.

      • GaussianSplattingEditorLibrary: Function interface related to 3DGS processing.
      • GaussianSplattingEditorSettings: Plugin-related configuration.
      • GaussianSplattingHLODBuilder: HLOD builder using 3DGS.
      • Editor mode related (left toolbar panel):
        • GaussianSplattingEdMode
        • SGaussianSplattingEdModePanel: UI panel of EdMode.
        • GaussianSplattingStep: Core logic of EdMode.
      • Asset editor related:
        • GaussianSplattingPointCloudEditor
        • SGaussianSplattingPointCloudEditorViewport
        • SGaussianSplattingPointCloudEditorViewportClient
        • SGaussianSplattingPointCloudFeatureEditor

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
As a fundamental graphical element in modern games, Landscape has become increasingly complex with the growing sophistication of graphics engineering and the "younger" composition of R&D teams. Focusing solely on effect implementation and editor usage while ignoring critical details can​埋​下​ significant hidden issues. This article aims to address these aspects.

In most graphics projects, the most widely used graphical element is undoubtedly the Static Mesh, which uses vertex geometry data (spatial coordinates, UVs, normals...) combined with material textures to render graphical effects:

Static Meshes play a pivotal role in modern game development, serving as the basic unit for constructing game world geometry. Professional modeling software (such as 3dsMax, Maya, Blender, Zbrush) provides designers with great convenience and freedom to quickly create their desired graphical effects.

In contrast, Landscape is a more specialized graphical element that does not directly use triangular vertex data like Static Meshes. Instead, it relies on heightmaps:

This image is generated by https://manticorp.github.io/unrealheightmap

Each pixel in the heightmap corresponds to an actual vertex coordinate, with the following mapping relationship:

  • Pixel coordinates (XY) > Vertex horizontal coordinates (XY)
  • Pixel grayscale value > Vertex height (Z)

A heightmap can be regarded as a 2D numerical array, where the basic element type is typically a 16-bit unsigned integer. The corresponding C++ structure is:

uint16_t HeightMap[Height][Width];

Actual conversion rules may vary slightly between software. Unreal Engine uses centimeters (cm) as its base unit, with the following conversion rules:

  • Vertex horizontal coordinates are directly converted from pixel coordinates. Without any scaling, the minimum horizontal precision of UE Landscape is 1 cm.
  • Pixel grayscale values are stored as 16-bit unsigned integers, meaning they can distinguish 65536 different height levels. UE does not directly map this to cm; instead, it remaps the values to the floating-point range [-256.0, 255.992]. This means that without any scaling, the vertical height range representable by UE Landscape is -256.0 cm ~ 255.992 cm, with a minimum height precision of 0.0078125 cm.

Given the above, some readers may have the following question:

  • Static Meshes offer high precision and freedom for achieving the same graphical effects, while Landscape has many limitations. Why do we still use Landscape?

In fact, the use of Landscape essentially involves a trade-off between scene scale and high precision.

First, let's discuss the disadvantages of Landscape:

  • Limited horizontal precision: For example, the maximum heightmap size supported by UE5 non-WP maps is 8129. Without scaling, this means the horizontal width it can represent is 81.29 m. To represent a larger area (e.g., stretching by 100x to cover 66.08 km), the minimum horizontal precision becomes 1 m, meaning any geometric details smaller than 1 m will be lost.
  • Limited height range: Without scaling, the height range is -256.0 cm ~ 255.992 cm. To represent a 2000 m mountain, the height must be stretched by 1000x, reducing the minimum height precision to 7.8125 cm and introducing at least a 7 cm error in collision calculations.
  • Single topology: Landscape is essentially a "continuous heightfield grid" that only supports "single-layer undulations" and cannot achieve complex topologies like Static Meshes (e.g., floating platforms, intersecting terrain, underground caves).
  • Coarse editing granularity: Landscape editing relies on "brush painting" (e.g., raising, lowering, smoothing), making it difficult to precisely control individual bumps or depressions through "vertex-level editing" like Static Meshes.
  • Complex collaborative development: Heightmaps and weightmaps are single files, so simultaneous editing by multiple people can cause data overwrites, requiring strict management via version control tools.

Despite these drawbacks, Landscape remains the only solution for large-scale scenes under current hardware constraints.

For example, to build a 1 km² scene with a grid plane and ensure an average geometric precision of 10 cm × 10 cm (already a low precision), we would need 100 million (10000×10000) triangular vertices. A single vertex in UE5 Static Meshes typically occupies 28 bytes (position: 12 + tangent X: 4 + tangent Z: 4 + UV: 8), so the uncompressed space required for the entire terrain mesh would be approximately:

  • 28 x 10000 x 10000 ÷ 1024³ ≈ 2.61 GB

This is just geometric data. Without using Tiled Textures, a 10 cm texel precision would clearly fail to ensure visual quality (resulting in blurriness or pixelation). To guarantee "close-up visual clarity" (e.g., 1 texel per 1 cm × 1 cm of ground), the total number of texture pixels would reach 10 billion. Using 4 channels (ARGB_8888) for color representation, the uncompressed space required would be approximately:

  • 4 x 100000 x 100000 ÷ 1024³ ≈ 37.25 GB

And this is just for a 1 km² scene!

In my recent experience, many teams (not just in the game industry) lack a deep understanding of the data scale of graphics scenes. Especially from the perspective of planners/product managers, open scenes are simply about "filling the scene with enough elements to make it larger."

Against this backdrop, Landscape is almost an inevitable choice when building larger scenes. Beyond the disadvantages mentioned above, it also has several notable advantages:

  • Memory efficiency: Each Landscape vertex requires only 4 bytes (RG channels for height, BA channels for compressed normals), while Static Meshes typically consume 6 to 7 times more memory.
  • Textures: Landscape uses "world-space mapping independent of height." Regardless of how the terrain undulates (raised, flattened, or mountainous), the texture tiling precision remains unchanged, making it easy to use tiled textures. This is difficult for Static Meshes, as modifying the model shape (e.g., changing flat ground to a slope) stretches the texture with the model. Additionally, Static Mesh details rely heavily on texture and UV precision, while Landscape can overlay multiple texture layers (e.g., detail textures, slope textures) on tiled textures to improve depth.
  • LOD: Landscape LOD uses "dynamic simplification based on heightfields." The GPU automatically switches to lower-resolution texture Mip levels via Mipmaps, ensuring rendering efficiency at a distance while avoiding texture stretching. Static Mesh LOD requires creating independent low-precision models for each level.
  • Collision: Landscape uses generated Heightfield Colliders that support destructibility. Their data structure makes collision calculations far more efficient than mesh collision, and their gap-free nature provides better protection against collision penetration than Static Meshes.
  • Workflow: In game engines, Landscape is treated as a basic graphical carrier, with numerous tools and workflows built around it (e.g., vegetation systems, procedural generation of terrain attachments, light baking).

The official documentation provides detailed instructions on using Landscape, covering concepts, LOD, and collision management:

  • https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/landscape-outdoor-terrain-in-unreal-engine

For an in-depth analysis of Landscape principles, refer to this article:

  • Unreal Engine Landscape System Principle and Source Code Analysis - MarsZhou: https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/668278748

docs.title: Planning
docs.text: For actual game projects, understanding Landscape implementation principles and tool usage is often insufficient. Planning should be established during early design.

docs.title: Define Scene Scale
docs.text:
Scene size determines the volume of game content to some extent. Taking the UE standard character as an example (default movement speed: 600 cm/s), moving 1000 m takes 2 minutes and 46 seconds. Use this to estimate the required scene scale based on actual game content.

When the scene size exceeds 1 km² and contains numerous GameObjects, consider using World Partition to organize scene streaming.

Note that for very large playable areas (e.g., 64 km²), avoid using a single Landscape for the entire scene. Excessively large scenes significantly increase asset management, map editing, gameplay, and level design complexity, severely slowing project iteration.

While UE WP maps currently support a maximum Landscape size of 65281, it is recommended that individual Landscape sizes do not exceed 4 km². Iterate on game content in independent sub-levels, with a main map responsible for connecting sub-maps via elements like oceans, rivers, or mountains:

After UE 5.4, many issues with Level Instances have been effectively resolved, enabling this workflow. The following sections focus on individual Landscape tiles.

docs.title: Determine Resolution
docs.text:
After defining the scale of a single Landscape, determine the minimum geometric precision. A horizontal precision of 1 m typically suffices for RPG projects. To add surface details, use the following methods:

  • Normal Map: Modify surface normal directions to affect light reflection, making flat terrain appear to have​凹凸​ details.
  • Parallax Occlusion Mapping: Calculate "virtual depth offsets" for pixels to give textures apparent thickness, creating a more three-dimensional effect than normal maps.
  • Displacement Mapping: Leverage Nanite and tessellation technology to achieve true geometric​凸起​ (modify pixel-level height) via displacement maps.
  • Terrain Attachments: Place Static Meshes and decals on the terrain surface to add details. Pay attention to collision performance impacts.

Define the vertical depth early, as modifying it later after extensive content iteration is cumbersome. Additionally, avoid over-stretching the Z-axis to ensure collision precision. For tall mountains, consider using Static Meshes for filling.

docs.title: Balance Streaming Proxies, Components, and Sections
docs.text:
The core structure corresponding to UE Landscape is ALandscape, which manages global data and component hierarchy, including holding basic resources like heightmaps and weightmaps, and controlling overall properties (e.g., physics settings, global LOD parameters).

To divide ALandscape responsibilities and enable finer-grained LOD management, visibility checks, DrawCalls, collision detection, and material management, the Landscape system introduces Landscape Components (ULandscapeComponent) and Sections.

Suppose we assign all fine-grained functions to Landscape Components without introducing Sections, using a 2017×2017 resolution heightmap to build a 4 km² scene. Component division faces a dilemma:

  • Few components (e.g., 1 component covering 4 km²): Large vertex data per component makes frustum culling unable to precisely exclude "invisible areas." LOD switching can only be done "globally" (e.g., switching the entire component from LOD0 to LOD3 at a distance, causing significant detail loss). Collision calculations must process full data, reducing efficiency.
  • Many components (e.g., 100 components covering 4 km²): While enabling precise culling and LOD switching, component scheduling (loading/unloading), DrawCall submission, and collider filtering introduce additional overhead, reducing frame rates.

To resolve this, the UE Landscape system introduces Sections—not a further division of components, but a way to handle fine-grained DrawCalls, LOD, culling, and collision within components. This allows merging component responsibilities to balance reducing component count and fine-grained management.

Streaming Proxies (ALandscapeStreamingProxy) are a new concept introduced in UE5 World Partition. Since World Partition streams at the Actor level (not Component), streaming proxies divide ULandscapeComponents originally attached to ALandscape into different streaming proxies. A streaming proxy can contain one or more Landscape Components, with division based on the project's desired streaming granularity.

Notably, streaming proxies have reduced the importance of Sections. In early projects, Landscape Components were typically fully loaded, with optimization via culling, so Sections helped reduce components.

With World Partition Streaming, combined with HLOD merging, component count can be reduced while significantly optimizing merged geometry and texture data. Thus, Sections have minimal value for WP maps.

In summary, the relationships between Landscape-related structures are as follows:

Hierarchical Object Core Responsibilities Dependencies Landscape (ALandscape) Manages global data (heightmaps/weightmaps) and unified scheduling Contains 1 or more streaming proxies (WP maps) Streaming Proxy Minimum streaming unit for WP,​承载​ Landscape Components Contains 1 or more Landscape Components Landscape Component Manages local data copies (e.g., 100 m×100 m areas) and materials (layer parsing, physical materials, holes) Can be divided into multiple Sections Section Handles DrawCalls, LOD, fine-grained culling, and collision calculations Belongs to a single Landscape Component

docs.title: Define Scene Ecological Structure
docs.text:
Landscape consists of heightmaps and weightmaps. Heightmaps describe geometric shape, while weightmaps control material expression.

Most artists have misunderstandings about layer management:

  • One-to-one binding of material effects to layers

In practice, artists often add layers based on effect requirements (e.g., adding a Grass layer for grass, a Snow layer for snow, followed by Gravel, Dirt, Rock, Mud, Water, Path...). To transition to another scene style, they continue adding materials and layers...

This incorrect approach leads to the following issues:

  • Limited effects: Landscape weight layers have a maximum count (8 in UE4, 16 in UE5).
  • Poor performance: Excessive weightmap sampling severely degrades Landscape material rendering performance.

The correct approach is to clarify the relationship between weight layers and Landscape materials:

  • Weight layers are not one-to-one with materials. Landscape materials essentially act as resolvers for weight data. An ALandscape is not limited to one material; the minimum granularity for material management is the Landscape Component (ULandscapeComponent).

For example, to achieve an effect where each numbered area has specific colors, vegetation, and physical materials, the incorrect approach would use 4 Landscape layers. However, the correct approach uses only 1 layer, with each Landscape Component having its own material:

UE5 non-WP maps do not expose Landscape Component editing entries; editing requires C++ access. WP map ALandscapeStreamingProxies also manage component properties in batches via specialized property panels, which is why misuse is common.

Thus, when managing Landscape layers, divide them based on ecological structure (not material effects). Use different materials to parse layers for different ecological communities, avoiding excessive layers and optimizing rendering overhead.

Since this workflow has a high entry barrier, develop corresponding toolchains to simplify iteration.

docs.title: LOD, Nanite, RVT, HLOD
docs.text:
Landscape LOD strategies can be adjusted in the ALandscape property panel.

UE5 now supports Nanite Landscape, which offers higher culling efficiency and geometric detail. Combined with VSM, Nanite typically outperforms LOD in rendering performance on mid-to-high-end hardware.

Since Nanite's geometry processing path is incompatible with RVT sampling, Nanite meshes usually do not support RVT writing. However, because Landscape retains original heightmap and weightmap data, the engine submits RVT rendering data via non-Nanite auxiliary channels:

  • https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/using-nanite-with-landscapes-in-unreal-engine

The latest UE5 version has adjusted the Landscape HLOD generation strategy, implemented in ULandscapeHLODBuilder:

  • Merge all Landscape Components in an ALandscapeStreamingProxy (selecting one LOD level) into a ULandscapeMeshProxyComponent (inheriting from UStaticMeshComponent).

This approach is inefficient, as it equates streaming granularity with batching granularity. For example, if a Landscape Component is 100 m in size, the streaming proxy range might need to be 200 m (containing 4 components) to allow HLOD merging, significantly increasing streaming costs. A better approach would be one streaming proxy per component, with actual batching based on mesh division granularity.

Landscape HLOD materials do not require re-baking textures. In practice, projects often use RVT on Landscape and enable SVT for RVT to store low-level Mip levels. Thus, the HLOD material can be specified directly in ALandscape via HLOD Material Override.

Therefore, Landscape HLOD materials do not need texture inputs; they can directly sample the RVT SVT:

RVT is widely used in Landscape. For example, distant surface details (e.g., decals, grass) can be baked into the RVT SVT to ensure HLOD material quality at a distance.

Writing height to RVT is useful for effects like:

  • Rain, snow, water flow: Dynamically control natural effect distribution based on terrain height (elevation) and normal direction (slope).
  • Footprints/stepping effects: Generate footprints matching terrain undulations at character contact points.
  • Explosion/impact marks: Generate dents or scorch marks matching the terrain contour at explosion points.
  • Fog/smoke distribution: Control fog density using terrain height and slope to simulate valley fog or climbing fog.
  • Ground wet/dry transitions: Simulate post-rain drying based on terrain drainage (slope).

For steps to enable SVT for Landscape RVT, refer to:

  • https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/zh-cn/unreal-engine/runtime-virtual-texturing-in-unreal-engine

Note: The article mentions selecting the Use Streaming Low Mips in Editor property in the RVT volume Details panel. In the latest engine version, this property has been renamed to View In Editor. Ensure it is enabled; otherwise, RVT will not read SVT data in the editor.

docs.title: Underlying Interfaces
docs.text:
After reading this, you might think, "Wow, Landscape has so many considerations! What if my project is already in trouble?" Don't worry—there's a solution!

While UE Landscape scheduling and management seem complex, they essentially process underlying textures. Bypassing the UE editor to directly manipulate these images offers great freedom.

Heightmap and weightmap management are unified in ULandscapeInfo, which can be obtained as follows:

ULandscapeInfo* LandscapeInfo = LandscapeActor->GetLandscapeInfo();

The UE heightmap structure is EditLayers, supporting multiple heightmap overlays. Import/export operations are as follows:

void ExportAllEditLayers(ALandscape* LandscapeActor, FString OutputDir){
    ULandscapeInfo* LandscapeInfo = LandscapeActor->GetLandscapeInfo();
    for (int i = 0; i < LandscapeActor->GetLayerCount(); i++) {
        const FLandscapeLayer* Layer = LandscapeActor->GetLayerConst(i);
        FString ExportFilename = FString::Printf(
            TEXT("%s_%s.%s"),
            *Filename,
            *Layer->Name.ToString().Replace(TEXT(" "), TEXT("_")),
            *Extension
        );
        FScopedSetLandscapeEditingLayer Scope(LandscapeActor, Layer->Guid);             // Set the current editing height layer in context
        LandscapeInfo->ExportHeightmap(FPaths::Combine(OutputDir, ExportFilename));     // Export the current height layer
    }
}

void ImportSingleEditLayer(ALandscape* LandscapeActor, int LayerIndex, FString ImportFilename){
    ULandscapeInfo* LandscapeInfo = LandscapeActor->GetLandscapeInfo();
    const FLandscapeLayer* Layer = LandscapeActor->GetLayerConst(LayerIndex);
    FImage Image;
    FImageUtils::LoadImage(*ImportFilename, Image);
    if (Image.Format != ERawImageFormat::Type::G16) {                                   // Only G16 format is supported
        return;
    }
    FIntRect TargetResolution;
    LandscapeInfo->GetLandscapeExtent(TargetResolution);
    if (Image.SizeX != TargetResolution.Width() + 1 || Image.SizeY != TargetResolution.Height() + 1) {
        FImage ScaledImage;                                                             // Resize the imported image to the terrain resolution
        Image.ResizeTo(ScaledImage, 
                       TargetResolution.Width() + 1,
                       TargetResolution.Height() + 1, 
                       ERawImageFormat::Type::G16, 
                       Image.GammaSpace);
        Image = ScaledImage;
    }
    FScopedSetLandscapeEditingLayer Scope(LandscapeActor, Layer->Guid, [&] {
        LandscapeActor->RequestLayersContentUpdate(ELandscapeLayerUpdateMode::Update_Heightmap_All);
    });
    FHeightmapAccessor<false> HeightmapAccessor(LandscapeInfo);
    HeightmapAccessor.SetData(TargetResolution.Min.X,
                              TargetResolution.Min.Y, 
                              TargetResolution.Max.X, 
                              TargetResolution.Max.Y, 
                              (uint16*)Image.RawData.GetData());
}

The weightmap structure is TargetLayers, with simpler operations than heightmaps. Here is pseudocode:

ULandscapeInfo* LandscapeInfo = LandscapeActor->GetLandscapeInfo();
FIntRect TargetResolution;
LandscapeInfo->GetLandscapeExtent(TargetResolution);

for (auto Layer : LandscapeInfo->Layers) {
    // Export
    LandscapeInfo->ExportLayer(Layer.LayerInfoObj, ExportFilename);

    // Import
    FAlphamapAccessor<false, false> AlphamapAccessor(Landscape->GetLandscapeInfo(), Layer.LayerObject);
    AlphamapAccessor.SetData(TargetResolution.Min.X,
                             TargetResolution.Min.Y, 
                             TargetResolution.Max.X,
                             TargetResolution.Max.Y, Data.GetData(),    // Data format is uint8
                             ELandscapeLayerPaintingRestriction::None);
}

These interfaces allow extracting core data from UE, processing it with more flexible tools (e.g., Photoshop, Houdini), and reimporting it into Unreal Engine.

docs.title: 18.​开放​世界
docs.text:
Mobile Game Performance White Paper: https://blog.uwa4d.com/archives/BlueBook_2023.html

In the field of software engineering, there is a very classic saying — "Premature optimization is the root of all evil"

docs.title: 2.​插件​开发
docs.text:
Plugins exist independently of the engine and project code. They are the primary way to extend program functionality in UE.

Essentially, a plugin is a modular code design. Following this design reduces dependencies between code modules, making subsequent iterations and maintenance easier.

The standard file structure of a plugin in UE is as follows:

  • Binaries: Stores compiled output files
  • Content: Stores the plugin's asset content
  • Intermediate: Stores intermediate files generated during compilation
  • Resources: Stores the plugin's resource files (e.g., icons) that are not UE assets

  • Source: Stores source code files and can contain multiple Modules

  • *.uplugin: The plugin's structural organization file

The basic content of *.uplugin is as follows:

{
    "FileVersion": 3,               // File version
    "Version": 1,                   // Version number
    "VersionName": "1.0",           // Version name
    "FriendlyName": "CustomPlugin", // Alias
    "Description": "",              // Description
    "Category": "Other",            // Category
    "CreatedBy": "",                // Author
    "CreatedByURL": "",             // Author URL
    "DocsURL": "",                  // Documentation URL
    "MarketplaceURL": "",           // Marketplace URL
    "SupportURL": "",               // Support URL
    "CanContainContent": false,     // Whether to include content directory
    "IsBetaVersion": false,         // Whether it is a beta version
    "IsExperimentalVersion": false, // Whether it is an experimental version
    "Installed": false,             // Whether it is embedded
    "Modules": [                    // Module definitions
        {
            "Name": "CustomPlugin",     // Module name
            "Type": "Editor",           // Module type
            "LoadingPhase": "Default"   // Loading phase
        }
        //,                             // Other modules
        //{
        //  ...    
        //}
    ]
}

For configuration of these parameters, see:

  • https://docs.unrealengine.com/5.2/en-US/unreal-engine-modules

The common workflow for developing plugins in UE is:

  • Click Edit - Plugins to open the plugin panel

  • Add a new plugin

  • Create a blank plugin

  • Since the project structure has changed, you need to regenerate the IDE project files at this point

A blank plugin is a good starting point. Other plugin templates just add some​附带​ code templates. If you are not familiar with them, you can try adding them to see what specific code is added. Once you understand their functions, you can add the required code to the blank plugin.

These are the necessary files in a C++ plugin:

// MyPlugin.h

#pragma once

#include "CoreMinimal.h"
#include "Modules/ModuleManager.h"

class FMyPluginModule : public IModuleInterface
{
public:

    /** IModuleInterface implementation */
    virtual void StartupModule() override;
    virtual void ShutdownModule() override;
};

// MyPlugin.cpp

#include "MyPlugin.h"

#define LOCTEXT_NAMESPACE "FMyPluginModule"

void FMyPluginModule::StartupModule()
{
    // This code will execute after your module is loaded into memory; the exact timing is specified in the .uplugin file per-module
}

void FMyPluginModule::ShutdownModule()
{
    // This function may be called during shutdown to clean up your module.  For modules that support dynamic reloading,
    // we call this function before unloading the module.
}

#undef LOCTEXT_NAMESPACE

IMPLEMENT_MODULE(FMyPluginModule, MyPlugin)     // Define plugin entry point

UE calls StartupModule() when loading the plugin and ShutdownModule() when unloading the plugin.

The code workflow for plugin development is mainly:

  • In StartupModule(), call core module function interfaces or use core module global singletons to perform operations, or mount some logic to core module entry points for extensions.
  • In ShutdownModule(), clean up the operations performed in StartupModule().

Some common function modules include:

  • FFileHelper: File operations
  • FPlatformProcess: Platform-related operations
  • FBlueprintEditorUtils: Blueprint operations
  • FKismetEditorUtilities: Editor operations
  • FEdGraphUtilities: Graph operations
  • FComponentEditorUtils: Component editor operations
  • FEnumEditorUtils: Enum operations
  • FStructureEditorUtils: Structure operations
  • FEditorFolderUtils: Editor folder operations
  • FMaterialEditorUtilities: Material operations
  • FPluginUtils: Plugin operations
  • UGameplayStatics: Gameplay-related operations
  • ...

Global singletons include:

  • GEngine, GEditor, GWorld: Common global singletons in the engine
  • FModuleManager::LoadModuleChecked<FAssetToolsModule>("AssetTools").Get(): Asset creation, deletion, renaming, import/export...
  • FModuleManager::LoadModuleChecked<FAssetRegistryModule>(TEXT("AssetRegistry")).Get(): Asset search, enumeration...
  • FModuleManager::LoadModuleChecked<ISettingsModule>("Settings"): Configuration file management
  • FModuleManager::LoadModuleChecked<FPropertyEditorModule>("PropertyEditor"): Property editor operations
  • FModuleManager::LoadModuleChecked<FLevelEditorModule>(TEXT("LevelEditor")): Level editor operations
  • FModuleManager::LoadModuleChecked<FBlueprintEditorModule>("Kismet"): Blueprint editor operations
  • ...

Core module entry points generally refer to:

  • Callback function callbacks
  • Delegate

Common delegate definition collections include:

  • FCoreUObjectDelegates: UObject-related delegates

  • FCoreDelegates: Core module-related delegates

  • FEditorDelegates: Editor module-related delegates

  • FWorldDelegates: Game world-related delegates

  • FGameDelegates
  • ...

When you finish writing the plugin and execute compilation, the following files will be generated in the plugin's Binaries directory:

  • *.module: Defines basic information about the module library
  • *.dll: Dynamic library
  • *.pdb: Program database for source-level breakpoint debugging of the library. See here for details.

The content of the *.module file is as follows:

{
    "BuildId": "a36b278a-b317-44c3-8743-b82361b74343",
    "Modules": 
    {
        "MyPlugin": "UnrealEditor-MyPlugin.dll"
    }
}

docs.title: Menu Bar and Toolbar Extension
docs.text:
During engine development, there are often requirements to extend the engine editor's menu bar and toolbar by adding a button to perform some convenient operations, like this:

In UE4, the main way to extend menus is through FExtender. In UE5, there is a new and easier way — UToolMenus.

UToolMenus is a singleton class. You can get the singleton instance with the following code:

UToolMenus* ToolMenus = UToolMenus::Get();

In UE5, all extensible menu bars and toolbars call the function UToolMenus::RegisterMenu for registration during initialization:

UToolMenu* UToolMenus::RegisterMenu(const FName InName,
                                    const FName InParent = NAME_None,
                                    EMultiBoxType InType = EMultiBoxType::Menu,
                                    bool bWarnIfAlreadyRegistered = true)

This function is used to register an extensible ToolMenu. The meanings of each parameter are as follows:

  • InName: The chain field used for registration, in the form of LevelEditor.LevelEditorToolBar.User. You can later use this field as a key to get the UToolMenu.
  • InParent: Specifies the parent of the tool menu.
  • InType: Specifies the type of the ToolMenu. This type determines how the menu can be extended. It can be one of the following values:
    • MenuBar: Menu bar, supports extending menus
    • ToolBar: Toolbar, can add tool buttons
    • VerticalToolBar: Vertical toolbar
    • SlimHorizontalToolBar: Horizontal toolbar, a slim version of the toolbar that aligns icons and text elements horizontally
    • UniformToolBar:
    • Menu: Menu, can add menu items
    • ButtonRow: Buttons arranged in rows, with a maximum number of buttons per row. Similar to a toolbar but can have multiple rows.
  • bWarnIfAlreadyRegistered: Boolean value. If the field is already registered, a warning is issued.

When the menu needs to be previewed, the function UToolMenus::GenerateWidget is called to generate the ToolMenu control:

TSharedRef<SWidget> UToolMenus::GenerateWidget(const FName Name, const FToolMenuContext& InMenuContext)

After the ToolMenu is registered, we can extend the menu content at any time before preview by calling the function UToolMenus::ExtendMenu.

UToolMenu* UToolMenus::ExtendMenu(const FName InName)

There are many extension references in the code above, and here is a simple plugin extension example:

#pragma once

#include "Modules/ModuleManager.h"

class FCustomPluginModule : public IModuleInterface
{
public:
    virtual void StartupModule() override {
        // Add a callback to UToolMenus' startup when the plugin starts
        UToolMenus::RegisterStartupCallback(FSimpleMulticastDelegate::FDelegate::CreateRaw(this, &FCustomPluginModule::RegisterMenus));
    }

    virtual void ShutdownModule() override {
        // Remove UToolMenus' startup callback and reset some states
        UToolMenus::UnRegisterStartupCallback(this);
        UToolMenus::UnregisterOwner(this);
    }
private:
    void RegisterMenus() {
        FToolMenuOwnerScoped OwnerScoped(this);
        UToolMenu* Menu = UToolMenus::Get()->ExtendMenu("LevelEditor.LevelEditorToolBar.PlayToolBar");
        FToolMenuSection& Section = Menu->FindOrAddSection("PluginTools");
        FToolMenuEntry& MenuEntry = Section.AddEntry(
            FToolMenuEntry::InitToolBarButton(          // Add toolbar button
                "CustomToolbarButton",
                FUIAction
                (
                    FExecuteAction::CreateLambda([]() {
                        FMessageDialog::Open(EAppMsgType::Ok, NSLOCTEXT("CustomNs", "HelloWorld", "Hello World!"));
                    })
                )
            )
        );
        MenuEntry.InsertPosition = FToolMenuInsert(NAME_None, EToolMenuInsertType::First);
    }
};

This code adds a button to the toolbar of the level editor main panel. When clicked, it pops up a Hello World dialog box:

We can add a breakpoint at UToolMenus::Get() and use VS's debug window to get the list of all extensible fields:

docs.title: Undo and Redo
docs.text:
UObject has a transaction mechanism. If a UObject has the flag RF_Transactional, you can use the following code:

GEditor->BeginTransaction(NSLOCTEXT("NS", "Transaction", "Transaction"));       // Start transaction
Object->Modify();               // This operation stores the current state of Object in the transaction

SomeChange(Object);             // Modify some properties of Object

GEditor->EndTransaction();      // End transaction and commit the new state of Object

The above operation allows SomeChanged to be undone and redone.

For details, see: https://blog.csdn.net/qq_29523119/article/details/96778797

In editor development, it is often necessary for an object or window to respond to changes (e.g., rebuild) when undo/redo is performed. UE provides the interface FEditorUndoClient for listening to undo/redo events. A simple code example is as follows:

class FUndoRedoListener: public FEditorUndoClient{
public:
    FUndoRedoListener(){
        if (GEditor)
            GEditor->RegisterForUndo(this);     // Register the listener at the appropriate time, not necessarily in the constructor
    }
    ~FUndoRedoListener(){
        if (GEditor)
            GEditor->UnregisterForUndo(this);   // Unregister
    }
protected:
    virtual void PostUndo(bool bSuccess) override{      // Called after the editor performs undo
        RebuildSomething();
    }
    virtual void PostRedo(bool bSuccess) override{      // Called after the editor performs redo
        RebuildSomething();
    }
};
