docs.title: Particle System
docs.text:
A Particle System refers to a technology in 3D computer graphics used to simulate specific fuzzy phenomena that are difficult to achieve realistic physical motion laws with other traditional rendering techniques. Phenomena often simulated using particle systems include fire, explosions, smoke, water flows, sparks, falling leaves, clouds, fog, snow, dust, meteor trails, or abstract visual effects like glowing trajectories.

Baidu Encyclopedia (Baidu Encyclopedia) — Particle System

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
Particle systems are mainly used to render large numbers of moving objects. Their core workflow is not complex. Those familiar with graphics APIs know that rendering an object with the GPU requires calling DrawCall. Since particle systems contain a huge number of tiny particles, a conventional approach might look like this:

for(int i = 0; i < particles.num(); i++){
    drawParticle(particles[i]);
}

While this achieves the effect, the numerous DrawCall invocations and repeated data between particles lead to very high rendering costs for the particle system, limiting the number of particles that can be rendered.

To maximize data reuse between particles and reduce DrawCall, the solution is Instancing.

For details on the concept and usage of instancing, see:

  • Learn OpenGL - Instancing

Instancing allows merging DrawCall operations for particle systems and reusing identical data between particles.

Understanding the above concepts makes it clear that a particle system is essentially a workflow using instanced rendering. When considering how to create particle effects from this perspective, we focus on:

  • How to construct the instanced data (Instance Data) required by the particle system.
  • How to use the instanced data to render the particle effect.

Starting from these two angles, it should be easy to build the workflow of a particle system. The following sections mainly explain the details of particle system architecture:

For a simple particle, it might use a data structure like this:

struct Particle{        // Particle attribute structure 
    vec3 position;
    vec3 rotation;
    float size;
    float age;
    //...
}

In most particle system architectures, a structure called a Particle Emitter is used. It maintains a Particle Pool for storing data and is responsible for Spawning, Updating, and Recycling particles. Using a Particle Renderer to render the data in the particle pool produces the particle effect. This process can be visualized as:

class ParticleEmitter{
protected:
    void Tick() override{
        Spawn();                // Spawn phase: Create new particles
        UpdateAndRecycle();     // Update phase: Update each particle's state data and recycle dead particles
        Render();               // Render phase: Use the particle renderer to render the particle effect
    }
private:
    vector<Particle> mParticlePool;
    ParticleRenderer mParticleRenderer;
};

docs.title: Particle Pool
docs.text:
Since computer memory resources are limited, the particle system must ensure that the memory occupied by the particle pool does not keep expanding as the program runs. To this end, particle systems typically use the following methods to avoid this issue:

  • Limit the number of particles emitted.
  • Particles have a lifecycle; particles exceeding their lifecycle are promptly recycled.

This also provides a foundation for memory optimization in the particle pool:

  • Knowing the number of particles emitted and their lifecycle, combined with the current maximum frame rate of the computer, it is easy to estimate the maximum number of particles for the emitter. The memory for this number is often allocated to the particle pool at the start, avoiding overhead from memory reallocation of the particle pool.
  • To allow parallel recycling of the particle pool (avoiding the need to shift subsequent elements to fill the position when removing an element from the array), two particle pools of the same size are often used for alternating iteration.

If we want to update and recycle particles, we might write code like this:

vector<Particle> ParticlePool;
ParticlePool.reserve(10000);            // Pre-allocate memory for 10000 particles

int index = -1;
for(int i = 0; i < ParticlePool.size(); i++){
    if(ParticlePool[i].isAlive()){
        index++;
        ParticlePool[index] = ParticlePool[i];
        ParticlePool[index].position = ...;
        ParticlePool[index].size = ...;
        ...;
    }
}
ParticlePool.resize(index);

Its logical complexity is O(n). If further optimization is needed, we can process the for loop in parallel, but the above code structure cannot do this because:

  • The internal loop logic reads and writes the external shared variable index.
  • Reading and writing different regions of ParticlePool simultaneously can cause data chaos due to out-of-order execution in parallel.

To solve this problem, we usually use two ParticlePool for alternating processing and use atomic operations to read and write index in local threads. Therefore, the structure code of ParticleEmitter might become:

class ParticleEmitter{
protected:
    void InitPool(){
        mParticlePool[0].reserve(...);
        mParticlePool[1].reserve(...);
        mCurrentPoolIndex = 0;
        mNextPoolIndex = 1;
        mCurrentNumOfParticle = 0;
    }
    void Tick() override{
        Spawn();                
        UpdateAndRecycle();     
        Render();               
    }
private:
    vector<Particle> mParticlePool[2];
    int mCurrentPoolIndex;
    int mNextPoolIndex;
    int mCurrentNumOfParticle;

    ParticleRenderer mParticleRenderer;
};

docs.title: Spawn Phase
docs.text:
The particle spawn phase mainly involves creating new particles, storing them in the particle pool, and initializing them. This process can be visualized as:

void Spawn(){ 
    SpawnPerFrame(mParticlePool[mCurrentPoolIndex], mCurrentNumOfParticle, 100);        // Spawn 100 particles per frame
}

// Emission mechanism (customizable)
void SpawnPerFrame(vector<Particle>& ParticlePool, int& NumOfParticle, int NumOfNewParticle){
    for(int i = 0; i < NumOfNewParticle ; i++ ){            // NumOfNewParticle is the number of new particles
        Particle& NewParticle =  ParticlePool[NumOfParticle];   
        NumOfParticle++;
        InitializeParticle(NewParticle);
    }
}

// Initialization mechanism (customizable)
void InitializeParticle(Particle& particle){
    particle.position = vec3(0.0f, 0.0f, 0.0f);
    // particle...
}

Note here that the Spawn function is called every frame. In addition to the emission mechanism of spawning a fixed number of particles per frame, the emitter may also spawn a "fixed" number per second. However, since the number of frames per second in the game is unpredictable under different system environments, the number of particles for such time-based emission mechanisms is difficult to control precisely.

docs.title: Update and Recycle Phase
docs.text:
The pseudocode for this phase can be visualized as:

void UpdateAndRecycle(){    
    int IndexOfNextBuffer = -1;             // Initial index
    for_each_thread(int i = 0 ; i < mCurrentNumOfParticle ; i++){       // Parallel for loop
        const Particle& CurrentParticle = mParticlePool[mCurrentPoolIndex][i];
        if(CurrentParticle.isActive()){ 
            int CurrentIndex = atomicAdd(IndexOfNextPool, 1);           // Use atomic operations to read/write external shared variables
            Particle& NextParticle = mParticlePool[mNextPoolIndex][CurrentIndex];
            UpdateParticleStatus(CurrentParticle, NextParticle);
        }
    }
    CurrentParticlesBufferSize = IndexOfNextBuffer; // Update the number of currently alive particles
    swap(mCurrentPoolIndex, mNextPoolIndex);            // Swap the indices of the current particle pools
}

// Particle state update mechanism (customizable)
void UpdateParticleStatus(const Particle& CurrentParticle, Particle& NextParticle){
    NextParticle.position = CurrentParticle.position;
    // NextParticle...
}

docs.title: Rendering Phase
docs.text:
Rendering itself only uses particle data for rendering. Its basic process can be visualized as:

void Render(){
    mParticleRenderer.BindAttribute("position", mParticlePool[mCurrentPoolIndex], offset0, stride0);
    mParticleRenderer.BindAttribute("color", mParticlePool[mCurrentPoolIndex], offset1, stride1);
    ...;
    mParticleRenderer.drawInstancing();
}

This phase reflects the essence of particles: particles are just a collection of data, and the particle system (emitter) simply processes this data in batches and binds it to the attribute slots of the particle renderer to complete the rendering of the particle effect.

docs.title: CPU VS GPU
docs.text:
As mentioned above, particle systems essentially revolve around processing a collection of particle data, which can be mainly divided into:

  • Spawn Phase and Update and Recycle Phase: These two phases mainly process particle data. Niagara provides visual scripting to enable custom operations for these two phases. The final script will:
  • CPU: C++ code generated by node concatenation runs in Niagara's virtual machine.
  • GPU: Niagara translates the node graph into corresponding HLSL code via NiagaraHlslTranslator for ComputeShader calls.
  • Rendering Phase: Both CPU and GPU particles can use the same renderer. The difference is that CPU particles need to upload data to the GPU, while GPU particle data resides on the GPU and requires no transfer.

The logic of the above processes is largely similar. One thing to note is the recycling of GPU particles. GPU particles use ComputeShader to process each particle in parallel, but during the update and recycle phase, data relocation is involved. The reason GPU can achieve efficient parallelism is that data on each branch is independent and does not interfere with each other. To implement GPU particle recycling, we must "break" this rule. Currently, there are two main ways to achieve this effect:

  • Graphics Rendering Pipeline: Disable rasterization, use TransformFeedback (OpenGL)/Stream Output (DX), and recycle (not submit) dead particles in the Geometry Shader.

The Geometry Shader itself has linear operations because this process generates an indefinite number of new vertices. The GPU must lock and relocate data when writing it to memory during execution. This is why some people use TransformFeedback and Stream Output to create GPU particles. Of course, this is also why GS should be avoided in games. Incidentally, Stream Output is an official feature of DX, while TransformFeedback is not well-supported by Khronos—Vulkan does not even provide official support, and Metal lacks corresponding API functions.

  • General Computing Pipeline: SSBO Atomic. With hardware updates, most modern rendering drivers support SSBO (Shader Storage Buffer Object). Our main focus here is that SSBO supports atomic operations. With this support, we can process particles in parallel in CS and use atomic operations to relocate particle data (i.e., NewIndex in the pseudocode above). For new particle data, another feature—indirect rendering (Indirect Draw)—can be used: directly call DrawCall using data on the GPU. This avoids particle data transfer between CPU and GPU throughout the process. Below is a simple GLSL code example:
layout (local_size_x = LOCAL_SIZE) in;
struct Particle {
    vec3 position;
    vec3 rotation;
    vec3 scaling;
    vec3 velocity;
    float life;
};
layout(std140,binding = 0) buffer InputParticlesBuffer{
    Particle inputParticles[PARTICLE_MAX_SIZE];
};
layout(std140,binding = 1) buffer OutputParticlesBuffer{
    Particle outputParticles[PARTICLE_MAX_SIZE];
};
layout(std140,binding = 2) buffer ParticleRunContext{
  int inputCounter;           // Initial value is the current number of particles
  int outputCounter;          // Initialized to -1
  float duration;
  float lifetime;
};

#define inID  gl_GlobalInvocationID.x
#define inParticle inputParticles[inID]

void main(){                                              // Note: GPU parallelism is unordered
    if(inID >= inputCounter || inParticle.life > lifetime)        // Can be optimized using the step function
        return;
    uint outID = atomicAdd(outputCounter, 1);             // atomicAdd is a native GLSL function but requires the operand to come from SSBO
    outputParticles[outID].life = inParticle.life + duration;
}

Shader Storage Buffer Object (Shader Storage Buffer Object) is used to provide readable and writable buffer data.

Its usage is almost identical to UniformBuffer. The main differences are:

  • Storage Buffer can allocate very large video memory: The OpenGL specification guarantees that Uniform Buffer can be up to 16KB, while Storage Buffer can be up to 128MB.
  • Storage Buffer is writable and even supports atomic operations: Reads and writes to Storage Buffer may be out of order, so memory barriers are often needed to ensure synchronization.
  • Storage Buffer supports variable storage: This means that blocks in Storage Buffer can define unbounded arrays (like int arr[]), and the array length can be obtained using arr.length in the shader. In contrast, blocks in Uniform Buffer require explicitly specifying the array size when defining arrays.
  • SSBO access is slower than Uniform Buffer under the same conditions: Storage Buffer is usually accessed like a buffer texture, while Uniform Buffer data is read through internal shader-accessible memory.

Functionally, SSBO can be considered a better interface for buffer textures when accessed via Image Load Store.

OpenGL provides an AtomicCounter feature, which essentially leverages this characteristic.

The above completes the recycling of GPU particles, but it actually introduces a serious problem—each time particles are recycled, the number of particles changes. However, since the data is located on the GPU, the CPU must know this parameter when calling DrawCall.

Reading data back from the GPU is definitely not feasible because modern graphics APIs use command buffering to accelerate rendering. Simply put, at any moment, the GPU's command buffer may contain instructions from two or more frames that have not yet been processed. If we want to read data back, we must ensure that the current instructions are executed immediately, which means blocking the rendering thread and waiting for the data to return. This operation is fatal to the entire engine, but fortunately, there is a solution.

In the OpenGL 4.0 update, a new feature called Indirect Rendering (also known as Indirect Draw) was introduced, which allows using data on the GPU as DrawCall parameters. Here is the official definition:

Indirect Rendering

Indirect rendering allows directly using data on the GPU as DrawCall parameters. For example, the parameters of glDrawArrays include primitive type, number of vertices, and starting vertex. When using the indirect drawing command glDrawArraysIndirect, the corresponding parameters are obtained from a buffer object.

This feature avoids GPU->CPU->GPU round trips by letting the GPU determine the parameters to render, while the CPU only decides when to issue the drawing command and which Primitive the command uses.

Searching for "Indirect" in the Niagara source code reveals definitions of related usage. The main structures are located in:

  • NiagaraVertexFactories\Public\NiagaraDrawIndirect.h
  • Niagara\Private\NiagaraGPUInstanceCountManager.cpp

docs.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
docs.text:
• CPU Particles

  • Advantages

    • The CPU can access the complete game environment and interact with other particles or game logic.
    • No high hardware configuration is required; the graphics card only needs to support programmable pipelines and instanced rendering.

  • Disadvantages

    • Particle data can only be iterated linearly on the CPU, causing severe performance loss to the CPU.
    • Particle data resides in CPU memory and needs to be uniformly uploaded to the GPU during rendering. This transfer process is extremely costly.

  • GPU Particles

  • Advantages

    • Particle data is generated and processed on the GPU throughout, avoiding data transfer between CPU and GPU.
    • Leveraging parallel units in the GPU to process particle data greatly reduces the time required for particle processing.

  • Disadvantages

    • GPU particle data resides in video memory, making it impossible to calculate bounding box boundaries in real time. Therefore, we need to manually specify fixed boundaries for GPU particles.
    • Cannot interact well with the game environment, but effects can be approximated using depth, Scene Capture, or distance fields.
    • Requires certain hardware configurations, including support for CS, SSBO Atomic, and Indirect Draw (PCs with discrete graphics cards are generally fine, but mobile support is not particularly​完善​).

docs.title: Niagara
docs.text: Unreal Engine's Niagara system is very powerful. It essentially provides a programmable data processor (CPU or GPU) and instanced renderer. From this perspective, we can achieve many stunning effects.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
Most articles refer to these scopes as "namespaces." While they do serve to distinguish variable names, more importantly for developers, these variable scopes represent different lifecycles.

The following is the general structure of Niagara in UE, where the yellow parts represent the scopes of manageable variables in Niagara:

In the Niagara editor, you can add, delete, or modify variables in these scopes through the parameter panel:

  • EngineProvided: This scope is mainly used to read variables from the engine, such as DeltaTime.

  • System Attribute: Attribute variables held by a single particle system.

  • Emitter Attribute: Attribute variables held by a single particle emitter.

  • Particle Attribute: Attribute variables held by a single particle.

  • Module Inputs: Module input variables, i.e., variables exposed by the module for external settings. They will be displayed in the module's settings panel:

  • Static Switch Inputs: Module static branch input variables, used to optimize script logic branches during compilation.

  • Module Locals: Module local variables.

  • Module Outputs: Module output variables.

  • Stage Transients: Stage temporary variables.

  • User Expose: User-exposed variables, mainly for calling from modules outside Niagara (C++ or Blueprint). Fundamentally, they are different from other variables, which will be discussed in detail below.

For the detailed meaning of these scopes, refer to: UE4: Niagara Variables and HLSL - Zhihu (zhihu.com)

docs.title: Underlying Core — FNiagaraDataSet
docs.text:
Niagara attributes are essentially a collection of data. Their corresponding code structure is FNiagaraDataSet (except for User Expose). Its simplified structure is as follows:

class FNiagaraDataSet{
    /** Table of free IDs available to allocate next tick. */
    TArray<int32> FreeIDsTable;

    /** Number of free IDs in FreeIDTable. */
    int32 NumFreeIDs;

    /** Max ID seen in last execution. Allows us to shrink the IDTable. */
    int32 MaxUsedID;

    /** Tag to use when new IDs are acquired. Should be unique per tick. */
    int32 IDAcquireTag;

    /** Table of IDs spawned in the last tick (just the index part, the acquire tag is IDAcquireTag for all of them). */
    TArray<int32> SpawnedIDsTable;

    /** GPU buffer of free IDs available on the next tick. */
    FRWBuffer GPUFreeIDs;

    /** Number of IDs allocated for the GPU simulation. */
    uint32 GPUNumAllocatedIDs;

    /**
    Actual data storage. These are passed to and read directly by the RT.
    This is effectively a pool of buffers for this simulation.
    Typically this should only be two or three entries and we search for a free buffer to write into on BeginSimulate();
    We keep track of the Current and Previous buffers which move with each simulate.
    Additional buffers may be in here if they are currently being used by the render thread.
    */
    TArray<FNiagaraDataBuffer*, TInlineAllocator<2>> Data;

        /** Buffer containing the current simulation state. */
    FNiagaraDataBuffer* CurrentData;

    /** Buffer we're currently simulating into. Only valid while we're simulating i.e between PrepareForSimulate and EndSimulate calls.*/
    FNiagaraDataBuffer* DestinationData;

    /* Max instance count is the maximum number of instances we allow. */
    uint32 MaxInstanceCount;
    /* Max allocation count is the maximum number of instances we can allocate which can be > MaxInstanceCount due to rounding. */
    uint32 MaxAllocationCount;
}

From the above structure, FNiagaraDataSet provides the data structures needed for the basic processes of the particle emitter mentioned at the beginning:

  • Maximum allocated storage (capacity, ID).
  • TArray<FNiagaraDataBuffer*, TInlineAllocator<2>> Data are two buffers for alternating iteration. FNiagaraDataBuffer* CurrentData and FNiagaraDataBuffer* DestinationData are pointers to the buffers for quick swapping.

The core storage structure is FNiagaraDataBuffer, whose focus is solely on memory data. Its simplified structure is as follows:

class FNiagaraDataBuffer : public FNiagaraSharedObject{
//////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
    // CPU Data
    /** Float components of simulation data. */
    TArray<uint8> FloatData;
    /** Int32 components of simulation data. */
    TArray<uint8> Int32Data;
    /** Half components of simulation data. */
    TArray<uint8> HalfData;

    /** Table of IDs to real buffer indices. */
    TArray<int32> IDToIndexTable;
    //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////
    // GPU Data
    /** Location in the frame where GPU data will be ready, for CPU this is always the first group, for GPU is depends on the features used as to which phase. */
    ENiagaraGpuComputeTickStage::Type GPUDataReadyStage = ENiagaraGpuComputeTickStage::First;
    /** The buffer offset where the instance count is accumulated. */
    uint32 GPUInstanceCountBufferOffset;
    /** GPU Buffer containing floating point values for GPU simulations. */
    FRWBuffer GPUBufferFloat;
    /** GPU Buffer containing integer values for GPU simulations. */
    FRWBuffer GPUBufferInt;
    /** GPU table which maps particle ID to index. */
    FRWBuffer GPUIDToIndexTable;
    /** GPU Buffer containing half values for GPU simulations. */
    FRWBuffer GPUBufferHalf;
#if NIAGARA_MEMORY_TRACKING
    int32 AllocationSizeBytes = 0;
#endif
    //////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////////

    /** Number of instances in data. */
    uint32 NumInstances;
    /** Number of instances the buffer has been allocated for. */
    uint32 NumInstancesAllocated;
    /** Stride between components in the float buffer. */
    uint32 FloatStride;
    /** Stride between components in the int32 buffer. */
    uint32 Int32Stride;
    /** Stride between components in the half buffer. */
    uint32 HalfStride;
    /** Number of instances spawned in the last tick. */
    uint32 NumSpawnedInstances;
    /** ID acquire tag used in the last tick. */
    uint32 IDAcquireTag;

    /** Table containing current base locations for all registers in this dataset. */
    TArray<uint8*> RegisterTable;//TODO: Should make inline? Feels like a useful size to keep local would be too big.
    RegisterTypeOffsetType RegisterTypeOffsets;
};

Classes in Niagara that hold FNiagaraDataSet include:

  • FNiagaraEmitterInstance: Niagara emitter instance
class FNiagaraEmitterInstance{
    struct FEventInstanceData
  {
      TArray<FNiagaraScriptExecutionContext> EventExecContexts;
      TArray<FNiagaraParameterDirectBinding<int32>> EventExecCountBindings;

      TArray<FNiagaraDataSet*> UpdateScriptEventDataSets;         // Data set for the update phase
      TArray<FNiagaraDataSet*> SpawnScriptEventDataSets;          // Data set for the spawn phase

      TArray<bool> UpdateEventGeneratorIsSharedByIndex;
      TArray<bool> SpawnEventGeneratorIsSharedByIndex;

      /** Data required for handling events. */
      TArray<FNiagaraEventHandlingInfo> EventHandlingInfo;
      int32 EventSpawnTotal = 0;
  };
    /** Particle simulation data. Must be a shared ref as various things on the RT can have direct ref to it. */
  FNiagaraDataSet* ParticleDataSet = nullptr;                     // Particle data
};
  • FNiagaraSystemInstance: Niagara system instance
class FNiagaraSystemInstance{
  // Registered events for each of the emitters
  typedef TPair<FName, FName> EmitterEventKey;
  typedef TMap<EmitterEventKey, FNiagaraDataSet*> EventDataSetMap;    
  EventDataSetMap EmitterEventDataSetMap;                         // Niagara system event set
};
  • FNiagaraDICollisionQueryBatch: Contains collision events
class FNiagaraDICollisionQueryBatch{
    FNiagaraDataSet *CollisionEventDataSet = nullptr;
};
  • FNiagaraScriptExecutionContextBase: Niagara script (Module) execution context
struct FNiagaraDataSetExecutionInfo{
    FNiagaraDataSet* DataSet;
  FNiagaraDataBuffer* Input;
  FNiagaraDataBuffer* Output;
}
struct FNiagaraScriptExecutionContextBase{
    UNiagaraScript* Script;
    TArray<FNiagaraDataSetExecutionInfo, TInlineAllocator<2>> DataSetInfo;
}

It can be seen that particle data and events in Niagara are both based on FNiagaraDataSet. Of course, there is an exception mentioned earlier: User Expose, which is stored in FNiagaraParameterStore and is invisible to modules. It can only be read in the Niagara system, i.e., bound to other attributes via FNiagaraParameterStoreBinding. It is mainly used to provide a means of interaction between Niagara and external data.

In Niagara\Classes\NiagaraDataSetAccessor.h, many template functions for internal reading and writing of FNiagaraDataSet are provided. Taking Int32 as an example:

template<typename TType>
struct FNiagaraDataSetAccessorInt32
{
    static FNiagaraDataSetReaderInt32<TType> CreateReader(const FNiagaraDataSet& DataSet, const FName VariableName) { }
    static FNiagaraDataSetWriterInt32<TType> CreateWriter(const FNiagaraDataSet& DataSet, const FName VariableName) { }
};

At the Niagara editor level, FNiagaraDataSet is not directly handled. Instead, FNiagaraVariable is managed and edited, stored in FNiagaraDataSetCompiledData, and finally compiled:

struct FNiagaraDataSetCompiledData
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

    /** Variables in the data set. */
    UPROPERTY()
    TArray<FNiagaraVariable> Variables;

    /** Data describing the layout of variable data. */
    UPROPERTY()
    TArray<FNiagaraVariableLayoutInfo> VariableLayouts;

    //...
};

Thus, the underlying core of Niagara is now covered. There is no need to delve deeper into the details.

docs.title: Data Interface — Data Interface
docs.text:
Basic data types (numbers, vectors, etc.) are insufficient for all application scenarios. In some cases, particle systems may need to access many complex data structures, such as skeletons, textures, distance fields, audio, etc.

To this end, Niagara provides a mechanism called Data Interface specifically for handling complex data structures. When creating attributes in any scope, you can see the following entries under DataInterface:

Its corresponding underlying code structure is UNiagaraDataInterface.

All the above interfaces are derived from it. The main reason for mentioning this is that we can also derive this class in a plugin for customization.

There are numerous derivation examples in the Niagara source code:

docs.title: Event Mechanism
docs.text:
Niagara's event mechanism is also based on the aforementioned FNiagaraDataSet.

Take GenerateLocationEvent as an example:

Opening its script, you can see:

The core of this script is calling the LocationEvent_V2 Write node. This node cannot be created manually because it is generated by engine serialization. Its node prototype is UNiagaraNodeWriteDataSet, whose structure is as follows:

class UNiagaraNodeDataSetBase : public UNiagaraNode
{
public:
    FNiagaraDataSetID DataSet;
    TArray<FNiagaraVariable> Variables;
    TArray<FString> VariableFriendlyNames;
};

class UNiagaraNodeWriteDataSet : public UNiagaraNodeDataSetBase{
    FName EventName;
};

Looking at its event handler Receive Location Event:

It can be seen that LocationEvent_V2_Read corresponds to the previous LocationEvent_V2 Write, with the node prototype being UNiagaraNodeReadDataSet.

Among them, events that can be created manually in Niagara include:

They also read and write FNiagaraDataSet via UNiagaraNodeDataSetRead / UNiagaraNodeDataSetWrite. Their execution logic is simple, but we only need to figure out:

  • Which FNiagaraDataSet do these two nodes read from and write to?
  • When are events processed?

docs.title: Holder of Event Data
docs.text:
The definition of FNiagaraSystemInstance includes the following function:

class FNiagaraSystemInstance{
 //...
    typedef TPair<FName, FName> EmitterEventKey;
    typedef TMap<EmitterEventKey, FNiagaraDataSet*> EventDataSetMap;    
    EventDataSetMap EmitterEventDataSetMap;                         // Niagara system event set
};

FNiagaraDataSet* FNiagaraSystemInstance::CreateEventDataSet(FName EmitterName, FName EventName)
{
    FNiagaraDataSet*& OutSet = EmitterEventDataSetMap.FindOrAdd(EmitterEventKey(EmitterName, EventName));
    if (!OutSet) {
        OutSet = new FNiagaraDataSet();
    }
    return OutSet;
}

When a Niagara emitter is initialized (possibly due to reset or recompilation), the following function is called:

void FNiagaraEmitterInstance::Init(int32 InEmitterIdx, FNiagaraSystemInstanceID InSystemInstanceID){
    const int32 UpdateEventGeneratorCount = CachedEmitter->UpdateScriptProps.EventGenerators.Num();
    const int32 SpawnEventGeneratorCount = CachedEmitter->SpawnScriptProps.EventGenerators.Num();
    const int32 NumEvents = CachedEmitter->GetEventHandlers().Num();

    if (UpdateEventGeneratorCount || SpawnEventGeneratorCount || NumEvents)
    {
        EventInstanceData = MakeUnique<FEventInstanceData>();
        EventInstanceData->UpdateScriptEventDataSets.Empty(UpdateEventGeneratorCount);
        EventInstanceData->UpdateEventGeneratorIsSharedByIndex.SetNumZeroed(UpdateEventGeneratorCount);
        int32 UpdateEventGeneratorIndex = 0;
        for (const FNiagaraEventGeneratorProperties &GeneratorProps : CachedEmitter->UpdateScriptProps.EventGenerators)
        {
            FNiagaraDataSet *Set = ParentSystemInstance->CreateEventDataSet(EmitterHandle.GetIdName(), GeneratorProps.ID);
            Set->Init(&GeneratorProps.DataSetCompiledData);

            EventInstanceData->UpdateScriptEventDataSets.Add(Set);
            EventInstanceData->UpdateEventGeneratorIsSharedByIndex[UpdateEventGeneratorIndex] = CachedEmitter->IsEventGeneratorShared(GeneratorProps.ID);
            ++UpdateEventGeneratorIndex;
        }

        EventInstanceData->SpawnScriptEventDataSets.Empty(SpawnEventGeneratorCount);
        EventInstanceData->SpawnEventGeneratorIsSharedByIndex.SetNumZeroed(SpawnEventGeneratorCount);
        int32 SpawnEventGeneratorIndex = 0;
        for (const FNiagaraEventGeneratorProperties &GeneratorProps : CachedEmitter->SpawnScriptProps.EventGenerators)
        {
            FNiagaraDataSet *Set = ParentSystemInstance->CreateEventDataSet(EmitterHandle.GetIdName(), GeneratorProps.ID);
            Set->Init(&GeneratorProps.DataSetCompiledData);

            EventInstanceData->SpawnScriptEventDataSets.Add(Set);
            EventInstanceData->SpawnEventGeneratorIsSharedByIndex[SpawnEventGeneratorIndex] = CachedEmitter->IsEventGeneratorShared(GeneratorProps.ID);
            ++SpawnEventGeneratorIndex;
        }

        EventInstanceData->EventExecContexts.SetNum(NumEvents);
        EventInstanceData->EventExecCountBindings.SetNum(NumEvents);

        for (int32 i = 0; i < NumEvents; i++)
        {
            ensure(CachedEmitter->GetEventHandlers()[i].DataSetAccessSynchronized());

            UNiagaraScript* EventScript = CachedEmitter->GetEventHandlers()[i].Script;

            //This is cpu explicitly? Are we doing event handlers on GPU?
            EventInstanceData->EventExecContexts[i].Init(EventScript, ENiagaraSimTarget::CPUSim);
            EventInstanceData->EventExecCountBindings[i].Init(EventInstanceData->EventExecContexts[i].Parameters, SYS_PARAM_ENGINE_EXEC_COUNT);
        }
    }
}

The main operations in this function are:

  • If the emitter contains event generators, FEventInstanceData is created.
  • All event handlers are initialized at the end.
  • The code iterates over CachedEmitter->UpdateScriptProps.EventGenerators and CachedEmitter->SpawnScriptProps.EventGenerators to generate EventDataSet. Tracing its definition leads to the following code:
void FNiagaraEmitterScriptProperties::InitDataSetAccess()
{
  EventReceivers.Empty();
  EventGenerators.Empty();

  if (Script && Script->IsReadyToRun(ENiagaraSimTarget::CPUSim))
  {
      //UE_LOG(LogNiagara, Log, TEXT("InitDataSetAccess: %s %d %d"), *Script->GetPathName(), Script->ReadDataSets.Num(), Script->WriteDataSets.Num());
      // TODO: add event receiver and generator lists to the script properties here
      //
      for (FNiagaraDataSetID &ReadID : Script->GetVMExecutableData().ReadDataSets)
      {
          EventReceivers.Add( FNiagaraEventReceiverProperties(ReadID.Name, NAME_None, NAME_None) );
      }

      for (FNiagaraDataSetProperties &WriteID : Script->GetVMExecutableData().WriteDataSets)
      {
          FNiagaraEventGeneratorProperties Props(WriteID, NAME_None);
          EventGenerators.Add(Props);
      }
  }
}

And its definition is as follows:

class FNiagaraVMExecutableData{
    UPROPERTY()
  TArray<FNiagaraDataSetProperties> WriteDataSets;
};

Among them, WriteDataSets is generated by FHlslNiagaraTranslator during script node compilation. The call stack is as follows:

void UNiagaraNodeWriteDataSet::Compile(...)
{
    //...
  Translator->WriteDataSet(AlteredDataSet, Variables, ENiagaraDataSetAccessMode::AppendConsume, Inputs, Outputs);
}

void FHlslNiagaraTranslator::WriteDataSet(...)
{
    //...
  TMap<int32, FDataSetAccessInfo>& Writes = DataSetWriteInfo[(int32)AccessMode].FindOrAdd(DataSet);
}

 FNiagaraTranslateResults FHlslNiagaraTranslator::Translate(...){
    for (TPair <FNiagaraDataSetID, TMap<int32, FDataSetAccessInfo>> InfoPair : DataSetWriteInfo[0]){
        CompilationOutput.ScriptData.WriteDataSets.Add(SetProps);
    }
}

Thus, we can conclude:

  • In a Niagara Module Script, any script containing UNiagaraNodeWriteDataSet will be defined as an event generator.
  • The holder of event data is FNiagaraSystemInstance.

docs.title: Timing of Event Processing
docs.text:
In FNiagaraEmitterInstance::Tick, there is the following code:

void FNiagaraEmitterInstance::Tick(float DeltaSeconds)
{
    //...
    if (EventInstanceData.IsValid())
    {
        // Set up the spawn counts and source datasets for the events. The system ensures that we will run after any emitters
        // we're receiving from, so we can use the data buffers that our sources have computed this tick.
        const int32 NumEventHandlers = CachedEmitter->GetEventHandlers().Num();
        EventInstanceData->EventSpawnTotal = 0;
        for (int32 i = 0; i < NumEventHandlers; i++)
        {
            const FNiagaraEventScriptProperties& EventHandlerProps = CachedEmitter->GetEventHandlers()[i];
            FNiagaraEventHandlingInfo& Info = EventInstanceData->EventHandlingInfo[i];

            Info.TotalSpawnCount = 0;//This was being done every frame but should be done in init?
            Info.SpawnCounts.Reset();

            //TODO: We can move this lookup into the init and just store a ptr to the other set?
            if (FNiagaraDataSet* EventSet = ParentSystemInstance->GetEventDataSet(Info.SourceEmitterName, EventHandlerProps.SourceEventName))
            {
                Info.SetEventData(&EventSet->GetCurrentDataChecked());
                uint32 EventSpawnNum = CalculateEventSpawnCount(EventHandlerProps, Info.SpawnCounts, EventSet);
                Info.TotalSpawnCount += EventSpawnNum;
                EventInstanceData->EventSpawnTotal += EventSpawnNum;
            }
        }
    }
}

The above code shows the logic of event processing:

  • When the emitter ticks, it iterates over all event handlers, reads the event's DataSet from the system instance ParentSystemInstance, and writes it to FNiagaraEventHandlingInfo for the script to read.

docs.title: Usage Recommendations
docs.text:
While pursuing artistic effects, special effects must also ensure:

  • The particle system has correct bounding boxes and scalability; otherwise, particles may disappear inexplicably in the scene.
  • Strictly control the lifecycle of spawned effects to avoid conflicts between the Pool Method and lifecycle processing operations (pre-culling, scalability culling, AutoDestroy).

For optimization, you need to understand:

  • How to reduce the number of particle emitters?

The ideal scenario is: as long as two emitters use exactly the same renderer parameters, they should use the same emitter.

Because one renderer in an emitter corresponds to one graphics rendering pipeline, and the particle system essentially processes the instanced data required by the graphics rendering pipeline.

One more emitter means one more set of rendering data and one more particle buffer to maintain.

If you just want to adjust the particle movement mechanism, you can extend it by customizing modules.

  • How to decide whether to use CPU or GPU particles?

CPU particles can dynamically calculate bounding box boundaries but are only suitable for rendering a small number of particles.

GPU particles can be used to render a large number of particles but must have accurate bounding box boundaries set.

The dividing line is mainly the number of particles. If the number is in the thousands or tens of thousands, GPU particles must be used.

For a small number of particles (e.g., a few), CPU particles are recommended.

  • When CPU particles must be used for effect purposes, two main points need to be considered:

  • CPU particles are executed serially. As the complexity of the particle system increases, performance loss multiplies.

  • The performance bottleneck of CPU particles in the rendering thread is mainly the transfer of particle data (limited bandwidth), which is why they are not suitable for rendering a large number of particles.

  • The working method of particle systems is different from conventional pipelines. If it is a single object placed in the scene, you need to consider using an Actor (Game Object) instead of a particle system.

  • In addition to controlling the complexity and number of particle systems, other methods can be used to reduce the performance consumption of particles:
  • Avoid particle crowding and reduce Overdraw.
  • Limit transparency.

  • ...

  • Generate data required for Niagara simulation offline (during editing).

  • Make good use of the Niagara Debugger and Insight.

docs.title: Niagara Performance Optimization
docs.text:
Niagara is a nearly all-powerful particle system provided by Unreal Engine. There are numerous high-quality tutorials online about how to use it to create certain effects, but the usage management and performance optimization of Niagara are often overlooked by effect artists.

Since the author has been plagued by these issues for a long time, this section will supplement relevant content, hoping that after understanding it, everyone can avoid such problems as much as possible =.=.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Particle System is an important means to enrich effects in 3D scenes. Unlike Mesh in scenes, its notable features are:

  • The quantity of particles is relatively large
  • Particles move over time

If these two features are not met (i.e., small quantity and static), artists need to consider whether to use MeshActor or particles.

In UE, effects can be mainly divided into two categories:

  • Spawned Effects: Effects dynamically spawned in the scene using SpawnSystemAtLocation and SpawnSystemAttached.
  • Scene Effects: Effects placed in the scene as Actors.

These two types of effects have different focus points and corresponding management measures.

docs.title: Bounding Box
docs.text:
In game engines, to reduce the rendering overhead of each frame, the engine culls some invisible objects so they do not participate in GPU rendering, as shown below:

This image is from: ​马克​·​加尔​维斯​ - Homepage (optus23.github.io)

If you understand 3D View Transformation, you should know that you can determine whether an object is within the camera's range by calculating all vertices of the object using the camera matrix.

However, obviously, an object may have thousands of vertices. If calculations are performed for each vertex, the game engine might turn into a PPT player~

To simplify this process, game engines use a clever method: replacing the object's vertices with a simple box that can enclose the object for camera culling calculations. Although the box has fewer vertices and visibility judgment is less precise, the performance improvement it brings is very significant.

Logically, it can be assumed that if this box is visible, the object must be visible.

Show object bounding box: ShowFlag.Bounds 1

So everyone should understand this: In the engine, to determine whether an object is within the camera's range or occluded, generally, the reference is not its own vertex information, but the object's bounding box.

For StaticMesh, its vertices are static, so the engine automatically generates bounding box information when creating the asset.

But for effects, since particles are dynamic, their bounding boxes cannot be generated statically.

In UE, for CPU particles, the engine recalculates the Niagara bounding box boundaries every frame:

However, due to the​特殊性​ of their implementation (all particle data is in the GPU, and the number of particles is often very large), GPU particles make it impossible for the CPU side to calculate the particle bounding box in real time. Developers must set a fixed boundary for them, i.e., manually set the size of the bounding box.

GPU particles use a GPU-driven rendering pipeline, and the entire process has almost no interaction with the CPU. The data in the graphics rendering pipeline can often be seen as one-way: CPU->GPU. Although data can also be read back from the GPU, this process has a certain delay and high performance cost.

In Niagara, you can set the bounding box of the particle emitter here:

The simplest way is to set the bounding box for the entire particle system:

Artists must ensure the correctness of the bounding box (the bounding box should cover the entire movement space of the effect with the smallest possible area), otherwise the following consequences will occur:

  • If the bounding box of the effect does not match the actual movement space, it will lead to incorrect visual culling:

  • If the bounding box of the effect is too large, it will cause effects that are clearly not within the field of view to fail to be culled and still be rendered, resulting in unnecessary overhead.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
For Scene Effects, their lifecycle is managed by the scene at the Actor level, so we generally don't need to care about it. For Spawned Effects, there are some details we must understand regarding lifecycle management:

Spawned Effects refer to effects generated using several functions under UNiagaraFunctionLibrary:

UNiagaraComponent* SpawnSystemAtLocation(const UObject* WorldContextObject,
                                         class UNiagaraSystem* SystemTemplate, 
                                         FVector Location, 
                                         FRotator Rotation = FRotator::ZeroRotator,
                                         FVector Scale = FVector(1.f), 
                                         bool bAutoDestroy = true,
                                         bool bAutoActivate = true, 
                                         ENCPoolMethod PoolingMethod = ENCPoolMethod::None,
                                         bool bPreCullCheck = true);

UNiagaraComponent* SpawnSystemAttached(UNiagaraSystem* SystemTemplate,
                                       USceneComponent* AttachToComponent,
                                       FName AttachPointName,
                                       FVector Location, 
                                       FRotator Rotation,
                                       FVector Scale, 
                                       EAttachLocation::Type LocationType, 
                                       bool bAutoDestroy, 
                                       ENCPoolMethod PoolingMethod, 
                                       bool bAutoActivate = true,
                                       bool bPreCullCheck = true);

SpawnSystemAtLocation is used to spawn a particle component at a specified location, while SpawnSystemAttached is used to attach to another scene component. Regarding the lifecycle, we mainly need to pay attention to several parameters:

  • bAutoActivate: Whether to activate automatically. True means the particle effect will play immediately afterward.
  • bAutoDestroy: Whether to destroy automatically. True will destroy the component after the particle finishes playing.
  • bPreCullCheck: Pre-culling. If true, and the bounding box of the spawned particle system is not within the view frustum, the particle component will not be spawned, i.e., returns null.
  • PoolingMethod: Pool operation, a mechanism to reuse particle components. Its values can be:
  • None
  • AutoRelease: Auto-release. After playing ends, it will be automatically stored in the effect pool for reuse.
  • ManualRelease: Manual release. The particle component can only be reused by manually calling ReleaseToPool.
  • ManualRelease_OnComplete: Non-public option, used for internal state control of Niagara. Do not use it.
  • FreeInPool: Non-public option, used for internal state control of Niagara. Do not use it.

docs.title: Effect Pool
docs.text: For detailed mechanism, refer to the article: 【UE4】Effect Pool - Zhihu (zhihu.com)

docs.title: Caching Mechanism
docs.text:
The main purpose of the effect pool is to reuse particle components. Its caching mechanism can be seen as:

  • If the spawn parameters include pool operation (i.e., PoolingMethod != ENCPoolMethod::None), Niagara will search the effect pool for reusable components of the same type. If found, it will use them; otherwise, it will create a new particle component and record its usage time.
  • Newly created particle components will not be released (meaning bAutoDestroy will be invalidated). They will be stored in the effect pool for management.
  • For AutoRelease particle components, when playback ends, the effect pool will mark them as reusable.
  • For ManualRelease particle components, when ReleaseToPool is called: if the particle has finished playing, it will be immediately marked as reusable; otherwise, the pool operation will be modified to ManualRelease_OnComplete, and it will also be marked as reusable when playback finishes.

docs.title: Cleaning Methods
docs.text:
UNiagaraComponentPool has a scheduled cleaning mechanism. The two main key parameters are:

  • GNiagaraSystemPoolKillUnusedTime: Default is 180.
  • GNiagaraSystemPoolingCleanTime: Default is 30.

The automatic cleaning mechanism corresponding to the above configuration can be roughly regarded as: UNiagaraComponentPool will clean up particle components that have not been reused for more than 180 seconds every 30 seconds.

Actually, it is not cleaned on Tick, but during each reuse. So it may not be exactly 30 seconds, and the deviation may be large.

When switching World, UNiagaraComponentPool will execute Cleanup.

You can also manually call UNiagaraComponentPool::ClearPool(UNiagaraSystem* System) for cleaning.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• If there is a pool operation (PoolingMethod), then bAutoDestroy will be invalidated.
  • The premise for the pool mechanism to work properly is that the particle system can finish playing. Please note:
  • Ensure there are no emitters with infinite lifecycle in the particle system.
  • Calling ResetParticles(true) will not reach Complete.
  • If the culling response is Dormant for scalability culling, the culled effect will not be reused, and OnSystemFinished will not trigger (strictly speaking, it is not completed).
  • For particle components with pool operations, do not call DestoryComponent. Particle components in the pool will be cleaned up when switching World or during scheduled cleaning.
  • If SpawnSystemAttached has a pool operation, the actual owner of the newly spawned particle component is the World, not the attached component. The particle component will not be destroyed when the attached component is destroyed.
  • Calling ReleaseToPool on an AutoRelease particle component will cause an error.
  • For particles with neither AutoRelease nor pool operation, their lifecycle must be strictly controlled.

docs.title: Scalability
docs.text:
By setting the bounding box, particles can be culled visually, but it should be noted that unlike ordinary scene objects, particle systems also have simulation costs!

This is a problem that many effect artists easily overlook when using Niagara. Many people think that particles stop when they are not visible, but in reality, they are still executing:

For spawned effects, since they have a certain lifecycle, their simulation consumption is mostly negligible in most cases.

However, for scene effects, if there are too many NiagaraActors placed in the scene, it will have a great impact on the entire program.

To solve this problem, UE provides an asset called NiagaraEffectType to control the simulation optimization strategy of Niagara System.

We can specify the effect type used by the NiagaraSystem here:

Using it can fulfill the following requirements:

  • Limit the maximum display distance of the particle system
  • Limit the maximum number of particle system instances displayed in the current viewport
  • Adjust particle effects according to performance budget
  • Adjust the scaling factor of emitter spawn count

Its configuration panel is as follows:

We can add system and emitter scalability configurations. Each configuration corresponds to the scalability strategy adopted under different performance levels:

The meanings of its parameters are as follows:

  • Culling applies to local player: Whether to allow culling effects generated, attached, or created by the local player.

  • Update frequency: Spawn Only, Low, Medium, High, Continuous.

Both NiagaraEffectType and NiagaraComponent are managed by NiagaraWorldManager. NiagaraEffectType will Tick separately. The update frequency here refers to the frequency at which it detects the current state of NiagaraSystem. The higher the frequency, the more timely the culling response, but the higher the performance overhead.

  • Culling response: Destroy, Destroy and Clear, Dormant, Dormant and Clear.

Clear will immediately kill all particles and then cull the NiagaraSystem. If not cleared, no new particles will be generated, and culling will be performed after all existing particles have finished their lifecycle.

The difference between Destroy and Dormant is that Destroy directly destroys the particles, while Dormant can be regarded as just hiding the particles waiting for activation.

For scene effects, since they are Actors placed in the scene and will not be regenerated after destruction, they are generally set to Dormant. The specific destruction and loading are managed by the large world.

For spawned effects, they are generally spawned once. If set to Dormant, they will occupy memory all the time, so they are generally destroyed.

  • Importance processor: Age, Distance.

The importance processor is mainly related to the Maximum System Instances below. The maximum system proxy determines how many instances of the same type of particle system are allowed to exist currently. The importance processor determines the priority of particle sorting. For example, if distance is the target, there are ten particle systems, and the maximum system instances is five, then NiagaraEffectType will only retain the five closest particle effects.

  • System scalability settings

Setting List: Each added setting item can configure under which environments this item takes effect.

  • Maximum distance: Cull particles according to the distance between the effect and the current player.
  • Cull proxy mode: Instanced Rendering. If Instanced Rendering is enabled, an invisible particle system will be created, and all other culled particle systems of the same type will use it for rendering, which can avoid a lot of simulation costs.
  • Maximum system proxies: Maximum number of system proxies.
  • Budget adjustment: Adjust the scalability strategy of the particle system according to a certain budget.
  • Visibility culling: Cull according to visibility.

For specific descriptions, refer to the Tooltip in the editor panel.

For scene effects, the author highly recommends that everyone uniformly set such an effect type for all scene effects:

The effect of this configuration is: when the particle system is invisible, it will stop both rendering and simulation.

When some effects need special culling strategies, Niagara supports scalability overrides for individual NiagaraSystem and NiagaraEmitter, which can override the configuration of NiagaraEffectType:

For detailed configuration examples of Niagara Effect Type, you can refer to: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-P3yaZNgeg0

docs.title: LOD
docs.text:
Niagara provides a built-in variable LODDistance. We can adapt Niagara's performance parameters based on its value for different distances.

For example, LOD is usually created for spawn count:

docs.title: Warmup Time
docs.text:
For loop effects placed in the scene, they often have a "warmup" period. In Niagara, we can set the system's warmup time to skip this warmup process:

For scene effects with visibility culling, dormant culling will reactivate the particles, and the warmup process will play again at this time:

But after setting the warmup time to skip the warmup process, the effect is like this:

docs.title: Control Emitter Count
docs.text:
Ideally, as long as two emitters use exactly the same renderer parameters, they should use the same emitter.

Because one renderer in an emitter corresponds to one graphics rendering pipeline, and the particle system essentially processes the instanced data required by the graphics rendering pipeline.

One more emitter means one more rendering data and one more particle buffer to maintain.

If you just want to adjust the particle movement mechanism, you can extend it by customizing Modules.

docs.title: Distinguish Between CPU and GPU Particles
docs.text:
CPU particles: Suitable for rendering a small number of particles. Since the data is located in the CPU, it can obtain information about the entire scene, easily interact with game logic, support event communication between particles, precise physical collisions, and dynamically calculate bounding box boundaries.

GPU particles: Have very low performance consumption and are suitable for rendering a large number (100,000-level) of particles.

When distinguishing, the first dimension to consider is the number of particles. If the number of particles is very small (such as a few or dozens), it is best to use CPU particles (because there is no need to increase GPU scheduling overhead for a few particles).

When the number exceeds 1,000, we consider: Does the functional requirement need to use the features of CPU particles? If not, then GPU particles are preferred.

When the number of particles is very large but the features of CPU particles are needed, the functionality of GPU particles needs to be extended at a lower code level.

docs.title: Optimization
docs.text:
Regarding performance optimization, most of the time we pursue: meeting artistic requirements without causing performance​卡顿​.

This indicator is very vague. For most beginners, all we can do is mend the fold after the sheep are lost.

So the first point is crucial: we need to be able to identify performance problems before we can further formulate optimization plans.

docs.title: Performance Localization
docs.text:
UE provides many commands and tools to detect the execution performance of scenes. The following videos can be used as references:

  • [Official Training]22-UE Asset Optimization | Epic Xiao Yue_Bilibili
  • [UnrealCircle Suzhou]UE4 Performance Optimization | Zhou Hua Suzhou Misha Digital Entertainment_Bilibili
  • 【Repost】UnrealFest2023 UE5 Performance Optimization_Bilibili

For engine programmers, they generally need to be proficient in using RenderDoc, Unreal Insight, and various Stat commands, from which we can obtain very detailed performance data.

For Niagara, UE provides a special tool to monitor the execution of Niagara —— Niagara Debugger.

We can open the NiagaraDebugger here:

It can also be started in the details panel of NiagaraSystem:

docs.title: Debug Hud
docs.text:
The Debug Hud page provides many configurable Niagara debug views.

Check Debug View Enabled to see the number of particles and memory of all particle systems currently executing in the scene:

You can check System Show Bounds to display the bounding box of NiagaraSystem:

Check Show System Properties and add Property Match String to add a debug preview view of the particle system:

Particle properties can also be previewed:

When there are many particle systems in the scene, to eliminate interference from other particle debug views, we can set Name Filter to select the particle systems that the debugger needs to focus on:

This configuration only focuses on particle systems whose names start with New.

docs.title: VFX Outline View
docs.text:
The VFX Outline is used to capture frames of Niagara in the scene. It supports three view modes:

Click Capture to capture the execution of Niagara (you can configure the capture delay time and number of frames):

In State mode, we can view the activation status, simulation type (CPU/GPU), and number of particles of all particle systems in the scene:

In Performance mode, we can further view the execution consumption of the particle system in the game thread and rendering thread:

In Debug mode, we can obtain specific particle data during the execution of the particle system:

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The Performance view provides some testing methods:

docs.title: Debug Spawn
docs.text: Debug Spawn provides an interface to spawn effect particles. Just configure the particle system and click Spawn System (needs to be in PIE mode):

docs.title: Module Performance
docs.text: The time consumption of each module can be obtained in the Niagara editor:

docs.title: Resource Occupation
docs.text: You can click Size Map in the asset's content menu to view the size of the referenced textures:

docs.title: Issues and Suggestions
docs.text:
• Before Unreal Engine 5.1, Niagara System had a recompilation BUG. Its manifestation is: when spawning particles in the game for the first time, the entire particle system will be recompiled. This is because saving resources in the Niagara System Editor stores some configurations different from those in the game mode, leading to inconsistent HashID of the particle system and thus invalidating the compilation cache. Therefore, if you need to evaluate the execution performance of the particle system in the game environment, the author recommends testing in the packaged environment.
  • Unreal Engine provides very complete supporting tools for Niagara, but for a large team, it is easy to use but not easy to manage. The author highly recommends further expanding on the basis of the above toolset and adding automated processes to complete macro particle system management.
  • For some​常规​ rendering optimizations, such as optimizing materials, simplifying models, and reducing Overdraw, they are also applicable to Niagara.

docs.title: Production Optimization
docs.text:
The optimization experience summarized in the process of mending the fold after the sheep are lost is precious. It can gradually let artists understand how to create high-performance particle effects.

The following are some insights that can help effect artists optimize production (mainly for GPU particles):

docs.title: Computing Power Awareness
docs.text:
1920 x 1080 is a common resolution for computer monitors nowadays. This means there are nearly 2 million pixels on the screen, which also means the computer needs to perform nearly 2 million pixel-level numerical processes to draw one frame. Currently, some mid-range hardware devices can easily draw hundreds or thousands of images per second. This amazing computing power benefits from the rapid development of the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU). Unlike the Central Processing Unit (CPU), which is the scheduling center of the computer and whose architecture needs to take all aspects of the system into account, the GPU is a specialized approach. Its architecture is filled with a large number of computing units to meet the needs of graphics operations.

Taking the current cutting-edge consumer graphics card GeForce RTX 4090 as an example, it has more than 76 billion transistors and more than 16,000 computing cores.

After understanding this upper limit, we can simply correspond a single GPU particle to a pixel point. That is, under normal circumstances, mid-range graphics cards can easily simulate millions of particle effects.

But it should be noted that the million-level is often the upper limit of the entire system. We usually cannot allocate all performance budgets to the particle system. So in general, if the total number of particles exceeds 100,000, it may cause performance pressure on the entire rendering system.

If these 100,000 particles are converted into the corresponding number of 1x1 pixels for tiling, it roughly corresponds to an image of 300x300 size:

The closer the screen occupation area of the particle system is to its tiling area, the better its performance (because there is less OverDraw).

The following is an ordinary NiagaraSystem with 140,000 particles, which fails to match the performance it should have for such a large number:

And as the view moves away, its OverDraw becomes more and more serious:

This problem can be optimized by using LOD curves based on distance to adjust the number of particles.

docs.title: Underlying Principles
docs.text:
Niagara itself is a programmable data processor provided by UE. In the NiagaraEditor, we can freely control the processing structure of this processor:

And in each Stage, use the visual nodes provided by the engine to write corresponding Modules to formulate data processing logic:

These visual node logics will be translated into ComputerShader code:

The results of data processing will be bound to the corresponding attribute slots of the renderer, providing the renderer to complete the final expression of the particle effect:

From the perspective of data processing, our key goal is how to create an efficient data processor. Therefore, mastering the principles of the underlying modules of Niagara is crucial for overall performance and effect control.

Here is a very excellent tutorial:

  • [Official Training]09-UE Particle Basics | Xiao Yue Epic Bilibili

docs.title: Sprite Sheet Baking
docs.text: Niagara Editor supports baking particle effects into sprite sheets. For some effects with fixed viewing angles, we can adopt this scheme to obtain a great degree of optimization.

docs.title: Procedural Content Generation
docs.text:
Particle systems are mainly suitable for simulating a large number of dynamic objects, but only under some specific requirements do we have to use particle systems for real-time simulation:

  • Creating interactive dynamic effects
  • Need to create a 3D effect with no visual dead angles
  • Very large number of large-scale clusters

Excluding the above usage scenarios, we can usually achieve the desired performance effect by baking static materials.

So when creating particle effects, we need to carefully examine: Is it necessary to use the particle system for real-time simulation?

If yes, then we further think: Can some real-time calculation stages in the particle system be replaced with pre-made static data?

For example, when creating effects related to the scene, the simulation of particles may need some scene information as input. Most of the time, this scene data is static. We don't need to calculate the relevant information of the scene in real time at runtime. We can generate this data statically in the editor. This way, we can create effects highly integrated with the scene with less performance cost. This improvement is particularly obvious when the number of particle systems is large.

We can also create Procedural Content Generation (PCG) assets on Niagara:

  • In the User Parameters of Niagara System, add the scene data required by the particle system (here, a variable named SpawnPositionArray is added):

  • Create a new Actor Blueprint, add NiagaraComponent, and specify Niagara System.

  • In the BeginPlay event of the blueprint, set the parameters we added in Niagara, and promote the parameter input to a variable (Partcile Spawn Position Array):

  • Add a function (e.g., named CalcParticleSpawnPositionArray) in the blueprint, check Call In Editor, and in this function, obtain scene information (no need to care about performance, you can scan Actors, cast rays...), and fill the blueprint variable value (Partcile Spawn Position Array):

  • Place the Actor blueprint in the scene, and you can find that the function we created earlier has become a clickable button in its details panel:

  • Clicking the button will execute the corresponding function logic, which will execute and fill the blueprint properties. These property values will be serialized when saved. When the game starts normally, BeginPlay will execute and submit this data to Niagara.

  • Then, we can write the corresponding Module in Niagara to use this part of the data.

It should be noted that we cannot directly set the Niagara parameters in CalcParticleSpawnPositionArray, but use the blueprint variable property serialization to store the scene data.

This is because the functions for setting Niagara parameters (starting with NiagaraSet...) directly upload the data to Niagara's data processor without storing it. Therefore, setting Niagara parameters through functions may not necessarily show parameter changes in the details panel of the NiagaraSystem (some property types do return synchronization of editor data, so changes can be seen in the details panel).

docs.title: Fluid Ninja
docs.text:
Fluid Ninja is an amazing interactive fluid simulation plugin that allows you to create stunning effects with extremely low performance overhead:

  • Author's YouTube: https://www.youtube.com/c/AndrasKetzer
  • Unreal Marketplace: https://www.unrealengine.com/marketplace/en-US/product/fluidninja-live
  • Discussion Community (Discord): https://discord.com/invite/rgEtwua2tu

The author has many video tutorials on YouTube:

  • FluidNinja LIVE - ALL IN ONE TUTORIAL and making FX from scratch - YouTube

  • FluidNinja Chinese Tutorial - Tao Renxian

docs.title: Acquisition
docs.text:
For student users, you can download the free student version from the Fluid Ninja Discord community:

For commercial users, please purchase the FluidNinja plugin from the Unreal Marketplace:

  • https://www.unrealengine.com/marketplace/en-US/product/fluidninja-live

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
There are numerous example levels in Content/FluidNinjaLive/Tutorial/Levels/, each with detailed descriptive text:

The best way to learn is to replicate these levels one by one and understand their parameter configurations:

docs.title: NinjaLiveComponent
docs.text:
NinjaLiveComponent is the core of Fluid Ninja. To use it, you must attach a static mesh (usually a plane, called the Trace Mesh). The final result of the fluid simulation will be output as the material of the trace mesh:

The red plane in the image above is the trace mesh

docs.title: NinjaLive
docs.text:
NinjaLive is a default Actor provided by Fluid Ninja. It wraps the parameters of NinjaLiveComponent, includes a trace plane that meets most usage requirements, simplifies the setup of NinjaLiveComponent, and adds some additional features, such as:

  • Culling and​休眠​ of NinjaFluid through ActivationVolume; NinjaLiveComponent will only activate when entering the ActivationVolume
  • Setting interaction areas with finer granularity through InteractionVolume.

docs.title: NinjaLive_Utilities
docs.text:
NinjaLive_Utilities (Blueprint Actor) provides some convenient debugging functions, such as:

  • Automatically controlling the player closest to this blueprint
  • Showing the mouse
  • Adjusting the quality of anti-aliasing, depth of field, and motion blur
  • Lifting the editor's 120FPS limit
  • ...

You can drag this blueprint into the scene and configure it:

docs.title: NinjaLive_PresetManager
docs.text:
NinjaLive_PresetManager (Blueprint Actor) is used to adjust parameter presets of NinjaLive.

Drag it into the scene and start PIE, and you will see the following panel:

docs.title: NinjaLive_MemoryPoolManager
docs.text: NinjaLive_MemoryPoolManager (Blueprint Actor) is used to configure the memory strategy of FluidNinja.

docs.title: Simulation Process
docs.text:
In the asset directory of FluidNinja, there is a blueprint named Help:

It contains a detailed flowchart describing the Fluid Ninja simulation:

The core of NinjaFluid lies in:

  • Constructing Density maps and Velocity maps
  • Overlaying Noise to increase the randomness of the fluid
  • Adjusting Brushes to control the shape of the fluid
  • Combining with Output Materials
  • Outputting the final result to the material surface of the Trace Mesh
  • Obtaining the desired result:

  • Density is a single-channel texture with a value range of [0,1], used to represent the density of the fluid at the current position.
  • Velocity is a two-channel texture with a value range of [0,1], used to represent the vector velocity of the fluid at the current position. Since it is normalized to [0,1], a velocity of 0 actually corresponds to an RG value of (0.5, 0.5). In the image above:
  • The R channel of the Velocity texture corresponds to horizontal velocity; when the value is <0.5, the fluid moves to the left; when it is >0.5, the fluid moves to the right
  • The G channel of the Velocity texture corresponds to vertical velocity; when the value is <0.5, the fluid moves upward; when it is >0.5, the fluid moves downward
  • FluidNinja allows input of three-channel materials, where the RG channels represent Velocity and the B channel represents Density

docs.title: Usage Workflow
docs.text:
During production, we essentially operate on the NinjaLiveComponent, whose Configuration Categories include:

  • Live Activation: Only has a Disable Component option, which can be dynamically set via blueprints for culling.
  • Live Interaction: All interaction-related configurations, such as filtering interaction targets, orientation and locking of the trace mesh, world coordinate offset, etc.
  • Live Brush Setting: Parameter configuration of the brush.
  • Live Generic: General configuration, mainly adjusting effect presets, inputs, and outputs.
  • Live Performance: Performance configuration, which can configure the number of effect iterations, FPS range limits, LOD, etc.
  • Live Compatibility: Compatibility configuration, which can configure collision channels, override inputs, etc.
  • Live Debug: Debug configuration, providing some checkboxes for printing prompt information.
  • Live Raymarching: Configure Raymarching.
  • Live Memory Management: Configure memory management.

docs.title: Building Inputs
docs.text:
The inputs here mainly refer to Density and Velocity. The relevant input configuration parameters are mainly located under the Live Generic category of the NiagaraComponent. The input sources of Fluid Ninja can be the following:

  • Static textures
  • Dynamic materials
  • Scene camera capture
  • Render Targets
  • Streaming videos
  • Mouse input
  • Scene interactions: static meshes, dynamic meshes, skeletal meshes, destructibles...

The above inputs are not independent; they can coexist. FluidNinja will mix multiple inputs together. For details, see the flowchart in Help.uasset.

In the map Content/FluidNinjaLive/Tutorial/Levels/NinjaLive_Level03_SimulationInputs_LIVE17.umap, there are complete NinjaFluid input examples. The key steps for these inputs are recorded below:

docs.title: Static Texture
docs.text:
The input settings for static textures are located in the NinjaPreset data table:

Normally, we do not directly modify the content of the data table. Instead, in the test level, we use the editor panel provided by NinjaLive_PresetManager to export the preset table:

docs.title: Dynamic Material
docs.text:
The input configuration for materials is located under the Live Generic category of the NinjaComponent:

  • You can add available input materials in the Input Materials parameter. You can add multiple materials so that you can switch and preview them in NinjaLive_PresetManager.
  • Adjust the Input Material Selected index to choose the currently used input material.
  • Checking RGB-Input Material will make the RG channels of the material serve as the Velocity texture and the B channel as the Density texture; otherwise, by default, only the R channel of the material will be used as the Density texture
  • Checking Input Material Clamp will crop the image where UV coordinates are outside [0,1].

For input materials of Ninja Fluid, you need to select the Material Domain as Post Process and disable Cast Ray Traced Shadows:

docs.title: Scene Capture 2D
docs.text:
FluidNinja can use a camera to capture the scene and use the image within the camera frame as input for the fluid simulation. The specific configuration is located under the Live Generic category of the NinjaComponent:

  • You can select an existing Actor in the current scene in Input Scene Capture Camera

Example:

  • Create a Ninja Live, a Cube, and a Scene Capture 2D, and aim the camera at the Cube to be captured

  • In the Ninja Component of Ninja Live, configure the Scene Capture 2D and select a more intuitive material output:

  • Execute PIE, and you will see the following effect:

  • You can adjust the capture configuration (camera parameters, object filtering...) in Scene Capture 2D, and use NinjaLive_PresetManager to adjust its parameter effects:

docs.title: Render Target
docs.text:
The input configuration for materials is located under the Live Generic category of the NinjaComponent:

  • Checking Use Render Target as Input will use the Input Render Target below as the input for the fluid simulation
  • Input Render Target is used to specify the Render Target to read

In Fluid Ninja, this solution can be used to create morphologically controllable 3D fluids

There is the following example in Level 3:

  • On the left is a Niagara particle system, in the middle is the projected RT, and on the right is the final effect displayed using RT + output material

Example:

  • Create a new [Niagara Particle System] in the Content Browser and select [Copy from Existing System]

  • Uncheck Library Only, and find NS_ParticleCaptureBasic in the Standard category:

  • After creation, open the particle system and you will find it contains two default emitters:

  • NE_ParticleCaptureBasic: Used to map particles from the Empty emitter to the RenderTarget through grid coordinates. You can select which emitter to capture in AttributeReader.

  • Empty: Particle emitter used for simulation

  • Below is an effect achieved by giving it an emission speed (60) and adding a scattered random initial velocity:

  • NE_ParticleCaptureBasic will use the captured particle data to "project" onto a RenderTarget based on the coordinates of all particles. We can set the strategy for this projection process in the user parameters:

  • In the user parameters, RT_PrevivewParticleCapture is used by default as the RT output. It may be shared by other particle systems, and using it directly will conflict with other logic (tutorial levels). Therefore, we need to create our own RT:

  • Specify it in the default parameters of the NiagaraSystem, and try adjusting the user parameters to understand the RT mapping rules:

  • Drag the configured NiagaraSystem into the scene, and place a NinjaLiveActor floating in the scene. Set TraceMeshSize to (5, 5, 1) in the details panel of NinjaLive, enable Camera Facing Trace Mesh in the details of NinjaLiveComponent, enable RT input, specify the RT just created, and select the output material as MI_DensityBuffer_Red:

  • Start PIE, and we can see the following effect:

  • In fact, we do not need to render the NiagaraSystem; we only need its simulation data. NS_ParticleCaptureBasic is enabled by default only for debugging convenience, so we can disable the renderer of the particle emitter:

  • In addition, since the rendering of RT also depends on the camera position, to obtain a more accurate planar image, we need to overlap the positions of NiagaraSystem and NinjaLive, select an appropriate output material effect, and then we can see:

docs.title: Video Input
docs.text:
To use a video file as input for NinjaFluid, you need to specify the following three parameters:

  • Input Media Player: Video player
  • Media Texture: Texture used for video rendering
  • Input Media Source: Video playback source

For how to play videos in UE, you can refer to the article https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/135963353

Example:

  • Add a NinjaLiveActor, specify a video as Density input, set an upward Velocity texture T_Crumple, and combine it with the output material MI_Candle1 to get the following effect:

docs.title: User Input
docs.text:
NinjaLiveActor enables mouse input by default, and its effect is as follows:

You can disable it here:

docs.title: Collision Interaction
docs.text:
Fluid Ninja can use physical collisions as input to achieve some interactive fluid effects. A simple example is as follows:

  • Add a NinjaLiveActor

  • Set Trace Mesh Size and Interaction Volume Size to (5,5,1)

  • Set NinjaLiveComponent\Live Bursh Settings; otherwise, the result may not be visible due to the collision brush being too small

    • Check Brush Scaled By Interacting Obj Size
    • Set Primitive Obj Brush Scale to 20

  • Add a Mannequin, and you can see the following effect:

This effect is achieved through UE's physical collision mechanism, and its complete parameters are all located in NinjaLiveComponent\Live Interaction:

  • Continuous Interaction with Owner Actor: Continuously interact with the Actor holding this component
  • Continuous Interaction incluisve Obj Type: Filter the collision object types for interaction
  • Continuous Interaction Component Name: Filter the component names for interaction
  • Continuous Interaction Bone Names Exact: Filter the bone names for interaction
