  • Single Target Mode: Single target mode; when enabled, FluidNinja considers that the images generated by collisions are all produced by one target, which can make the collision path smooth without​断层​ (interpolation)
  • Single Target Type
  • Single Target Mode Skeletal Mesh Index
  • Single Target Move Set Sim Speed
  • Speed Influence Factor: Speed influence factor
  • Clamp Max Velocity: Clamp maximum velocity
  • Camera Facing Tace Mesh: TraceMesh always faces the camera
  • Camera Facing Lock Y-Axis: Lock the Y-axis of the camera
  • Use Legacy Camera Facing
  • Trance Mesh Translucent Sort Prio
  • Use Custom Trace Source: Use a custom trace source; when enabled, it is equivalent to using the following position as the camera position for collision detection
  • Custom Trace Source Position: Position of the custom trace source
  • Trace Mesh Moving in World Space: TraceMesh is located in world space
  • Movement Not Quantized to Steps OnAxis
  • Movements is Locked on This axis: Lock movement on a certain axis
  • Force Trace Mesh to Custom Vertical Pos
  • Force Trace Mesh Vertical Position: Lock the position of the TraceMesh
  • Enable Paint Buffer Offset in World Spacing: Enable the world space mechanism of the paint buffer offset
  • Simple Painter Mode: Simple painter mode without collision input

For NinjaLiveActor, the above parameters are further encapsulated, and the following parameters can be adjusted:

  • Overlap Based Interaction: Enable collision interaction

  • Interaction Volume Size: Size of the interaction volume

  • The following parameters are used to filter which objects can "interact" with the interaction volume.

  • Track Actor Primitive Components With Tag: Track components with this tag
  • Track Actor Skeletal Mesh Components With Tag: Track skeletal mesh components with this tag
  • Overlap Filter Inclusive Obj Tab: Inclusive object collision types for filtering
  • Overlap Filter Inclusive Bone Name Exact: Inclusive bone names for filtering; if empty, all bones will be processed
  • Overlap Filter Inclusive Bone Name Partial: Partial bone names for filtering; for example, entering "Foot" will include all bones with names containing "Foot"
  • Exclude Specific Actors from Overlap: Actor types to exclude from overlap
  • Auto Exclude Large Overlapping Objects: Automatically exclude large overlapping objects

docs.title: Adjusting Brushes
docs.text:
Brushes are used to control the scaling factor of the action area of FluidNinja input maps. Their parameter configurations are as follows:

Some key parameters:

  • Brush Scaled Inversely by Trace Mesh Size: The brush scales inversely with the size of the trace mesh
  • Brush Scaled by Interacting Obj Size: The brush scales with the size of the interacting object
  • Use Obj Bounds Instead of Size: Use the bounds of the interacting object as the brush size
  • Global Brush Scale: Global brush scaling factor

If the effect of collision interaction is almost invisible, it is likely that the brush is too small

docs.title: Preset Configuration
docs.text:
The preset table contains parameters related to fluid simulation:

Read the prompt information of the parameters in NinjaLive_PresetManager, understand their relationship with the effect by adjusting them, and save them as a new table after configuring the parameters.

docs.title: Output Materials
docs.text:
The core materials used by FluidNinjaLive are defined in its content directory:

We can directly use the material instances in the Instance_* folder

Or create a new material instance and set the parent to the base material provided by FluidNinja (material file names start with M_NinjaOutput_):

  • M_NinjaOutput_Basic: Basic material
  • M_NinjaOutput_Advanced: Advanced material
  • M_NinjaOutput_TranslucentReflective: Translucent reflective material
  • M_NinjaOutput_WorldSpaceGeneric: World space material
  • ...

Taking M_NinjaOutput_Basic as an example, it provides many adjustable parameter presets:

In the Tutorial and Usercase levels of FluidNinja, there are many material examples for reference. The specific meanings of the parameters can be learned through replication.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
FluidNinja has an ingenious​思路​ and is a bit cumbersome to use, but the key steps are clear:

  • Construct the Density and Velocity maps required for the simulation process, use appropriate brushes and presets, and combine them with corresponding materials to present the final desired effect.

docs.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
docs.text:
• FluidNinja uses 2D planes to disguise 3D visual effects. Its performance overhead is much lower than conventional particle fluid simulations. However, to disguise sufficiently realistic 3D effects, you need sufficiently realistic 2D inputs; otherwise, the trace mesh plane of FluidNinja can be easily​识破​ from certain perspectives.
  • FluidNinja provides many ways to construct fluid inputs: textures, materials, RT, Niagara, cameras... which can meet most development needs. However, there are many details, and it is not easy to use. In-depth learning is required to freely create the desired effects.
  • FluidNinja cannot completely replace particles; it is more suitable for interactive fluid simulations, such as smoke, fire, water...

docs.title: Unreal Engine 5 Open World
docs.text:
The author previously compiled a non-technical chat about open worlds:

  • Game Development Chat - Open World - Zhihu / Italink

This article will explain in more detail what to pay attention to and what challenges you will face when creating an open world with UE5.

docs.title: World Partition
docs.text:
When creating an open world map in UE5, you need to clearly understand the concepts of Partition and Streaming. Here are some MUST-READ! MUST-READ! MUST-READ! resources:

  • Building Virtual Worlds in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.3 Documentation (unrealengine.com)
  • Unreal Fest 2023 - Building Bigger
  • [UFSH2023] Workflow Upgrade from Creating Small Scenes to Building Large Worlds | Chris Murphy Epic Games

There are also some easy-to-understand explanatory videos:

  • 【UE Terrain】What is World Partition? How to Use It? - bilibili
  • UE5 World Partition Part 1 Concepts - YouTube

In short, UE divides the map into many Cells, and Streams surrounding cells as the Player (streaming source) moves:

In the image above, we only see a four-directional division, but in fact, UE's World Partition uses a sparse quadtree approach for streaming, and it has multiple grid levels. What we see is only Level 0:

docs.title: Partition
docs.text:
World Partition determines which Grid Level and Cell an object belongs to based on its bounding box.

For example, suppose there are the following objects in our world partition, with red areas representing the horizontal Area of their Bounds:

When partitioning, World Partition starts from the lowest grid level and assigns objects to the smallest cell that can fully contain their area.

Therefore, the final partition of the above objects is as follows:

You can set partition-related parameters here:

Checking Preview Grid allows you to see the streaming view of the scene in the editor view:

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
By default, newly created Actors in the scene will participate in streaming, meaning they will be unloaded. You can adjust related settings in the Actor's Details panel:

  • Runtime Grid: Which World Partition grid the Actor belongs to. If set to None, it will be assigned to MainGrid.
  • Is Spatially Loaded: If checked, the Actor will participate in World Partition streaming. Unchecking it will keep the Actor permanently loaded in the scene and exclude it from streaming.

World Partition streaming is triggered by Streaming Sources.

The C++ interface corresponding to streaming sources is: IWorldPartitionStreamingSourceProvider

PlayerController is a default streaming source:

Suppose the character is located at the bottom right corner of the map. Combined with the partition above, the overall loading status might look like this:

We can also use the WorldPartitionStreamingSourceComponent to make other actors act as streaming sources:

docs.title: Debug Views
docs.text:
The official provides some commands to preview the streaming process:

  • wp.Runtime.ToggleDrawRuntimeHash2D

  • wp.Runtime.ToggleDrawRuntimeHash3D

  • After enabling the preview view:

  • Use the command wp.Runtime.ShowRuntimeSpatialHashGridLevel ${LevelIndex} to adjust the preview level.

  • Use the command wp.Runtime.ToggleDrawRuntimeCellsDetails to see the loading time of cells:

  • Use the command wp.Runtime.ShowRuntimeSpatialHashCellStreamingPriority 1 to view the streaming priority heatmap of cells:

docs.title: Multiplayer
docs.text:
In multiplayer, the server does not enable streaming by default; scene streaming is only a local behavior of players:

Use the command wp.Runtime.EnableServerStreaming 1 to enable streaming on the server:

docs.title: Streaming Optimization
docs.text:
World Partition enables streaming optimization by default, which means streaming status is not updated every frame. You can adjust the optimization strategy through the following configurations:

  • wp.Runtime.UpdateStreaming.EnableOptimization true: Defaults to true, enabling streaming optimization.
  • wp.Runtime.UpdateStreaming.ForceUpdateFrameCount 0: Defaults to 0, can set how many frames to fix for updating streaming status.
  • wp.Runtime.UpdateStreaming.LocationQuantization 400: Defaults to 400, triggers streaming status update when movement distance exceeds 400.
  • wp.Runtime.UpdateStreaming.RotationQuantization 10: Defaults to 10, triggers streaming status update when rotation angle exceeds 10.

docs.title: Code Flow
docs.text:
For developers, a deep understanding of the World Partition flow is crucial for overall project control! Artists can skip this section.

Here are some key steps explained.

The core structure of UE's World Partition is: UWorldPartition

It is stored in AWorldSettings and can be obtained through the following method:

UWorldPartition* UWorld::GetWorldPartition() const
{
    AWorldSettings* WorldSettings = GetWorldSettings(/*bCheckStreamingPersistent*/false, /*bChecked*/false);
    return WorldSettings ? WorldSettings->GetWorldPartition() : nullptr;
}

Actor's support for World Partition is mainly reflected in the addition of an editor-only virtual function in the Actor base class for creating World Partition Actor descriptions:

class AActor : public UObject
#if WITH_EDITOR
    virtual TUniquePtr<class FWorldPartitionActorDesc> CreateClassActorDesc() const;
#endif
}

It can be overridden by subclasses to populate the following structure:

class FWorldPartitionActorDesc
{
    // Persistent
    FGuid                           Guid;
    FTopLevelAssetPath              BaseClass;
    FTopLevelAssetPath              NativeClass;
    FName                           ActorPackage;
    FSoftObjectPath                 ActorPath;
    FName                           ActorLabel;
    FVector                         BoundsLocation;
    FVector                         BoundsExtent;
    FName                           RuntimeGrid;
    bool                            bIsSpatiallyLoaded;
    bool                            bActorIsEditorOnly;
    bool                            bActorIsRuntimeOnly;
    bool                            bActorIsHLODRelevant;
    bool                            bIsUsingDataLayerAsset; // Used to know if DataLayers array represents DataLayers Asset paths or the FNames of the deprecated version of Data Layers
    FName                           HLODLayer;
    TArray<FName>                   DataLayers;
    TArray<FGuid>                   References;
    TArray<FName>                   Tags;
    FPropertyPairsMap               Properties;
    FName                           FolderPath;
    FGuid                           FolderGuid;
    FGuid                           ParentActor; // Used to validate settings against parent (to warn on layer/placement compatibility issues)
    FGuid                           ContentBundleGuid;

    // Transient
    mutable uint32                  SoftRefCount;
    mutable uint32                  HardRefCount;
    UClass*                         ActorNativeClass;
    mutable TWeakObjectPtr<AActor>  ActorPtr;
    UActorDescContainer*            Container;
    TArray<FName>                   DataLayerInstanceNames;
    bool                            bIsForcedNonSpatiallyLoaded;
};

There are many overrides in the engine:

In the editor, creating a new Actor in a World Partition map will automatically create FWorldPartitionActorDesc:

In the editor, all created ActorDescs are stored in ActorDescContainer of UWorldPartition:

class UWorldPartition final 
    : public UObject
    , public FActorDescContainerCollection
    , public IWorldPartitionCookPackageGenerator
{

    UPROPERTY(Transient)
    TObjectPtr<UActorDescContainer> ActorDescContainer;     // Container storing ActorDescs, also known as **MainContainer**

    UPROPERTY()
    TObjectPtr<UWorldPartitionRuntimeHash> RuntimeHash;     // Used to customize Actor partition strategy

    UPROPERTY(Transient)
    TObjectPtr<UWorld> World;
};

Although ActorDescContainer is a transient variable and does not participate in serialization, it is stored during packaging:

bool UWorldPartition::GatherPackagesToCook(IWorldPartitionCookPackageContext& CookContext)
{
    TArray<FString> PackagesToCook;
    if (GenerateContainerStreaming(ActorDescContainer, &PackagesToCook))
    {
        FString PackageName = GetPackage()->GetName();
        for (const FString& PackageToCook : PackagesToCook)
        {
            CookContext.AddLevelStreamingPackageToGenerate(this, PackageName, PackageToCook);
        }
        return true;
    }
    return false;
}

docs.title: Partition
docs.text:
The Actor partition strategy of UWorldPartition is implemented by RuntimeHash. In the editor, RuntimeHash re-partitions every time the map is started, and during packaging, the partition data is also baked:

bool UWorldPartition::PrepareGeneratorPackageForCook(IWorldPartitionCookPackageContext& CookContext, TArray<UPackage*>& OutModifiedPackages)
{
    check(RuntimeHash);
    return RuntimeHash->PrepareGeneratorPackageForCook(OutModifiedPackages);
}

bool UWorldPartition::PopulateGeneratorPackageForCook(IWorldPartitionCookPackageContext& CookContext, const TArray<FWorldPartitionCookPackage*>& InPackagesToCook, TArray<UPackage*>& OutModifiedPackages)
{
    check(RuntimeHash);
    return RuntimeHash->PopulateGeneratorPackageForCook(InPackagesToCook, OutModifiedPackages);
}

bool UWorldPartition::PopulateGeneratedPackageForCook(IWorldPartitionCookPackageContext& CookContext, const FWorldPartitionCookPackage& InPackagesToCook, TArray<UPackage*>& OutModifiedPackages)
{
    check(RuntimeHash);
    return RuntimeHash->PopulateGeneratedPackageForCook(InPackagesToCook, OutModifiedPackages);
}

UWorldPartitionRuntimeCell* UWorldPartition::GetCellForPackage(const FWorldPartitionCookPackage& PackageToCook) const
{
    check(RuntimeHash);
    return RuntimeHash->GetCellForPackage(PackageToCook);
}

In the editor, when starting an open world map, UWorldPartition::OnBeginPlay is called:

void UWorldPartition::OnBeginPlay()
{
    TArray<FString> OutGeneratedStreamingPackageNames;
    GenerateStreaming((bIsPIE || IsRunningGame()) ? &OutGeneratedStreamingPackageNames : nullptr);

    // Prepare GeneratedStreamingPackages
    check(GeneratedStreamingPackageNames.IsEmpty());
    for (const FString& PackageName : OutGeneratedStreamingPackageNames)
    {
        // Set as memory package to avoid wasting time in UWorldPartition::IsValidPackageName (GenerateStreaming for PIE runs on the editor world)
        FString Package = FPaths::RemoveDuplicateSlashes(FPackageName::IsMemoryPackage(PackageName) ? PackageName : TEXT("/Memory/") + PackageName);
        GeneratedStreamingPackageNames.Add(Package);
    }

    RuntimeHash->OnBeginPlay();
}

The GenerateStreaming function further calls UWorldPartition::GenerateContainerStreaming, which recursively searches for all Containers and ActorDescs from the MainContainer.

Some ActorDescs hold their own Containers, such as FLevelInstanceActorDesc which is a special case—it is a Level Instance placed in the scene. Its main code definition is as follows:

class FLevelInstanceActorDesc : public FWorldPartitionActorDesc
{
public:
    FLevelInstanceActorDesc();
    virtual ~FLevelInstanceActorDesc() override;

    virtual bool IsContainerInstance() const override;
    virtual bool GetContainerInstance(const UActorDescContainer*& OutLevelContainer, 
                                      FTransform& OutLevelTransform, 
                                      EContainerClusterMode& OutClusterMode) const override;
protected:
    FTransform LevelInstanceTransform;
    ELevelInstanceRuntimeBehavior DesiredRuntimeBehavior;
    TWeakObjectPtr<UActorDescContainer> LevelInstanceContainer;  // ActorDescContainer for Level Instance
private:
    void RegisterContainerInstance(UWorld* InWorld);
    void UnregisterContainerInstance();
};

After collecting all Containers and ActorDescs, the following function is called:

bool UWorldPartitionRuntimeSpatialHash::GenerateStreaming(UWorldPartitionStreamingPolicy* StreamingPolicy,
                                                          const IStreamingGenerationContext* StreamingGenerationContext,
                                                          TArray<FString>* OutPackagesToGenerate);

The main flow of this function is:

  • Collect all grid configurations in the scene (not only WorldSettings contain grid configurations, some Actors also provide them, such as ASpatialHashRuntimeGridInfo, which is currently mainly used for HLOD).
  • Iterate through all ActorDescs and assign them to the corresponding Grid's FActorSetInstance based on the RuntimeGrid configuration in the ActorDesc.
  • For each Grid's FActorSetInstance, call:
FSquare2DGridHelper GetPartitionedActors(const FBox& WorldBounds, 
                                         const FSpatialHashRuntimeGrid& Grid, 
                                         const TArray<const FActorSetInstance*>& ActorSetInstances)

to assign all Actors in the Grid to specific Cells.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: The streaming logic is mainly located in:

docs.title: Key Issues
docs.text: World Partition allows us to easily implement seamless loading of large worlds, but the streaming feature also brings many limitations. This often requires developers to have a more mature production team and a professional engine team, fully consider the characteristics of World Partition during design, and need professionals to supervise the streaming strategy of World Partition.

docs.title: Cross-Boundary
docs.text:
Observe the previous object partitioning and streaming status:

You can see some "strange" phenomena:

  • Because the bounding box of object E is on the axis of the World Partition, it is assigned to Level 3, which means it will always be loaded, even though its bounding box area is very small.

This problem is very easy to occur:

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
The engine provides some commands to help alleviate this phenomenon:

  • wp.Runtime.RuntimeSpatialHashUseAlignedGridLevels: Whether to enable upward alignment of grid levels.
  • wp.Runtime.RuntimeSpatialHashSnapNonAlignedGridLevelsToLowerLevels: Assign non-aligned objects to lower grid levels.
  • wp.Runtime.RuntimeSpatialHashPlaceSmallActorsUsingLocation: Objects with bounding boxes smaller than the cell size will be partitioned directly using their Location.
  • wp.Runtime.RuntimeSpatialHashPlacePartitionActorsUsingLocation: Partition objects (vegetation, water, and terrain) with bounding boxes smaller than the cell size will be partitioned directly using their Location.

Here is a description of it:

  • Tech Note: World Partition Spatially Loaded Actors are Always Loaded - Epic Developer Community Forums

But this is not a perfect solution. To avoid these problems, UE allows development teams to customize the RuntimeHashClass according to their scene requirements. Replace it here:

Reference: Engine\Source\Runtime\Engine\Private\WorldPartition\RuntimeSpatialHash\RuntimeSpatialHashGridHelper.cpp

In UE5.3, the official exposed the above configurations to the editor and allowed adjusting the coordinate origin of the World Partition, which can meet most needs:

docs.title: Loading Priority
docs.text:
Due to World Partition streaming, some moving objects in the scene may behave abnormally. Gravity is one of the most common issues:

The problems in the image above are:

  • Some cubes are assigned to one cell, while the ground is assigned to another cell due to limitations of the partitioning algorithm. If the cell containing the ground is outside the loading range, the objects will fall through the ground.

Other situations can also trigger this problem:

  • World Partition streaming is performed per Cell, not per Actor. When a cell is within the loading range of the streaming source, all Actors in that cell are loaded asynchronously. The loading order is not guaranteed. If the cube is loaded before the ground and a physics tick occurs during this period, the object will fall through the ground. (This is more likely to happen when the scene is under heavy load.)

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
The main ideas to solve this problem are:

  • Make the World Partition grid containing gravity-bearing objects have a larger loading range.
  • Move gravity objects to a World Partition grid with lower loading priority than gravity-bearing objects.

docs.title: Data Persistence
docs.text:
Actors participating in World Partition do not have data persistence. When we modify a loaded object, the modified data will not be saved when the object is unloaded.

For example: There are a group of floating cubes in the World Partition. After loading, they fall to the ground due to gravity. After unloading and reloading, you can see that the cubes have correctly saved their previous state and are on the ground:

But when we enable the console command gc.ForceCollectGarbageEveryFrame 1 and look again:

When reloading the cubes this time, they return to their starting position.

The first example gives us the illusion that object modifications can be saved because cells outside the loading range are not immediately released but are in the Unloaded Still Around state. This ensures they can be reused immediately when loaded next time. The actual unloading of cells occurs during the next GC.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
This problem is caused by the characteristics of streaming:

  • Assets are loaded into memory when streaming in and unloaded (resources destroyed) when streaming out, without saving modifications to the assets.

Does this mean we need to save asset modifications when streaming out?

  • Obviously not, unless you want to make permanent modifications—meaning the previous modifications remain even after restarting the game and cannot be reverted.

Usually, such modifications only persist within a certain scope (lifecycle), such as after restarting the game, re-entering the level, or reloading a save, these modifications should be lost.

But what we want now is that streaming does not cause data loss.

In fact, we only need:

  • To prevent this part of the data from participating in streaming, i.e., store the data in a reasonable scope instead of in the Actor.

UE5.3 provides an experimental plugin LevelStreamingPersistence to help developers solve this problem.

This plugin uses ULevelStreamingPersistenceSettings to configure which properties in the engine require persistence:

When World Partition streams cells, it saves the persistent properties of the outgoing cells according to the above configuration. For incoming cells, it assigns values using previous historical values:

To solve the gravity problem above, we only need to add the following configuration to DefaultEngine.ini:

[/Script/LevelStreamingPersistence.LevelStreamingPersistenceSettings]
Properties=(Path="/Script/Engine.SceneComponent:RelativeLocation",bIsPublic=False)
Properties=(Path="/Script/Engine.SceneComponent:RelativeRotation",bIsPublic=False)

Using PropertyPath to determine which properties often results in a very broad scope. For example, the above configuration serializes the location and rotation of all Scene Components, but not all Scene Components need persistence. The plugin also provides some delegates to further filter which objects need serialization:

bIsPublic determines whether the saved value of the property can be modified manually, not just automatically serialized based on streaming. The main operation interfaces are located in ULevelStreamingPersistenceManager:

class ULevelStreamingPersistenceManager : public UWorldSubsystem
{
    GENERATED_BODY()

    // Serialization
    bool SerializeTo(TArray<uint8>& OutPayload);
    bool InitializeFrom(const TArray<uint8>& InPayload);

    // Sets property value and creates the entry if necessary, returns true on success.
    template <typename ClassType, typename PropertyType>
    bool SetPropertyValue(const FString& InObjectPathName, const FName InPropertyName, const PropertyType& InPropertyValue);

    // Sets the property value on existing entries, returns true on success.
    template <typename PropertyType>
    bool TrySetPropertyValue(const FString& InObjectPathName, const FName InPropertyName, const PropertyType& InPropertyValue);

    // Gets the property value if found, returns true on success.
    template<typename PropertyType>
    bool GetPropertyValue(const FString& InObjectPathName, const FName InPropertyName, PropertyType& OutPropertyValue) const;

    // Sets the property value converted from the provided string value on existing entries, returns true on success.
    bool TrySetPropertyValueFromString(const FString& InObjectPathName, const FName InPropertyName, const FString& InPropertyValue);

    // Gets the property value and converts it to a string if found, returns true on success.
    bool GetPropertyValueAsString(const FString& InObjectPathName, const FName InPropertyName, FString& OutPropertyValue);
};

docs.title: Runtime Spawning
docs.text:
World Partition partitioning is performed in the editor. Any objects spawned at runtime will not participate in World Partition streaming. Consider this scenario:

  • A gravity-enabled ball is spawned in the scene and falls to the ground. When the character moves away from the area, causing the ground to stream out, the ball will fall through the ground.

This is obviously not what we want. Generally, all persistent objects except the character should be placed in the map level from the beginning.

But sometimes there are special requirements:

  • Some scene objects may have runtime event dependencies and must be spawned at runtime.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
• If the object's position is fixed, you can place a placeholder Actor in the scene in advance, making it configurable at runtime.
  • If the object is located in a certain area, you can place a Trigger Volume in that area and control the object's lifecycle through trigger logic. If the trigger area is larger than the World Partition loading range, the trigger volume should be placed in a grid with higher loading priority and a streaming source component added.

docs.title: Character Teleportation
docs.text: When teleporting a character in World Partition, since streaming takes time, directly moving the character to the target location may cause the character to fall through the ground due to unloaded surrounding objects.

docs.title: Solutions
docs.text:
To solve this problem, we need to preload the target area and wait for loading to complete.

  • Solution 1: Disable the character's tick, teleport the character to the target point, use the character itself as a streaming source to trigger streaming of the surrounding area, and enable the tick when the target area finishes loading via polling (FTSTicker). There is a corresponding reference in the Matrix's Mass framework:

  • Solution 2: Spawn an Actor with a streaming source component at the target location, enable streaming, poll whether loading is complete, and teleport the character after completion:

docs.title: One File Per Actor
docs.text:
OFPA allows team members to edit different Actors in the same map simultaneously.

Traditional maps store all Actors in the asset package corresponding to the World, while UE's open world maps enable One File Per Actor (OFPA) by default, meaning each Actor corresponds to a separate file.

These files are stored in the project's Content directory under the corresponding map path in the __ExternalActors__ and __ExternalObjects__ folders. The image below shows all Actors in the map named OpenWorld:

You can get the real file path of an Actor in the Scene Outliner:

Generally, all Actors are stored in __ExternalActors__, while __ExternalObjects__ stores UObject (non-Actor) objects such as various Settings and Outliner groups.

docs.title: HLOD
docs.text:
Through World Partition streaming, we can reduce the performance pressure of the entire scene to only the area around the streaming source:

For game logic, this streaming is certainly an optimization, but for the scene, we don't want distant scenes to be unloaded due to streaming. HLOD solves this problem.

HLOD is used to display distant views in World Partition. Its usage in open world maps differs from HLOD in regular maps (UE4):

  • World Partition - Hierarchical Level of Detail in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.3 Documentation (unrealengine.com)

The official documentation also lacks detailed descriptions of HLOD. For those unfamiliar with its positioning, it's easy to misuse HLOD. The original intention of using HLOD in World Partition is:

  • Merge all Actors in a Cell into a low-precision cell model proxy. When the cell is outside the loading range of the streaming source, this simplified model can be used for display. This reduces rendering costs (using low-precision models and materials) while optimizing occlusion culling calculations (reducing the number of Actors).

You can set the default HLOD layer configuration for the entire map here:

Its asset configuration panel is as follows:

  • Layer Type: The strategy used to generate HLOD.
  • Instanced: Uses the lowest LOD of the corresponding model (if it's a Nanite model, it will generate new Nanite data using that LOD).
  • Merged: Merges static meshes within the partition.
  • Simplified: Merges meshes within the partition and performs mesh simplification on the merged mesh. It is more suitable for objects with complex geometries, such as leafy trees.
  • Approximated: Merges meshes within the partition and performs mesh approximation on the merged mesh. It is more suitable for objects with rounded geometries, such as buildings and stones.

  • Custom: Custom HLOD generation strategy.

  • Is Spatially Loaded: Whether the generated HLOD needs to enable streaming. If enabled, an HLOD Grid will be created for this HLOD layer, and the generated HLODActors will be placed in this Grid.

  • Cell Size: Configures the cell size of the HLOD Grid. The value should preferably be an integer multiple of the Main Grid cell size.
  • Loading Range: Configures the loading range of the HLOD Grid. The value should preferably be an integer multiple of the Main Grid cell size.
  • Parent Layer: Uses the parent HLOD layer to process the generated HLOD simplified model again to generate an even more simplified HLOD model, which usually has a larger loading range.

Notes:

  • The Matrix's scene objects are mostly angular buildings, which uniformly use a customized approximated mesh strategy. When the scene has more complex object types (such as trees, water, vegetation), more refined processing strategies need to be customized, which often requires very strict asset management strategies as support. Additionally, a deep understanding of the HLOD-related code flow and the mesh processing algorithms provided by UE is very valuable for performance optimization of open world projects.
  • HLOD merges the cells of a grid into a simplified model. However, if an area has multiple grids, multiple simplified models will be generated for that area, and models between different grids will not be merged. Therefore, usually, all scene objects should be placed in the MainGrid, and HLOD should be generated only for objects in the MainGrid. For small objects, they can be placed in a grid with a smaller loading range and excluded from HLOD generation.

docs.title: Data Layers
docs.text:
Data Layers are a feature provided by UE5 for open worlds, and their usage is similar to Outliner folders:

But unlike folders, it also provides two key features:

  • You can set default non-loading for this category of Layer when opening the map in the editor.
  • You can load and unload Layers at runtime through related interfaces.

Why use Data Layers?

  • Data Layers can be used to layer scene objects by category and block by region, which can alleviate the pressure of full-scene loading in the editor. During multi-person editing, each person can selectively load the regions they care about, which is crucial for large scene management and multi-person collaboration. If not handled properly, it will be the beginning of chaotic scene production processes.
  • Editor classification can provide an effective basis for subsequent scene optimization.
  • Data Layers are sub-levels participating in World Partition streaming.

You can open the Data Layers panel here:

Right-click to create a Data Layer for this map:

This creates a Data Layer Asset shared by all maps:

You can manually set which Actor a Data Layer belongs to here:

Or like this:

We can also set the Current Context of Data Layers. Newly created Actors will be automatically added to the current Data Layer:

Remove or clear the current Data Layer like this:

docs.title: Level Instances
docs.text:
UE5 provides the Level Instancing feature to improve and simplify the editing experience of World Partition.

  • Level Instancing in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.3 Documentation (unrealengine.com)

The original intention of Level Instances is to group a set of Actors so that Level Instances can be placed and reused throughout the world. However, since they can be embedded into the World Partition of the main level during packaging, and UE5's Data Layers are not yet widely adopted, many development teams accustomed to UE4 prefer to use them as sub-levels of open world maps.

UE5.3 also solved the previous problem of not being able to set Runtime Grid for Actors in Level Instances:

For Actors in Level Instances, there is an additional "Only in Main World" option. When checked, the Actor will only be loaded when the Level Instance map is opened. It will not be loaded when used as a Level Instance in other maps:

docs.title: Scene Production
docs.text:
Here is an article listing many related topics:

  • 【UE5】Directory and Asset Naming Conventions - Zhihu (zhihu.com)

Here are some suggestions:

  • UE is just an engine technology provider. It offers many excellent technical capabilities and general editors, but there is no standard scene production solution. This requires R&D teams to spend a lot of trial-and-error costs on technical accumulation and selection.

  • Understand that human capabilities are limited. Therefore, when creating assets, it is best to use procedural methods as much as possible. Use automation as much as possible in process control. Find suitable quantitative indicators to make the production process traceable and iterative:

  • Houdini and UE5's PCG framework:
    • [UE5 PCG] Official Public Course: In-depth Study of the Electric Dreams Environment Project
    • Electric Dreams PCG Technical Explanation (1) — Terminology, Tools, and Chart Introduction
    • Electric Dreams PCG Technical Explanation (2) — Ravines and Large Assemblies
    • Electric Dreams PCG Technical Explanation (3) — Forests, Rocks, and Scene Backgrounds
    • Electric Dreams PCG Technical Explanation (4) — Distant Views, Fog, Custom Nodes, and Subgraphs
  • Unreal Engine Automation System | Unreal Engine 5.3 Documentation (unrealengine.com)

  • Procedural Generation and Deep Learning | EA Studios

  • Performance optimization for open world scenes is different from optimizing individual assets. Since there are a large number of assets to maintain, it is difficult to rely on manual maintenance. Therefore, you should seek unified management strategies from a macro perspective as much as possible, and abandon some minor optimization requirements in exchange for greater performance balance. Proper classification and isolation of scene assets is very, very, very important—it is an important basis for performance optimization. R&D teams can formulate corresponding LOD Groups, Texture Groups, and HLOD generation strategies based on different classifications. Additionally, for assets that do require special treatment, the basis for specialization (whitelist) should be retained.

  • The scene production process will not be chaotic only if every participant strictly follows the scene production specifications. Therefore, R&D teams need to establish a public document repository for publishing and iterating scene specifications. Use tools as much as possible instead of manual checks to minimize the probability of errors caused by human intervention. If manual workload must be increased for relevant personnel, the most streamlined data and processes should be evaluated as much as possible.

  • Open world scene specifications are highly dependent on game design. Only after clarifying the core character gameplay can the development team formulate corresponding scene specifications, establish performance optimization indicators, and create corresponding toolchains. Take The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom as an example:

  • Customize terrain height, slope, and water body specifications based on the character's stamina (swimming, climbing, gliding) mechanics.

  • Customize terrain specifications based on the requirements of the Ascend skill.
  • Create interactive objects that meet the characteristics of abilities like Ultrahand, Fuse, and Recall.
  • Weapons (one-handed swords, two-handed swords, spears, shields, arrows) can be fused, and characteristics are bound to corresponding slots to formulate specifications for fuse items.
  • Based on known character state categories, create different scene effects such as lightning strikes, fire, cold, and heat, and provide corresponding solutions (clothing or food).
  • Create Zonai technology gameplay without conflicting with core gameplay design specifications.

For these specifications, engine developers can carry out development work similar to the following:

  • Customize debug views for "terrain climbable height", "water traversable area", and "Ascend usable area" (it would be great if UE supports extending debug views via plugins without modifying source code).

  • Verify the performance indicators of various effects and scene effects, adjust the balance between effect and performance, and create corresponding management and acceptance tools.

  • Here are some small suggestions for editor tools:

  • Trace the origin of problems as much as possible. Solving problems at the source has the lowest cost, such as when an asset is created (AssetCreated) or when an asset is saved (AssetSaved), when an Actor is created (NewActorsPlaced), etc.
  • Use ignorable Notifications instead of Dialogs that forcefully block user input.
  • Provide a friendly user experience with support for undo, redo, batch processing, and customization.

docs.title: Gameplay Design
docs.text:
Regarding open world level design, here are some related documents:

  • What Challenges Are There in Making an Open World Game? - TiMi Studios / Jiang Anxi
  • From Zero to One: Making an Open World - Game Grape / wenlon
  • Game Development Chat - Open World - Zhihu / Italink
  • Metaverse Chat - Zhihu

The underlying gameplay design of an open world is very important. It should be complete and full of ingenuity. Forcing unreasonable modules to achieve a certain effect will only cause destructive blows to subsequent development work.

  • After clarifying the upper limits of various budgets (time, energy, money, computing power), formulate resource scheduling and allocation. Trade-offs are inevitable.
  • If the underlying gameplay design is not rigorous, the entire production process will become chaotic or even out of control. As gameplay stacks up, the production difficulty of open scenes will increase exponentially. If some ingenious designs are not used to converge gameplay content, production costs will easily soar.

Here are two examples:

  • The Legend of Zelda uses underlying systematic gameplay to build the game's gameplay system, applying various templates to expand gameplay. Developers ensure that templates and systematic designs are within a manageable range. Artists and game creators derive game content within this limited range, which prevents project complexity from rising sharply as the scale increases.

  • In Black Myth: Wukong, Wukong can transform into various elite monsters through the 72 Transformations. This gameplay design allows the R&D team to invest more production costs into the design of elite monsters.

docs.title: Audio Development
docs.text:
For a long time, rendering has been the focus of graphics engines, while audio seems to struggle to attract developers' attention. However, in reality, audio not only enhances immersive interactive experiences but also further boosts visual expressiveness:

It was precisely this that ignited my passion for program development. To achieve better visual effects with audio, I finally dived into the world of graphics engines~

This article will start with basic audio knowledge, introduce commonly used audio interfaces in UE5, and some common Digital Signal Processing (DSP) algorithms. Finally, we will embrace Meta Sound.

I am not a professional audio developer. If there are any mistakes, please feel free to correct me~

docs.title: What is Audio?
docs.text:
As we all know, sound is produced by vibrations, like this:

Image source: How Does Sound Travel From One Medium To Another? (scienceabc.com)

Here are two excellent videos explaining the nature of sound:

  • What is Sound-The Dr. Binocs Show
  • What is Sound-BranchEducation

We usually regard sound as a continuous waveform, like this:

The storage precision of computers is limited (there are infinitely many decimals between 0 and 1). If we want to store sound data in a computer, we will face precision processing issues in two dimensions:

  • Time
  • Amplitude

This requires the use of Pulse Code Modulation (PCM) to convert the Continuous Signal of sound into a Discrete Signal.

First, we process the precision division in the time dimension through Sampling:

The sampling precision parameter in the time dimension is the Sample Rate, which represents the number of times the sound signal is sampled per unit time (1 second). Common sample rates include 44100 Hz, 48000 Hz, etc.

After obtaining the sampled data, we further process the precision division in the amplitude dimension through Quantization:

The sampling precision in the amplitude dimension is Bits Per Sample, which represents the bit storage precision of an audio sample. Common bit depths include 8 bit, 16 bit, 24 bit, and 32 bit. Taking 8 bit as an example, it is equivalent to 1 byte and can represent 256 (2^8) numbers. Including the sign bit, its value range is [-128, 127], which can be regarded as having 128 amplitude gradients.

Regarding sampling and quantization, here is an excellent article:

  • Introduction to Audio-Video Development Basics | Sound Capture and Quantization, Audio Digital Signal Quality, Audio Bit Rate - Zhihu (zhihu.com)

The final data we obtain is generally called a Wave Table. If we ignore the storage precision of the bit depth and use floating points to represent the amplitude, in C++, we can express it as the following storage structure:

std::vector<float> WaveTable = {
    sample0,sample1,sample2,sample3,sample4...
};

Opening the computer's sound settings, we can find that each audio device (input or output) has relevant configurations:

In the real world, a Sound Source emits a large number of moving particles in all directions. Some particles directly enter the human ear, while others collide with surrounding objects one or more times before entering the human ear. In such a complex surrounding environment, it usually causes the two ears to receive different audio data, which also creates the so-called Spatial Sense for audio.

Therefore, to retain this spatial sense when storing audio in a computer, we store multiple copies of audio data. The number of copies is usually called the Number Of Channels. Audio with only one channel is called Mono, and audio with 2 channels is called Stereo.

Audio samples from multiple channels are interleaved together, and each combination is called an Audio Block.

For stereo, its storage structure is as follows:

std::vector<float> WaveTable = {
    channel0_sample0, channel1_sample0,     // Block 0
    channel0_sample1, channel1_sample1,     // Block 1
    channel0_sample2, channel1_sample2,     // Block 2
    channel0_sample3, channel1_sample3,     // Block 3
    channel0_sample4, channel1_sample4,     // Block 4
    ...
};

The same applies to four channels:

std::vector<float> WaveTable = {
    channel0_sample0, channel1_sample0, channel2_sample0, channel3_sample0,     // Block 0
    channel0_sample1, channel1_sample1, channel2_sample1, channel3_sample1,     // Block 1
    channel0_sample2, channel1_sample2, channel2_sample2, channel3_sample2,     // Block 2
    channel0_sample3, channel1_sample3, channel2_sample3, channel3_sample3,     // Block 3
    channel0_sample4, channel1_sample4, channel2_sample4, channel3_sample4,     // Block 4
    ...
};

Under normal circumstances, a Wave Table cannot be directly played by an audio device because it is a bunch of waveform data without audio format information, such as sample rate, bit depth, number of channels, etc.

To make it playable, we need to further encode it into an audio file.

docs.title: WAV
docs.text:
*.WAV is one of the most common sound file formats. It is a standard digital audio file developed by Microsoft specifically for Windows. Unlike audio formats such as *.mp3, *.flac, and *.aac, it is an uncompressed audio format that only stores audio format information before the WaveTable data:

Here is a complete document:

  • WAV File Format Analysis and Processing - JianShu (jianshu.com)

Please read the above article carefully to understand the meaning of each data in the WAV format.

Afterwards, we can use the following memory alignment in C++ to describe the WAV file header structure:

struct WavFmtChunk {
    uint8_t chunkID[4] = { 'f','m','t',' ' };
    int32_t chunkSize;
    int16_t audioFormat;
    int16_t numChannels;
    int32_t sampleRate;
    int32_t byteRate;
    int16_t blockAlign;
    int16_t bitsPerSample;
};

struct WavDataChunkHeader {
    uint8_t chunkID[4] = { 'd','a','t','a' };
    int32_t chunkSize;
};

struct WavRiffChunk {
    uint8_t chunkID[4] = { 'R','I','F','F' };
    int32_t chunkSize;
    uint8_t format[4] = { 'W','A','V','E' };
    WavFmtChunk fmtChunk;
    WavDataChunkHeader dataChunkHeader;
};

typedef WavRiffChunk WavHeader;

When storing a segment of data in C++, we usually use std::vector<uint8_t>. If we want to write a segment of waveform data into a Wav file, we can use the following function:

void writeWavFile(std::string filePath, int numChannels, int sampleRate, int bitsPerSample, std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable) {
    WavHeader header;
    header.fmtChunk.audioFormat = 0x0001;           // The value corresponding to the PCM format is 0x0001
    header.fmtChunk.chunkSize = 16;                 // The audio format of the PCM format occupies 16 bytes. For other formats, it may be >16, which will cause the total file header size to be >44
    header.fmtChunk.numChannels = numChannels;
    header.fmtChunk.bitsPerSample = bitsPerSample;
    header.fmtChunk.sampleRate = sampleRate;
    header.fmtChunk.blockAlign = header.fmtChunk.numChannels * header.fmtChunk.bitsPerSample / 8;
    header.fmtChunk.byteRate = header.fmtChunk.sampleRate * header.fmtChunk.blockAlign;
    header.dataChunkHeader.chunkSize = waveTable.size();
    header.chunkSize = sizeof(header.format) + sizeof(header.fmtChunk) + sizeof(header.dataChunkHeader) + waveTable.size();
    std::ofstream out(filePath, std::ios::out | std::ios::binary);      // Be sure to use std::ios::binary, otherwise the data will be corrupted
    assert(out.is_open() && "Can`t Write File");
    out.write(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&header), sizeof(WavHeader));
    out.write(reinterpret_cast<char*>(waveTable.data()), waveTable.size());
    out.close();
}

Reading is also very simple:

std::vector<uint8_t> readWavFile(std::string filePath) {
    WavHeader header;
    std::ifstream in(filePath, std::ios::in | std::ios::binary);                // Be sure to use std::ios::binary, otherwise the data will be corrupted
    assert(in.is_open() && "Can`t Read File");
    in.read(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&header), sizeof(header));
    int waveTableSize = header.dataChunkHeader.chunkSize;                       // Get the size of the waveform data
    std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable(waveTableSize);      
    in.read(reinterpret_cast<char*>(waveTable.data()), waveTableSize);
    return waveTable;
}

Next, let's generate an audio waveform. The Sine Wave is one of the basic waveforms, and its function is as follows: $$ y(Time) = Amplitude * sin(2 * PI * Frequency * Time + PhaseOffset) + Bias $$

According to the function, we can write the following function:

const double M_PI = 3.1415926535;
std::vector<uint8_t> generateSineWave(int timeLengthSec,    // Duration of the sine wave in seconds
                                            int frequency,      // Frequency of the sine wave
                                            float amplitude,    // Amplitude of the sine wave
                                            int numChannels,    // Number of audio channels
                                            int sampleRate,     // Audio sample rate
                                            int bitsPerSample   // Bit depth of the audio
                                           ) {
    int numBlocks = timeLengthSec * sampleRate;                         // Number of audio blocks
    amplitude = std::clamp(amplitude, 0.01f, 1.0f);                     // Limit the amplitude, std::clamp requires C++17
    std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable;                             
    waveTable.resize(numBlocks * numChannels * bitsPerSample / 8);      // Calculate the memory size required for the audio data
    int step = bitsPerSample / 8;
    for (int i = 0; i < numBlocks; i++) {
        float time = i / (float)numBlocks * timeLengthSec;      // Time point
        float sampleValue = amplitude * std::sin(2 * M_PI * frequency * time);      // Calculate the sample value at the corresponding time point
        // We need to find a way to write sampleValue into waveTable
    }
    return waveTable;
}

We face a problem in the above code:

  • Through the sine wave function, we get a sample value of type float, but the bit depth may be 8 bit, 16 bit, 24 bit, or 32 bit. How do we convert the float to data of the corresponding bit depth?

A common approach is to use existing data types to assign corresponding data bits, like this:

const int PCMS16MaxAmplitude = 32767;    // The value range of 16 bit is [-32768, 32767]. Here we take the minimum absolute value (32767) to avoid overflow

void write16BitSampleValue(uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
    (*reinterpret_cast<int16_t*>(dataPtr)) = sampleValue * PCMS16MaxAmplitude;
}

We can also use bitwise operations for filling:

const int PCMS24MaxAmplitude = 8388607;
void write24BitSampleValue(uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
    int value = sampleValue * PCMS24MaxAmplitude;
    dataPtr[0] = value & 0xFF;
    dataPtr[1] = (value >> 8) & 0xFF;
    dataPtr[2] = (value >> 16) & 0xFF;
}

To sum up, we can organize a conversion function table like this:

const int PCMS8MaxAmplitude = 127;
const int PCMS16MaxAmplitude = 32767;
const int PCMS24MaxAmplitude = 8388607;
const int PCMS32MaxAmplitude = 2147483647;

typedef std::function<void(uint8_t*, float)> SampleValueWriteFunction;
static std::map<uint8_t, SampleValueWriteFunction> SampleValueWriteFunctions = {
    {8,[](uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
         // I don't know why we need to add an offset here for the waveform to be correct =.=
        (*reinterpret_cast<int8_t*>(dataPtr)) = sampleValue * PCMS8MaxAmplitude + PCMS8MaxAmplitude;  
    }},
    {16,[](uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
        (*reinterpret_cast<int16_t*>(dataPtr)) = sampleValue * PCMS16MaxAmplitude;
    }},
    {24,[](uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
        int value = sampleValue * PCMS24MaxAmplitude;
        dataPtr[0] = value & 0xFF;
        dataPtr[1] = (value >> 8) & 0xFF;
        dataPtr[2] = (value >> 16) & 0xFF;
    }},
    {32,[](uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
        (*reinterpret_cast<int32_t*>(dataPtr)) = sampleValue * PCMS32MaxAmplitude;
    }}
};

typedef std::function<float(uint8_t*)> SampleValueReadFunction;
static std::map<uint8_t, SampleValueReadFunction> SampleValueReadFunctions = {
    {8,[](uint8_t* dataPtr) {
        return ((*reinterpret_cast<int8_t*>(dataPtr)) - PCMS8MaxAmplitude) / float(PCMS8MaxAmplitude);
    }},
    {16,[](uint8_t* dataPtr) {
        return (*reinterpret_cast<int16_t*>(dataPtr)) / float(PCMS16MaxAmplitude);
    }},
    {24,[](uint8_t* dataPtr) {
        int value = dataPtr[2];
        value <<= 8;
        value |= dataPtr[1];
        value <<= 8;
        value |= dataPtr[0];
        return value / float(PCMS24MaxAmplitude);
    }},
    {32,[](uint8_t* dataPtr) {
        return (*reinterpret_cast<int32_t*>(dataPtr)) / float(PCMS32MaxAmplitude);
    }}
};

To sum up, with the test code, the complete code is as follows:

#include <stdint.h>
#include <assert.h>
#include <map>
#include <vector>
#include <functional>
#include <string>
#include <fstream>
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>

struct WavFmtChunk {
    uint8_t chunkID[4] = { 'f','m','t',' ' };
    int32_t chunkSize;
    int16_t audioFormat;
    int16_t numChannels;
    int32_t sampleRate;
    int32_t byteRate;
    int16_t blockAlign;
    int16_t bitsPerSample;
};

struct WavDataChunkHeader {
    uint8_t chunkID[4] = { 'd','a','t','a' };
    int32_t chunkSize;
};

struct WavRiffChunk {
    uint8_t chunkID[4] = { 'R','I','F','F' };
    int32_t chunkSize;
    uint8_t format[4] = { 'W','A','V','E' };
    WavFmtChunk fmtChunk;
    WavDataChunkHeader dataChunkHeader;
};

typedef WavRiffChunk WavHeader;

const int PCMS8MaxAmplitude = 127;
const int PCMS16MaxAmplitude = 32767;
const int PCMS24MaxAmplitude = 8388607;
const int PCMS32MaxAmplitude = 2147483647;

typedef std::function<void(uint8_t*, float)> SampleValueWriteFunction;
static std::map<uint8_t, SampleValueWriteFunction> SampleValueWriteFunctions = {
    {8,[](uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
        (*reinterpret_cast<int8_t*>(dataPtr)) = sampleValue * PCMS8MaxAmplitude + PCMS8MaxAmplitude;   // I don't know why we need to add an offset here for the waveform to be correct =.=
    }},
    {16,[](uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
        (*reinterpret_cast<int16_t*>(dataPtr)) = sampleValue * PCMS16MaxAmplitude;
    }},
    {24,[](uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
        int value = sampleValue * PCMS24MaxAmplitude;
        dataPtr[0] = value & 0xFF;
        dataPtr[1] = (value >> 8) & 0xFF;
        dataPtr[2] = (value >> 16) & 0xFF;
    }},
    {32,[](uint8_t* dataPtr, float sampleValue) {
        (*reinterpret_cast<int32_t*>(dataPtr)) = sampleValue * PCMS32MaxAmplitude;
    }}
};

typedef std::function<float(uint8_t*)> SampleValueReadFunction;
static std::map<uint8_t, SampleValueReadFunction> SampleValueReadFunctions = {
    {8,[](uint8_t* dataPtr) {
        return ((*reinterpret_cast<int8_t*>(dataPtr)) - PCMS8MaxAmplitude) / float(PCMS8MaxAmplitude);
    }},
    {16,[](uint8_t* dataPtr) {
        return (*reinterpret_cast<int16_t*>(dataPtr)) / float(PCMS16MaxAmplitude);
    }},
    {24,[](uint8_t* dataPtr) {
        int value = dataPtr[2];
        value <<= 8;
        value |= dataPtr[1];
        value <<= 8;
        value |= dataPtr[0];
        return value / float(PCMS24MaxAmplitude);
    }},
    {32,[](uint8_t* dataPtr) {
        return (*reinterpret_cast<int32_t*>(dataPtr)) / float(PCMS32MaxAmplitude);
    }}
};

const double M_PI = 3.1415926535;

std::vector<uint8_t> generateSineWave(int timeLengthSec, int frequency, float amplitude, int numChannels, int sampleRate, int bitsPerSample) {
    int numBlocks = timeLengthSec * sampleRate;                         // Number of audio blocks
    amplitude = std::clamp(amplitude, 0.01f, 1.0f);                     // Limit the amplitude, std::clamp requires C++17
    std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable;                             
    waveTable.resize(numBlocks * numChannels * bitsPerSample / 8);
    int step = bitsPerSample / 8;                                       // Calculate the byte span of each sample
    uint8_t* waveTablePtr = waveTable.data();
    SampleValueWriteFunction writer = SampleValueWriteFunctions.at(bitsPerSample);
    for (int i = 0; i < numBlocks; i++) {
        float time = i / (float)numBlocks * timeLengthSec;              // Time corresponding to the current audio block
        float sampleValue = amplitude * std::sin(2 * M_PI * frequency * time);      // Sine value corresponding to the current time
        for (int channelIndex = 0; channelIndex < numChannels; channelIndex++) {    // All channels use the same value
            writer(waveTablePtr, sampleValue);
            waveTablePtr += step;
        }
    }
    return waveTable;
}

void writeWavFile(std::string filePath, int numChannels, int sampleRate, int bitsPerSample, std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable) {
    WavHeader header;
    header.fmtChunk.audioFormat = 0x0001;           // The value corresponding to the PCM format is 0x0001
    header.fmtChunk.chunkSize = 16;                 // The audio format of the PCM format occupies 16 bytes. For other formats, it may be >16, which will cause the total file header size to be >44
    header.fmtChunk.numChannels = numChannels;
    header.fmtChunk.bitsPerSample = bitsPerSample;
    header.fmtChunk.sampleRate = sampleRate;
    header.fmtChunk.blockAlign = header.fmtChunk.numChannels * header.fmtChunk.bitsPerSample / 8;
    header.fmtChunk.byteRate = header.fmtChunk.sampleRate * header.fmtChunk.blockAlign;
    header.dataChunkHeader.chunkSize = waveTable.size();
    header.chunkSize = sizeof(header.format) + sizeof(header.fmtChunk) + sizeof(header.dataChunkHeader) + waveTable.size();
    std::ofstream out(filePath, std::ios::out | std::ios::binary);      // Be sure to use std::ios::binary, otherwise the data will be corrupted
    assert(out.is_open() && "Can`t Write File");
    out.write(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&header), sizeof(WavHeader));
    out.write(reinterpret_cast<char*>(waveTable.data()), waveTable.size());
    out.close();
}

std::vector<uint8_t> readWavFile(std::string filePath) {
    WavHeader header;
    std::ifstream in(filePath, std::ios::in | std::ios::binary);                // Be sure to use std::ios::binary, otherwise the data will be corrupted
    assert(in.is_open() && "Can`t Read File");
    in.read(reinterpret_cast<char*>(&header), sizeof(header));
    int waveTableSize = header.dataChunkHeader.chunkSize;                       // Get the size of the waveform data
    std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable(waveTableSize);      
    in.read(reinterpret_cast<char*>(waveTable.data()), waveTableSize);
    return waveTable;
}

int main() {
    assert(sizeof(WavHeader) == 44 && "WAV Header Size Error");

    int numChannels = 2;            // Mono
    int sampleRate = 48000;         // Sample rate is 48000 Hz
    int bitsPerSample = 16;         // Each audio sample occupies 16 bits, i.e., 2 bytes
    int auidoLengthSec = 2;         // Generate a 2-second sine wave
    int sineFrequency = 440;        // Frequency of the sine wave
    float sineAmplitude = 0.8f;     // Amplitude of the sine wave

    std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable = generateSineWave(auidoLengthSec, sineFrequency, sineAmplitude, numChannels, sampleRate, bitsPerSample);

    writeWavFile("./sineWave.wav", numChannels, sampleRate, bitsPerSample, waveTable);

    std::vector<uint8_t> readData = readWavFile("./sineWave.wav");

    assert(readData == waveTable && "Audio Data Error");

    return 0;
}

Executing this program will generate a sineWave.wav audio file in the output directory. Try playing it~

You can also modify the parameters to regenerate the audio and listen to the differences between sine waves of different frequencies.

In addition, you can try to simulate the effect of spatial audio:

std::vector<uint8_t> generateSineSurroundWave(int timeLengthSec, int frequency, float amplitude, int numChannels, int sampleRate, int bitsPerSample) {
    assert(numChannels == 2);

    int numBlocks = timeLengthSec * sampleRate;                         // Number of audio blocks
    amplitude = std::clamp(amplitude, 0.01f, 1.0f);                     // Limit the amplitude, std::clamp requires C++17
    std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable;
    waveTable.resize(numBlocks * numChannels * bitsPerSample / 8);
    int step = bitsPerSample / 8;                                       // Calculate the byte span of each sample
    uint8_t* waveTablePtr = waveTable.data();
    SampleValueWriteFunction writer = SampleValueWriteFunctions.at(bitsPerSample);

    float leftEarPos[2]  = { -5,0 };                                    // Position of the left ear (X, Y)
    float rightEarPos[2] = {  5,0 };                                    // Position of the right ear (X, Y)
    float radiusOfSurround = 10;                                        // Radius of the surround audio
    float audioAttenuationFactor = 0.7;                                 // Sound attenuation factor, e.g., 0.7 means the audio attenuates to 0.7 times the original every unit length
    float periodSec = 2;                                                // Time taken to rotate one circle in seconds, 2 means one circle every two seconds

    for (int i = 0; i < numBlocks; i++) {
        float time = i / (float)numBlocks * timeLengthSec;                          // Time corresponding to the current audio block
        float sampleValue = amplitude * std::sin(2 * M_PI * frequency * time);      // Sine value corresponding to the current time

        float angle = 2 * M_PI * time / periodSec;                                  // Calculate the current rotation angle
        float audioSourcePos[2] = {                                                 // Calculate the current position of the sound source
            radiusOfSurround * std::cos(angle),
            radiusOfSurround * std::sin(angle)
        };

        float leftEarDistance  = sqrt(pow(leftEarPos[0] - audioSourcePos[0], 2) + pow(leftEarPos[1] - audioSourcePos[1], 2));       // Distance from the sound source to the left ear
        float leftSampleValue = sampleValue * pow(audioAttenuationFactor, leftEarDistance);                                         // Calculate the attenuated audio sample value based on the distance
        writer(waveTablePtr, leftSampleValue);                                                                                      // Write to the left channel
        waveTablePtr += step;

        float rightEarDistance = sqrt(pow(rightEarPos[0] - audioSourcePos[0], 2) + pow(rightEarPos[1] - audioSourcePos[1], 2));     // Distance from the sound source to the right ear
        float rightSampleValue = sampleValue * pow(audioAttenuationFactor, rightEarDistance);                                       // Calculate the attenuated audio sample value based on the distance
        writer(waveTablePtr, rightSampleValue);                                                                                     // Write to the right channel
        waveTablePtr += step;
    }
    return waveTable;
}

int main() {
    assert(sizeof(WavHeader) == 44 && "WAV Header Size Error");
    int numChannels = 2;            // Mono
    int sampleRate = 48000;         // Sample rate is 48000 Hz
    int bitsPerSample = 16;         // Each audio sample occupies 16 bits, i.e., 2 bytes
    int auidoLengthSec = 2;         // Generate a 2-second sine wave
    int sineFrequency = 150;        // Frequency of the sine wave
    float sineAmplitude = 0.8f;     // Amplitude of the sine wave
    std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable = generateSineSurroundWave(auidoLengthSec, sineFrequency, sineAmplitude, numChannels, sampleRate, bitsPerSample);
    writeWavFile("./sineWave.wav", numChannels, sampleRate, bitsPerSample, waveTable);
    std::vector<uint8_t> readData = readWavFile("./sineWave.wav");
    assert(readData == waveTable && "Audio Data Error");
    return 0;
}

On this website, you can upload files to view the audio waveform:

  • Musiscope (sciencemusic.org)

At this point, we should have a general understanding of the original form of audio on a computer.

docs.title: Audio IO Interfaces
docs.text:
With audio, we also need to know how to interact with audio devices. Common audio devices include:

  • Input: Microphone
  • Output: Speaker, sound system, headphone

These device manufacturers will provide or support relevant audio drivers. Usually, we do not need to directly interact with audio drivers, but use the audio interfaces provided by the operating system to handle audio input and output, such as:

  • Windows: DirectSound, ASIO, WASAPI
  • Linux: native ALSA, Jack, OSS
  • Mac OS: CoreAudio, Jack

For cross-platform audio processing, many frameworks also uniformly encapsulate these interfaces, such as:

  • Audio IO module in Qt Multimedia: Audio Overview | Qt Multimedia 6.6.1
  • RtAudio introduced by UE: http://www.music.mcgill.ca/~gary/rtaudio/

docs.title: Fourier Transform Libraries
docs.text:
Fourier Transform is an important tool for signal processing.

We know that sound is a continuous signal that changes over time, like this:

But the sound we hear often does not have only one frequency. In fact, it may be a stack of many frequency sound waves, like this:

Fourier Transform can help us analyze the Time Domain Signal that has mixed a large number of different frequency waveforms over a period of time to obtain the frequency distribution of the sound waveform during that period, i.e., the Frequency Domain Signal. The entire process looks like this:

Here is a very good video explaining the principle of Fourier Transform:

  • 【Official Bilingual】Animated Fourier Transform | 3Blue1Brown

Some seemingly chaotic time-domain signals are easier to find data features after being converted to the frequency domain, such as this real-time analysis result of a piece of music:

Although you can't hear the sound, I believe you can see the rhythm changes of the music from the jumping graphics.

In addition, Fourier Transform is not only a mathematical processing tool but also guides us to think about problems in the frequency domain. If you like playing with Shader Toy or GLSL Sandbox, many of the codes inside are actually based on frequency domain thinking.

Here is an interesting video where each line rotates at a fixed frequency:

  • The Beauty of Fourier Transform | Science Short Video

Here are some mature Fourier algorithm implementations:

  • fftw3: The Fastest Fourier Transform in the West
  • pffft: A small Fourier Transform library
  • ffts: The Fastest Fourier Transform in the South (doge)

If you also like audio visualization like me, here are two recommended open-source libraries:

  • adamstark/Gist: A C++ Library for Audio Analysis (github.com)
  • jmerkt/rt-cqt: Real-Time Constant-Q Transform (github.com)

docs.title: DSP Algorithm Libraries
docs.text:
DSP stands for Digital Signal Processing.

In the "Understanding Audio" section, we generated a sine wave and wrote it to a WAV file. Usually, these functions are included in DSP libraries. In addition, they often provide other functions, such as:

  • Filters
  • Resampling
  • Audio synthesis
  • Spectrum analysis
  • ...

Open-source DSP libraries include:

  • KFR | Fast, modern C++ DSP framework (kfrlib.com)
  • Maximilian | C++ Audio and Music DSP Library

docs.title: Audio Development Engines
docs.text:
Usually, for audio developers of game projects, there is no need to understand some of the underlying interfaces and frameworks above. Generally, game engines provide basic audio modules. For complex audio mechanisms, we will directly use the editors provided by audio engines for development.

Common audio engines include:

  • CRIWARE ADX: ADX has almost no learning curve because its creation tools make full use of the functions provided by the DAW paradigm and add intuitive functions to create interactive sounds. When project scales are getting larger and deadlines are getting tighter, use ADX to improve your work efficiency!
  • FMOD: FMOD is an end-to-end solution for adding sound and music to any game. Build adaptive audio with FMOD Studio and play it in your game with the FMOD Engine.
  • Wwise | Audiokinetic: Provides a complete set of interactive audio design and development tools, helping you easily complete prototyping regardless of the project scale, and on this basis, turn your audio creation ideas into reality.

These audio software all provide unique editors and plugin support in relevant game engines (UE, Unity, Cocos, etc.).

Regarding the choice of audio engines, there are some related discussions on Zhihu:

  • Which domestic games use audio engines for audio development? Such as FMOD and Wwise? - Zhihu (zhihu.com)
  • Using Unity5 to develop mobile games, what are the benefits of using FMOD or Wwise audio plugins instead of the built-in sound system? - Zhihu (zhihu.com)

Meta Sound is a built-in audio engine provided by UE5. Although its current functions cannot compare with the above audio engines, this one-stop solution will undoubtedly make UE more and more powerful.

Just like UE5's modeling tools, their greatest value is not allowing artists to model in UE, but essentially the biggest beneficiaries are developers (should be TA?).

Developers can quickly verify algorithm effects in the editor for scene assets of their own projects. After the strategy is stable, use a series of mesh processing algorithms provided by the UE underlying layer to build an automated pipeline from DCC models to high-quality engine assets.

As mentioned in the previous open-world chapter, HLOD synthesizes all models in a Cell into a low-precision model. Using a unified strategy in scenes with complex categories often makes it difficult to get good results. After being familiar with the UE underlying mesh processing algorithms, if there is appropriate asset classification, it is not difficult to generate high-quality HLOD.

docs.title: UE Audio
docs.text:
At Unreal Fest 2023, experts introduced UE's audio architecture:

  • Sounds Good: Unreal Engine Audio | Unreal Fest 2023

We can obtain some information from the following sites, but unfortunately, the documentation about audio in Unreal is relatively scarce and mixed with a large number of outdated documents:

  • Working with Audio in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.3 Documentation (unrealengine.com)
  • Latest unreal-engine topics in Audio - Epic Developer Community Forums (unrealengine.com)

docs.title: Audio Devices
docs.text:
Audio devices are divided into input devices and output devices. Their relevant information is stored in UE's Audio::FCaptureDeviceInfo and Audio::FAudioPlatformDeviceInfo respectively. We can obtain all devices through the following interfaces:

// Get all input devices
Audio::FAudioCapture AudioCapture;
TArray<Audio::FCaptureDeviceInfo> CaptureDevices;
AudioCapture.GetCaptureDevicesAvailable(CaptureDevices);
for (auto InputDeviceInfo : CaptureDevices) {
    UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning,TEXT("[Input Device] Name: %s, Device Id: %s, Num Channels: %u, Sample Rate: %u, Supports Hardware AEC: %u, "),
        *InputDeviceInfo.DeviceName,
        *InputDeviceInfo.DeviceId,
        InputDeviceInfo.InputChannels,
        InputDeviceInfo.PreferredSampleRate,
        InputDeviceInfo.bSupportsHardwareAEC);
}

// Get the current (default) audio input device
Audio::FCaptureDeviceInfo CurrentInputDevice;
AudioCapture.GetCaptureDeviceInfo(CurrentInputDevice);
UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("[Current Input Device] %s"),
    *CurrentInputDevice.DeviceName);

// Get all output devices
Audio::FMixerDevice* AudioMixerDevice = FAudioDeviceManager::GetAudioMixerDeviceFromWorldContext(GWorld);       // Use the current GWorld as the WorldContentObject
if (AudioMixerDevice){
    if (Audio::IAudioMixerPlatformInterface* MixerPlatform = AudioMixerDevice->GetAudioMixerPlatform()){
        uint32 NumOutputDevices = 0;
        MixerPlatform->GetNumOutputDevices(NumOutputDevices);
        for (uint32 i = 0; i < NumOutputDevices; ++i){
            Audio::FAudioPlatformDeviceInfo OutputDeviceInfo;
            MixerPlatform->GetOutputDeviceInfo(i, OutputDeviceInfo);
            UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("[Output Device] Name: %s, Device Id: %s, Num Channels: %u, Sample Rate: %u, "),
                *OutputDeviceInfo.Name,
                *OutputDeviceInfo.DeviceId,
                OutputDeviceInfo.NumChannels,
                OutputDeviceInfo.SampleRate);
        }

        // Get the current (default) audio output device
        Audio::FAudioPlatformDeviceInfo CurrentOutputDevice = MixerPlatform->GetPlatformDeviceInfo();
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("[Current Output Device] %s"),
            *CurrentOutputDevice.Name);
    }
}

docs.title: Output Audio
docs.text:
The base class of sound sources in UE is USoundBase:

There are many derivatives in the engine:

Our focus is mainly on USoundWave, which transmits waveform data to the audio device for playback.

Combined with the sine wave generation function we wrote earlier, we can also play our custom waveform data in UE, like this:

void UTestBlueprintLibrary::PlayTestAudio(UObject* WorldContext)        // Blueprint function library for testing
{
    int numChannels = 2;            // Mono
    int sampleRate = 48000;         // Sample rate is 48000 Hz
    int bitsPerSample = 16;         // Each audio sample occupies 16 bits, i.e., 2 bytes
    int auidoLengthSec = 2;         // Generate a 2-second sine wave
    int sineFrequency = 440;        // Frequency of the sine wave
    float sineAmplitude = 0.8f;     // Amplitude of the sine wave

    USoundWaveProcedural* Wave = NewObject<USoundWaveProcedural>();
    Wave->NumChannels = numChannels;
    Wave->SampleByteSize = bitsPerSample / 8;       // UE only supports int16
    Wave->SetSampleRate(sampleRate);
    std::vector<uint8_t> waveTable = generateSineWave(auidoLengthSec,
                                                      sineFrequency, 
                                                      sineAmplitude, 
                                                      numChannels, 
                                                      sampleRate, 
                                                      bitsPerSample);
    Wave->QueueAudio(waveTable.data(), waveTable.size());
    UGameplayStatics::PlaySound2D(WorldContext, Wave);
}

Here, the function UGameplayStatics::PlaySound2D is used. We can look at its internal implementation:

void UGameplayStatics::PlaySound2D(const UObject* WorldContextObject, 
                                   USoundBase* Sound, 
                                   float VolumeMultiplier,
                                   float PitchMultiplier, 
                                   float StartTime, 
                                   USoundConcurrency* ConcurrencySettings, 
                                   const AActor* OwningActor,
                                   bool bIsUISound)
{
    if (!Sound || !GEngine || !GEngine->UseSound())
    {
        return;
    }

    UWorld* ThisWorld = GEngine->GetWorldFromContextObject(WorldContextObject, EGetWorldErrorMode::LogAndReturnNull);
    if (!ThisWorld || !ThisWorld->bAllowAudioPlayback || ThisWorld->IsNetMode(NM_DedicatedServer))
    {
        return;
    }

    if (FAudioDeviceHandle AudioDevice = ThisWorld->GetAudioDevice())   // Get the audio output device of the current world
    {
        FActiveSound NewActiveSound;                                    // Create an active audio
        NewActiveSound.SetSound(Sound);
        NewActiveSound.SetWorld(ThisWorld);

        NewActiveSound.SetPitch(PitchMultiplier);
        NewActiveSound.SetVolume(VolumeMultiplier);

        NewActiveSound.RequestedStartTime = FMath::Max(0.f, StartTime);

        NewActiveSound.bIsUISound = bIsUISound;
        NewActiveSound.bAllowSpatialization = false;

        if (ConcurrencySettings)
        {
            NewActiveSound.ConcurrencySet.Add(ConcurrencySettings);
        }

        NewActiveSound.Priority = Sound->Priority;
        NewActiveSound.SubtitlePriority = Sound->GetSubtitlePriority();

        // If OwningActor isn't supplied to this function, derive an owner from the WorldContextObject
        const AActor* ActiveSoundOwner = OwningActor ? OwningActor : GameplayStatics::GetActorOwnerFromWorldContextObject(WorldContextObject);

        NewActiveSound.SetOwner(ActiveSoundOwner);

        TArray<FAudioParameter> Params;
        UActorSoundParameterInterface::Fill(ActiveSoundOwner, Params);

        AudioDevice->AddNewActiveSound(NewActiveSound, &Params);    // Throw the active audio to the output device for processing
    }
}

The Wave data we add by calling USoundWaveProcedural::QueueAudio will be stored in the internal AudioBuffer, and later the audio device will call USoundWaveProcedural::GeneratePCMData to receive it and play the sound.

int32 USoundWaveProcedural::GeneratePCMData(uint8* PCMData, const int32 SamplesNeeded)
{
    // ...
    FMemory::Memcpy((void*)PCMData, &AudioBuffer[0], BytesToCopy);
}

Using USoundWaveProcedural, we can play PCM data. But if it involves some complex audio generation strategies, we may need to derive USoundWaveProcedural. The implementation of UMetaSoundSource is a good reference example. We just need to customize an ISoundGenerator and override its audio generation function:

class ISoundGenerator
{
public:
    ENGINE_API ISoundGenerator();
    ENGINE_API virtual ~ISoundGenerator();

    // Called when a new buffer is required. 
    virtual int32 OnGenerateAudio(float* OutAudio, int32 NumSamples) = 0;

    // Returns the number of samples to render per callback
    virtual int32 GetDesiredNumSamplesToRenderPerCallback() const { return 1024; }

    // Optional. Called on audio generator thread right when the generator begins generating.
    virtual void OnBeginGenerate() {}

    // Optional. Called on audio generator thread right when the generator ends generating.
    virtual void OnEndGenerate() {}

    // Optional. Can be overridden to end the sound when generating is finished.
