    virtual bool IsFinished() const { return false; }

    // Retrieves the next buffer of audio from the generator, called from the audio mixer
    ENGINE_API int32 GetNextBuffer(float* OutAudio, int32 NumSamples, bool bRequireNumberSamples = false);

    virtual Audio::AudioTaskQueueId GetSynchronizedRenderQueueId() const { return 0; }

protected:

    // Protected method to execute lambda in audio render thread
    // Used for conveying parameter changes or events to the generator thread.
    ENGINE_API void SynthCommand(TUniqueFunction<void()> Command);

private:

    ENGINE_API void PumpPendingMessages();

    // The command queue used to convey commands from game thread to generator thread 
    TQueue<TUniqueFunction<void()>> CommandQueue;

    friend class USynthComponent;
};

Then derive your own USoundWaveProcedural and override:

virtual ISoundGeneratorPtr USoundBase::CreateSoundGenerator(const FSoundGeneratorInitParams& InParams) { return nullptr; }

When the UE audio device plays an audio source, if it is procedural audio (USoundWave.bProcedural == true), it will call CreateSoundGenerator to create a SoundGenerator for it:

When actually parsing the audio, the following interface will be called to generate the audio:

For detailed implementation, refer to UMetaSoundSource and FMetasoundGenerator.

docs.title: Capture Audio
docs.text:
There are few requirements for audio capture in game projects, so only a brief introduction is given here.

Regarding audio capture, it is mainly divided into two categories:

  • Capture system audio
  • Capture in-game audio

docs.title: System Audio Capture
docs.text:
System audio capture specifically refers to the collection of input devices (microphones). UE currently does not support the capture of output devices. If there is a corresponding requirement, you need to use a lower-level API to implement it (such as WASAPI).

TSharedPtr<Audio::FAudioCapture> AudioCapture = MakeShared<Audio::FAudioCapture>();
Audio::FOnCaptureFunction OnCapture = [](const float* AudioData,
                                             int32 NumFrames, 
                                             int32 InNumChannels,
                                             int32 InSampleRate, 
                                             double StreamTime, 
                                             bool bOverFlow) {
    // Process the captured audio data, which is in an asynchronous thread at this time
};
Audio::FAudioCaptureDeviceParams Params;                                    // Parameter configuration for audio capture. If no device is filled, the default input device will be used
if (mAudioCapture->OpenCaptureStream(Params, MoveTemp(OnCapture), 1024)) {  // Start audio capture
    Audio::FCaptureDeviceInfo Info;
    if (mAudioCapture->GetCaptureDeviceInfo(Info)){
        OnAudioFormatChanged.ExecuteIfBound(Info.InputChannels, Info.PreferredSampleRate);  // Notification signal for audio format change
    }
}

docs.title: In-Game Audio Capture
docs.text:
In-game audio capture uses the interface ISubmixBufferListener provided by UE:

/** Abstract interface for receiving audio data from a given submix. */
class ISubmixBufferListener
{
public:
    virtual ~ISubmixBufferListener() = default;

    /**
    Called when a new buffer has been rendered for a given submix
    @param OwningSubmix The submix object which has rendered a new buffer
    @param AudioData        Ptr to the audio buffer
    @param NumSamples       The number of audio samples in the audio buffer
    @param NumChannels      The number of channels of audio in the buffer (e.g. 2 for stereo, 6 for 5.1, etc)
    @param SampleRate       The sample rate of the audio buffer
    @param AudioClock       Double audio clock value, from start of audio rendering.
    */
    virtual void OnNewSubmixBuffer(const USoundSubmix* OwningSubmix, float* AudioData, int32 NumSamples, int32 NumChannels, const int32 SampleRate, double AudioClock) = 0;

    /**
     * Called if the submix is evaluating disabling itself for the next buffer of audio in FMixerSubmix::IsRenderingAudio()
     * if this returns true, FMixerSubmix::IsRenderingAudio() will return true.
     * Otherwise the submix will evaluate playing sounds, children submixes, etc to see if it should auto-disable
     *
     * This is called every evaluation.
     * ISubmixListeners that intermittently render audio should only return true when they have work to do.
     */
    virtual bool IsRenderingAudio() const
    {
        return false;
    }
};

We just need to derive from ISubmixBufferListener, override OnNewSubmixBuffer to process audio data, and register it to the USoundSubmix of the FAudioDevice that needs to be captured. This code has many dependencies and would be messy to paste in the article. For the specific implementation, please refer to FNiagaraSubmixListener.

docs.title: DSP
docs.text:
UE has a very comprehensive built-in DSP module called SignalProcessing

You can find almost everything you need in it:

Here are some commonly used structures and functions:

  • Audio::TCircularAudioBuffer: A circular buffer, often used for streaming audio storage.
  • Audio::TSampleBuffer: Used to convert RawPCM data into sampleable data of the corresponding bit depth, similar to the SampleValueWriteFunction we provided earlier, but only supports int16 and float.
  • Audio::FResampler: A resampler used to modify the sampling rate of audio.
  • Audio::FWindow: Used to generate window functions, supporting Hamming, Hann, and Blackman.
  • Audio::TSlidingWindow: A sliding window.
  • Audio::IFFTAlgorithm: Provides basic FFT algorithms, created via FFFTFactory::NewFFTAlgorithm(...).
  • Audio::FBiquadFilter: A biquad filter.
  • Audio::FSpectrumAnalyzer: A spectrum analyzer that supports amplitude spectrum and CQT spectrum.
  • Audio::FAsyncSpectrumAnalyzer: An asynchronous spectrum analyzer that runs in a separate thread, with the same functionality as above.
  • ConstantQ.h: Provides a series of structures supporting Constant Q Transform (CQT). CQT is often used for music spectrum visualization and has better rhythm representation compared to FFT.

For spectrum analysis, UE also has a module AudioSynesthesia to extend related functions.

It supports analysis of CQT, Onset, Loudness, and Meter. Unfortunately, most of them are NRT (Non-Real-Time) interfaces, which require audio data to be imported as assets during editing. However, many of its algorithm structures can be referenced.

docs.title: MetaSound
docs.text:
MetaSound is a new-generation audio system introduced in UE5. Compared to the old Sound Cues, MetaSound not only has better performance but also supports Procedural functionality, which is more important.

Currently, MetaSound shows great potential in UGC (User-Generated Content):

  • Mix Universe: Event Speech | Bringing Music to "Mix Universe" (Official Subtitles)
  • Fortnite: Fortnite - AR Arrangement

If you are not familiar with MetaSound, it is highly recommended to watch this basic video:

  • Event Speech | MetaSound Guide for Beginners (Official Subtitles)

Create a new MetaSoundSource, build the following graph, and click play. You will hear the familiar sine wave:

The MetaSound graph is a data flow graph that executes every frame. Each node is a functional block that accepts inputs, combines them with the current context of MetaSound execution to populate output data, and the audio generated each frame is stored in the AudioBuffer of MetaSoundSource, waiting for the audio engine to play it.

Trigger Pin can be simply treated as a bool variable. Output nodes will set it to true, and input nodes will read its value to determine whether to execute the node's logic.

Taking the sine wave above as an example, when the engine plays MetaSound, the following steps are performed:

  • First, an asynchronous task to build the MetaSound graph is created, with the corresponding function stack as follows:

  • In the asynchronous task, all nodes are loaded (nodes without dependencies are removed), and the remaining nodes are topologically sorted according to their dependencies. The corresponding code stack is as follows:

  • Finally, IOperator is created through the INodeOperatorFactory inside the node. The partial definition of IOperator is as follows. It provides BindInput, ResetFunction, ExecuteFunction, and PostExecuteFunction to write related logic:

    class IOperator
{
public:
    /** FResetOperatorParams holds the parameters provided to an IOperator's 
     * reset function.
     */
    struct FResetParams
    {
        /** General operator settings for the graph. */
        const FOperatorSettings& OperatorSettings; 

        /** Environment settings available. */
        const FMetasoundEnvironment& Environment;
    };

    virtual ~IOperator() {}

    /** BindInputs binds data references in the IOperator with the FInputVertexInterfaceData.
     *
     * All input data references should be bound to the InVertexData to support
     * other MetaSound systems such as MetaSound BP API, Operator Caching, 
     * and live auditioning. 
     *
     * Note: The virtual function IOPerator::BindInputs(...) will be made a
     * pure virtual when IOperator::GetInputs() is removed at or after release 5.5
     *
     * Note: Binding an data reference may update the which underlying object 
     * the reference points to. Any operator which caches pointers or values 
     * from data references must update their cached pointers in the call to 
     * BindInputs(...).  Operators which do not cache the underlying pointer 
     * of a data reference do not need to update anything after BindInputs(...)
     *
     * Example:
     *  FMyOperator::FMyOperator(TDataReadReference<float> InGain, TDataReadReference<FAudioBuffer> InAudioBuffer)
     *  : Gain(InGain)
     *  , AudioBuffer(InAudioBuffer)
     *  {
     *      MyBufferPtr = AudioBuffer->GetData();       
     *  }
     *
     *  void FMyOperator::BindInputs(FInputVertexInterfaceData& InVertexData)
     *  {
     *      InVertexData.BindReadVertex("Gain", Gain);
     *      InVertexData.BindReadVertex("Audio", AudioBuffer);
     *
     *      // Update MyBufferPtr in case AudioBuffer references a new FAudioBuffer.
     *      MyBufferPtr = AudioBuffer->GetData();
     *  }
     */
    virtual void METASOUNDGRAPHCORE_API BindInputs(FInputVertexInterfaceData& InVertexData);

    /** BindOutputs binds data references in the IOperator with the FOutputVertexInterfaceData.
     *
     * All output data references should be bound to the InVertexData to support
     * other MetaSound systems such as MetaSound BP API, Operator Caching, 
     * and live auditioning. 
     *
     * Note: The virtual function IOPerator::BindOutputs(...) will be made a
     * pure virtual when IOperator::GetOutputs() is removed at or after release 5.5
     *
     * Note: Binding an data reference may update the which underlying object 
     * the reference points to. Any operator which caches pointers or values 
     * from data references must update their cached pointers in the call to 
     * BindOutputs(...).  Operators which do not cache the underlying pointer 
     * of a data reference do not need to update anything after BindOutputs(...)
     *
     * Example:
     *  FMyOperator::FMyOperator(TDataWriteReference<float> InGain, TDataWriteReference<FAudioBuffer> InAudioBuffer)
     *  : Gain(InGain)
     *  , AudioBuffer(InAudioBuffer)
     *  {
     *      MyBufferPtr = AudioBuffer->GetData();       
     *  }
     *
     *  void FMyOperator::BindOutputs(FOutputVertexInterfaceData& InVertexData)
     *  {
     *      InVertexData.BindReadVertex("Gain", Gain);
     *      InVertexData.BindReadVertex("Audio", AudioBuffer);
     *
     *      // Update MyBufferPtr in case AudioBuffer references a new FAudioBuffer.
     *      MyBufferPtr = AudioBuffer->GetData();
     *  }
     */
    virtual void METASOUNDGRAPHCORE_API BindOutputs(FOutputVertexInterfaceData& InVertexData);

    /** Pointer to initialize function for an operator.
     *
     * @param IOperator* - The operator associated with the function pointer.
     */
    using FResetFunction = void(*)(IOperator*, const FResetParams& InParams);

    /** Return the reset function to call during graph execution.
     *
     * The IOperator* argument to the FExecutionFunction will be the same IOperator instance
     * which returned the execution function.
     *
     * nullptr return values are valid and signal an IOperator which does not need to be
     * reset.
     */
    virtual FResetFunction GetResetFunction() = 0;

    /** Pointer to execute function for an operator.
     *
     * @param IOperator* - The operator associated with the function pointer.
     */
    using FExecuteFunction = void(*)(IOperator*);

    /** Return the execution function to call during graph execution.
     *
     * The IOperator* argument to the FExecutionFunction will be the same IOperator instance
     * which returned the execution function.
     *
     * nullptr return values are valid and signal an IOperator which does not need to be
     * executed.
     */
    virtual FExecuteFunction GetExecuteFunction() = 0;

    /** Pointer to post execute function for an operator.
     *
     * @param IOperator* - The operator associated with the function pointer.
     */
    using FPostExecuteFunction = void(*)(IOperator*);

    /** Return the FPostExecute function to call during graph post execution.
     *
     * The IOperator* argument to the FPostExecutionFunction will be the same IOperator instance
     * which returned the execution function.
     *
     * nullptr return values are valid and signal an IOperator which does not need to be
     * post executed.
     */
    virtual FPostExecuteFunction GetPostExecuteFunction() = 0;
};

  • After the above process, the graph is built. Remember what we mentioned earlier: if bProcedural of USoundWave is true, it will create a corresponding ISoundGenerator and call ISoundGenerator::OnGenerateAudio every frame of the audio engine to fill data. Exactly, MetaSound follows this process:

  • Let's see what our sine wave node does during this frame's execution:

    Each frame, it increments Phase according to DeltaPhase, then retrieves the relevant sample value from the WaveTable of FSineWaveTableGenerator and fills it into the output AudioBuffer.

By now, you should have a basic understanding of the fundamental principles of MetaSound.

However, to use MetaSound well, you need more professional audio knowledge. The author is also a novice in this area and can't be of much help~

It provides many function nodes. Give them a try—your computer won't explode:

But sometimes it can't fully meet our needs. Now, you can try making some custom extensions.

docs.title: Blueprint Interaction
docs.text:
MetaSound is different from Blueprints; it supports relatively limited variables:

You can also extend these variables in C++ by finding appropriate references.

These parameters are not directly exposed to the property editor, so modifying their values is a bit complicated. We can use UAudioComponent to simplify this process. It derives from IAudioParameterControllerInterface, which provides many convenient interfaces for setting audio parameters:

If you don't want to use UAudioComponent, you can refer to the specific implementation of related functions.

It's worth mentioning the Trigger in UE's audio system, which is different from the Delegate commonly used in C++ code. We can simply treat it as a bool variable, like in this graph:

As we know, each node is executed according to the topological order of dependencies. When the Input executes, it sets the output delegate When Playing to true. When AD Envelope executes, it reads the node connected to its input delegate Trigger (i.e., When Playing). If it finds the value is true, it executes the node. After AD Envelope finishes executing, it sets the output delegate When Done to true. At this point, when the Output node executes, it detects that the input delegate When Done is true and notifies MetaSoundSource to stop playing, which happens here:

docs.title: Vegetation Optimization Techniques in Open Worlds
Vegetation Optimization Techniques in Open Worlds
docs.text:
I believe that in some large-scale games, we have all more or less witnessed some breathtaking natural scenery and can't help but marvel at the artistic effects displayed by these games:

Ghost of Tsushima

Horizon Forbidden West

Shadow of the Tomb Raider

Kena: Bridge of Spirits

YanCloud 16

Assassin's Creed: Odyssey

And none of these games were made with UE...

It must be acknowledged that although Unreal Engine 5 is very powerful, it is not omnipotent. To build natural scenes that meet the performance requirements of game projects like the ones above, we will face many challenges beyond engine technology.

In open natural scenes, the frequency and impact of performance issues caused by vegetation are often no less than those caused by lighting and special effects.

When it comes to vegetation optimization in UE5, the first things that come to mind might be reducing polygons, instancing, distance culling, optimizing materials, using LOD, or Nanite...

These asset-level optimizations and complex specialized methods often struggle to support the lush vegetation ecosystems in open scenes.

Therefore, this article will elaborate on some strategies and perspectives regarding vegetation optimization.

docs.title: Plant Asset Production
docs.text:
Most 3D modeling software can create plant assets, but in the game industry, Speed Tree is the mainstream vegetation production tool.

Unlike common models such as rocks, items, and buildings, plants often have a large number of stems and leaves. Geometrically, this means plant models usually have a large number of dense vertices and faces, which brings very high rendering costs. Here is an example:

  • Such a not-so-lush tree has up to two million triangles. This huge amount of vertex data and numerous repeated draws will keep the GPU busy.

This method of using model geometry to represent plant structures is generally called model trees/grass. Usually, assets of this specification cannot be used in large quantities in game projects.

In existing game projects, plant assets are more often made using the card/mask method. By pressing some branches and leaves onto a texture sheet and inserting a large number of cards on the branches to show a lush appearance, this is a very clever production method. Although there are some flaws in the effect, the performance benefits it brings are very objective.

The card method has long been recognized as the most efficient way for vegetation rendering in the game industry, but it also has some defects:

  • Visual defects, easy to be exposed in close-up shots.
  • Using mask materials, although the number of vertices is reduced, there is still a lot of OverDraw, and the shadow rendering cost is higher.
  • Plant models lack vertex features of branches and leaves, resulting in loss of global illumination effects.

With the emergence of UE5's virtual geometry technology - Nanite, this situation has changed somewhat.

The advantage of Nanite lies in using a GPU-driven pipeline, which can quickly switch geometric details and timely cull invisible triangles, greatly improving vertex utilization (screen space ratio) without affecting the visual effect as much as possible.

The model tree used earlier has only one million pixels in the image but two million vertices. Obviously, most vertices contribute little to the​画面​ effect.

Regarding Nanite, here is a good official usage guide:

  • Documentation | Nanite Virtualized Geometry (epicgames.com)
  • [Official Training] 23 - Creating Art Assets for UE | Epic Li Wenlei

The official also made a more detailed comparison for Nanite vegetation:

  • Vegetation Best Practices for UE5 | Epic Developer Community (epicgames.com)

In the official test report, with Nanite enabled, results completely different from traditional rendering methods were shown - using model trees performed better than card trees.

Based on this analysis result, does it mean that we can use the model tree method with the help of Nanite to render vegetation more efficiently?

The answer is no.

A valid argument is: The screenshots of those games listed earlier did not use virtual geometry technology like Nanite, but they still built stunning natural ecological scenery. In contrast...

docs.title: The Downside of Nanite
docs.text:
The reason for the negative answer is not about the vertex data volume and video memory usage, because vegetation in the scene is usually drawn in an instanced way, especially in open world scenes. We are very concerned about the load balance of performance between partitions. Although a single model tree using Nanite may indeed have better performance, it will also hinder us from building a unified vegetation strategy with superior performance.

The following will elaborate on the problems of using Nanite from several aspects. The views may be somewhat subjective. If there are any mistakes, please correct them~

  • Higher effect expectations, accompanied by more difficult performance balance control
  • Unable to specialize model optimization strategies, and not the most performance-optimal model optimization processing method
  • Static data with fixed precision gradients is easier to organize into high-performance dense vegetation

docs.title: Higher effect expectations, accompanied by more difficult performance balance control
docs.text:
When UE5 was released, I believe many friends were shocked by the​画面​ effect shown in the demo. At that time, many people might have thought that we were about to usher in the next generation of game graphics:

Believe it or not, I did (dog head). Many teams I know also believed it.

Those who believed have been official guinea pigs for the past few years and have suffered a lot. This has an even more significant impact on a commercial project.

But complaints aside, Nanite is indeed a breakthrough technology with absolute advantages over traditional LOD. With the official optimization iterations over the years, its reliability has gradually improved.

Currently, it can indeed be widely used in actual game projects, but the problems brought by Nanite usually do not lie in itself.

I'm using Nanite, so it's not too much to make a small stone with one million triangles, right? Anyway, it will automatically reduce polygons.

Is this the number of vertices you call a tree? The details are gone. How dare you say you use UE5? Do you look down on me?

This situation usually occurs in emerging teams using UE. In fact, the popularity of UE is not that long ago, and most teams using UE do not have deep engine technology accumulation (especially in China). For such emerging technologies, such teams are prone to​盲从​ marketing rhetoric, thereby weakening or even ignoring the iteration and accumulation of content production pipelines.

Precisely because of the blessing of Nanite, bosses and development teams often have higher requirements for game graphics. From the optimization perspective, although Nanite can improve vertex utilization, if source assets with more details are used, it will mean larger disk usage, and the entire scene will have more and denser vertices than before.

The number of vertices will seriously affect the performance consumption of some rendering stages:

  • Shadow Map construction
  • Velocity buffer drawing

And disk usage not only affects the final package size but also significantly increases the difficulty of project scene management.

Take Ghost of Tsushima as an example. You may think its map is not particularly large (28.62 km2), with few model types and low precision, but its package size is over 50 GB. What's more alarming is the size of its development assets:

I highly recommend watching this GDC to get a concept of asset management for large-scale projects:

  • Zen of Streaming: Building and Loading 'Ghost of Tsushima' (youtube.com)

Imagine if we use UE's Nanite to replicate a scene like Ghost of Tsushima. Conservatively, if we increase the asset precision by four or five times, we can imagine how high the management cost of such a huge project asset will be.

Therefore, for game projects, I still suggest managing the expectations of scene art effects as much as possible. It should not affect or even drag down the iteration of gameplay.

If the game scene cannot run stably at 80 frames on the development machine, and seriously encroaches on the performance budget and iteration space of gameplay or other modules, no matter how good it looks, if it lacks gameplay, what's the use? I believe most players will not pay for a game just because it has photo-realistic graphics.

docs.title: Unable to specialize model optimization strategies, and not the most performance-optimal model optimization processing method
docs.text:
There are usually two ways to optimize models:

  • Reduce:​删减​ the geometric data of the source model to get a simplified model.
  • Remesh: Approximate the source model with a certain voxel precision through voxelization model algorithms to get a simplified model.

These two strategies have different application scenarios:

  • Reduce: Suitable for planes, usually used for models with high requirements for geometric edges and corners, such as terrain, buildings, plants, water planes...
  • Remesh: Suitable for closed models with relatively rounded geometric shapes, which can usually ensure the geometric shape of the source model with very few vertices, such as stones, buildings, props...

For trees, if we use these two strategies to generate simplified models with the same number of triangles:

Nanite uses the Reduce algorithm. It can be understood that the reduced model will be a certain precision gradient of Nanite. The Nanite strategy is to prioritize ensuring that the​画面​ is not distorted. If this tree uses Nanite directly, how far do you think it needs to be to display such precision? Obviously, it has to be very far, and there are still many vertices at this time.

Both strategies have their own problems:

  • Remesh: The model becomes fluffy, and black blocks appear where UV mapping is abnormal. (In fact, to generate a good Remesh model, the parameters of the voxel algorithm need a lot of fine-tuning and specialization)
  • Reduce: A lot of leaf details are lost.

In this regard, I have done many attempts and can clearly say that it is difficult to get excellent plant LOD through automated model processing algorithms with unified strategies.

Why is vegetation optimization so difficult? Because many times people treat it as a regular model in the engine's rendering mechanism for optimization, but the most critical part of making good vegetation in games is the production skills.

For manually making LOD, art students can use as few main branches as possible to create a larger coverage area, use secondary branches to add local details to the main branches, and when making low-level LOD, only need to cut off a certain number of secondary branches.

You can also adjust the vertex color to distinguish between main and secondary branches, and finally use the vertex color weight-based reduction method for plants.

Usually, vertex colors are painted on trees as weights for the vertex offset amplitude during plant wind calculation. This weight factor can also be used as the weight for regional simplification.

This method can be used to generate several high-precision LODs of plant models, but unfortunately, the simplified models generated in this way still often have a high number of vertices (when simplified to more than 1500 vertices, the model is already unrecognizable). To further reduce the number of vertices significantly (without cutting the main branches, otherwise there will be great visual defects) while ensuring the model's performance effect, it is obvious that the simplification method cannot do this. We must break the original geometric structure of the model. However, the Remesh method often makes a tree very fluffy and has UV mapping abnormalities. Its performance effect is not good. Is there any other way to solve this problem?

The answer is yes. Our ultimate goal is to ensure the display effect of the model, not the geometric structure. This also leads to another strategy for model optimization - Impostor.

Impostor is my own translation. Translating it as "proxy" is easy to confuse with Proxy, and translating it as "impostor" is not very nice.

We usually use Impostor as the last level LOD of vegetation models. Common Impostor strategies include the following:

  • Billboard: Draw the model from a specific angle onto a texture.
  • Flipbook: Draw the model from multiple angles onto a texture, and finally switch the displayed texture according to the player's perspective in the material.
  • Billboard Cloud/ Mesh Card Cloud: Draw the model on many mesh cards to stack up the perspective effect similar to the source model.
  • Octahedron: Draw the model with a certain perspective distribution onto a texture, and finally interpolate images from multiple angles in the material to present a reliable perspective transition effect.

  • Game Scene Vegetation Optimization —— Impostor - Italink's video - Zhihu

The implementation principles of these Impostor strategies are not complicated. After understanding their principles, we can easily build an Impostor generation pipeline. However, there are some specialized SDKs available for us to use:

  • Simplygon - Setting the Standard for 3D Game Content Optimization
  • InstaLOD - Everything You Need to Produce and Automatically Optimize 3D Content

I used InstaLOD (free for personal use) for testing. This is the UE plugin it provides, which includes many model processing algorithms:

For Octahedron, UE provides a special plugin:

For its usage, you can check this article:

  • 【Performance Optimization】Use of Impostor in Unreal (Vegetation Optimization) - Zhihu (zhihu.com)

For those interested in the principle, you can check this blog:

  • https://shaderbits.com/blog/octahedral-impostors

The most valuable thing for an actual project is not the editor, but the code interface related to model processing inside, which helps the project team build a model generation pipeline that meets their own project specifications.

With so many Impostor strategies, some friends may ask, which one has better performance and effect?

Billboard and Flipbook have very few vertices, small texture sizes, and simple shader programs. Their performance effects are undoubtedly the best, but their performance effects are often not good.

The most controversial are the Billboard Cloud and Octahedron methods. In many previous 3A projects, the Billboard Cloud method was basically used, but I found in the UE forum that many people recommend using Octahedron.

I did a simple comparison test here. Who is better may need more data support:

Source Model

  • Number of triangles: 639639
  • Texture size: 4096
  • GPU time: 15.52ms

Billboard Cloud

  • Number of triangles: 32
  • Texture size: 2048
  • GPU time: 10.81ms

Octahedron

  • Number of triangles: 32
  • Texture size: 2048
  • GPU time: 7.75ms

It can be clearly seen that the performance and​画面​ performance of Octahedron are better than those of Billboard Cloud. However, if it is only used as the last level LOD, the texture size of Billboard Cloud still has a lot of optimization space. The specific plan may vary from person to person.

If Octahedron is used, we can make such an LOD chain without affecting the tree effect:

This precision gradient, combined with instancing, can achieve very low performance consumption. In contrast, it is very difficult to achieve the same goal with Nanite, because the current automatic reduction algorithm used by Nanite has low degradation efficiency for models like trees. To ensure that the​画面​ is not distorted, it will comprehensively consider the average distribution of precision to ensure that the​画面​ is not distorted, lacking the distinction of important parts. It usually has more vertex details, and the performance improvement brought by Impostor is completely incomparable to Nanite.

This is a simple comparison test I did:

  • Nanite undoubtedly has the most​保真​ effect details, but its performance consumption is much higher than that of LOD. Moreover, because Nanite is based on camera perspective geometric scheduling, when the perspective rotates rapidly (which is very common in game projects), the GPU consumption will fluctuate severely!

The above LOD chain also leads us to think about another problem:

  • For the problem of multi-quality compatibility, in the traditional LOD strategy, we usually adjust the Bias of LOD to do compatibility for different qualities. For example, in high quality, the LOD chain starts from LOD0, and in low quality, the LOD chain can start from LOD1 or LOD, which can greatly reduce the number of vertices, thereby improving scene performance. But in Nanite, what should we do?

The LOD of a model is usually manually supervised, which needs to ensure clear optimization range and smooth transition effect. To achieve this, each model's LOD usually needs to be manually made or use non-unified parameter model simplification strategies.

Nanite is different. Nanite uses a unified reduction strategy for all models. This strategy optimizes vertices as much as possible while ensuring the visual effect. This strategy will lead to some models having high degradation efficiency and some having low degradation efficiency due to different model characteristics.

Although Nanite can also adjust the offset and degradation multiplier, using unified parameters will definitely break the above strategy, leading to the visual effect of the model not being guaranteed, and some abnormalities or even broken faces that users cannot accept.

This is not just for vegetation, but for all models using Nanite.

docs.title: Static data with fixed precision gradients is easier to organize into high-performance dense vegetation
docs.text:
My understanding of Nanite has gone through several stages:

  1. "Use it as much as possible": Turn on Nanite for everything.
  2. Encountered a pitfall: Grass should not use Nanite. There are some bugs when using Nanite for objects with dense instanced rendering.
  3. Encountered another pitfall: The characteristics of Nanite cannot fit the HISM mechanism. Theoretically, objects that need HISM for efficient rendering cannot use Nanite.
  4. After in-depth understanding of the production methods of some projects - who uses Nanite for vegetation seriously?

Let's talk about the first pitfall. Nanite's reduction is friendly to individual instances. It can easily reduce a model with millions of triangles and a relatively rounded geometry to empty pixels and finally be culled. However, for grass or trees that have tens of thousands of instances through instancing, the degradation of Nanite cannot efficiently reduce instances, and a large number of vertices will undoubtedly generate huge overhead for Nanite's scheduling calculation, further occupying the computing resources of other GPU tasks. This is especially obvious on some mid-to-low-end models.

When the number of Nanite instances in the current​画面​ exceeds a certain threshold, it may even cause​画面​ abnormalities, although there are some engine commands that help improve this phenomenon.

The second pitfall should be discussed in combination with the HLOD of world partitioning. HLOD is a distant proxy used to display outside the streaming loading range in the open world. Ordinary models can generate distant HLOD through Merge + Remesh in the partition. However, for vegetation, using the voxelized Remesh algorithm for objects with many fragmented planes will generate marshmallows. The Merge + Reduce method cannot guarantee the​画面​ quality of distant vegetation while greatly reducing the number of vertices and DrawCall. Therefore, the HLOD of vegetation can only use Instancing. The instancing optimization in world partitioning, in addition to regional​切块​ for instanced vegetation, also needs to use Hierarchical Instanced Static Mesh (HISM), which is different from Instanced Static Mesh (ISM). Hierarchical instanced meshes allow switching LOD inside the instanced mesh. For example, all the trees below are drawn with one HISM:

HISM essentially divides the instanced mesh into ClusterTree, each Cluster has its own independent LOD level, and finally generates multiple levels of ISM. Through some engine commands, we can control the division strategy of HISM. For specific implementation details, you can refer to:

  • UHierarchicalInstancedStaticMesh (HISM) Principle Analysis - CSDN Blog
  • HISM Large-scale Vegetation Rendering Solution - CSDN Blog

Unlike traditional LOD schemes, Nanite does not have a few models with fixed precision gradients. Its LOD gradient is not at the model level, but at the cluster level. Therefore, the HISM mechanism cannot work normally on models using Nanite.

docs.title: Production Reference
docs.text:
For the production standard of LOD, you can refer to the GDC sharing of Horizon, except that the last level LOD becomes Octahedron:

  • Between Tech and Art: The Vegetation of Horizon Zero Dawn (youtube.com)
  • Interactive Wind and Vegetation in 'God of War' (youtube.com)

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
I have said a lot of trivial information above, and here is a unified summary:

  • For plants with the same lushness, using the model tree method will generate a large number of vertices, and the performance and memory consumption it brings are much higher than those of the card tree method.
  • The current reduction strategy of Nanite has low degradation efficiency for leaves, while manually controlling the LOD precision gradient and using Impostor can usually produce vegetation with better performance.
  • Whether it is a model tree or a card tree, turning on Nanite will definitely have optimization improvements, but Nanite is contrary to HISM. Therefore, if there is a lot of vegetation in the project scene, it is not recommended to use Nanite vegetation, but to use traditional LOD production processes with ISM and HISM for optimization.
  • For emerging teams, everyone is crossing the river by feeling the stones, and it is difficult to say which solution is optimal. Once it is determined, you can rest assured by laying out the quantity according to this specification. Facing this problem of uncertain solutions, our best management plan is to build our own content generation pipeline to minimize the sunk cost in the iteration and verification process as much as possible.

It is recommended to build a preview level for scene assets:

docs.title: Vegetation Organization
docs.text: After determining the vegetation production pipeline, we also need to consider the planning method of vegetation in the scene.

docs.title: Construction Methods
docs.text:
In UE, there are mainly the following ways to create a large number of vegetation:

  • Foliage EdMode

  • Landscape Foliage Type

  • Procedural Content Generation Framework

These methods have their own application scenarios:

  • Foliage EdMode: For a serious game project, I can only say that Foliage EdMode is something that cannot be touched at all. This way of painting vegetation has a huge rework cost and is difficult to do cross-platform performance adaptation.

  • PCG: The PCG framework is undoubtedly the best vegetation editing method. Using it can easily and quickly build ecological communities, and can customize some scalable parameters for multi-platform adaptation.

  • Landscape Foliage Type: It is suitable for dense grass drawing. The implementation in UE should refer to the management process of procedural grass in Ghost of Tsushima. It generates grass clusters through asynchronous tasks during preview. Although it is very efficient, using Landscape Foliage Type will occupy a terrain layer to describe the density of grass, which is not suitable for large-scale use.

docs.title: Partitioning and Streaming
docs.text:
First, let's review the content about UE5 world partitioning. I have sorted out a related article before:

  • Unreal Engine 5 Development — Open World Production - Zhihu (zhihu.com)

Some key construction guidelines were also given by the official some time ago:

  • World Construction Guide (qq.com)
  • Advanced World Building in Unreal Engine - Chris Murphy / Epic Games for WA Games Week 2023 - YouTube

I believe everyone has a certain concept of Streaming:

This is the grid configuration used in my personal test project:

GirdName Cell Size Loading Range Priority BlockOnSlowStreaming MainGrid（Default） 12800 25600 0 false DeferGrid 25600 25600 -9 true AdvanceGrid 51200 51200 9 true SmallGrid 6400 12800 -9 false

Usually, a loading range of 256 m can ensure that most of the performance effects in the field of view are normal. The following is the effect in the 3D view (the character in the distance is a small black dot under 256 m):

Scene models are generally placed in Main Grid, but considering that the cell size (CellSize) will also affect the distance of HLOD batching, I recommend putting vegetation in AdvanceGrid.

Unlike other regular static models, vegetation cannot generate a high-quality distant proxy by Merge+Remesh in open world scenes. But vegetation cannot be Merge into a Mesh, or after Merge into a Mesh, there is no good strategy to ensure the effect of vegetation while greatly reducing its vertices and optimizing its materials. Therefore, if you want to make a large range of vegetation, you can only use the instanced way to lay it. To ensure the load balance of performance between the world partition units, we must strictly control the number of plant types. There will definitely be some compromises in the art effect.

Distance culling usually causes serious visual defects. If we can use some means (such as fog, corners) to block the vegetation at a distance, we do not need to consider the problem of distant proxies in this case. In this case, treat the plant as a regular Mesh, turn on Nanite, and combine with the unloading or distance culling of world partitioning to achieve good performance effects.

Usually, vegetation uses HISM for organization at close range. After exceeding the loading range:

  • For small vegetation, you can directly not display the distant proxy. If you use terrain grass, you usually need to ensure that the color of the grass is basically the same as the terrain color, so that there will be no particularly obvious visual defects at a distance. If you do not use terrain grass but use procedural grass, you can bake a color texture from the top view in the procedural blueprint in the editor and render it as a decal as the distant proxy of the grass.
  • For large vegetation, usually referring to trees, after exceeding the loading range, HISM can be degraded to ISM using the lowest level LOD as HLOD (HISM has the overhead of cluster division and LOD switching scheduling), like this:

The LOD of vegetation needs to be able to transition smoothly. Since HISM will become ISM when exceeding the loading range, it is necessary to ensure that the LOD levels on the left and right sides of the loading distance are consistent, which means that the LOD gradient of the model is distributed within the loading distance. Since UE currently uses the screen space size as the basis for model LOD switching, it needs to be converted to the corresponding distance during production.

Although with the blessing of world partitioning, it does not mean that we can build an infinitely large scene. Its advantage is more about seamless loading. The real-time computing resources of the computer are limited. Although this batching mechanism can further expand the distance, the larger the range, the greater the performance overhead, and the less budget left for gameplay. Therefore, the distance that the character can see should still be maintained within a certain distance, such as 768 m:

Not only trees, but also other models, particles, dynamic material effects, etc. are recommended to follow this rule.

docs.title: Shadow Optimization
docs.text:
The shadow consumption of vegetation is often a large part of the entire scene, because it has a large number of dense and overlapping triangles.

So how to optimize shadows?

First, we need to think about a question: Why do we need shadows? If we turn off the shadows, we will see:

If players are asked after watching the above comparison​画面​: Do you like the​画面​ with shadows or the one without shadows?

Most players will probably answer: I choose the​画面​ with shadows.

Further question: Why do you like the​画面​ with shadows?

Most answers may be: Because without shadows, the​画面​ looks very​违和​.

Indeed, when we turn off the shadows, the spatial hierarchy of the​画面​ becomes much worse, which violates people's intuitive feeling of space.

In the process of game development, we need to learn to​揣摩​ the real intentions of players. Just like here, essentially, players do not care about shadows. They may not even care what shadows are. They just don't like the​违和​画面​ after losing shadows.

Usually, pursuing physical or academic correctness in game projects is usually meaningless, or its cost performance is not high. Here, as long as we can ensure the deep-seated needs of players and fully show the sense of hierarchy of the​画面​ in a performance-superior way, it is enough.

Looking at such a flat​画面​:

To increase its sense of hierarchy, what can you think of?

SSAO!

SSAO is not enabled by default after using Lumen. You can use the following commands to enable it:

r.Lumen.ScreenProbeGather.ShortRangeAO 0

r.Lumen.DiffuseIndirect.SSAO 1

  • If we can increase the weight gain of AO on the​画面​, the sense of hierarchy of the​画面​ will be much better, but this idea is contrary to the current Lumen. Interested friends can try it.

Improving AO can only increase the subtle sense of space in the​画面​. Without large-area spatial shadows, the​画面​ may still look strange.

For grass, we can directly turn off the dynamic shadow of the grass and turn on the contact shadow. The contact shadow can be regarded as a screen-space-based shadow algorithm, which is almost a shadow strategy tailored for grass:

After enabling contact shadow in the model component, you can set the length of the contact shadow in the directional light.

For trees, it cannot use screen-space shadow algorithms like grass, but we can optimize the vertex data submitted to the shadow. Because we use the LOD method to render trees, if the​画面​ shows LOD0, we can completely use LOD2 or LOD3 to draw the shadow instead of LOD0...

For developers, creating products that receive praise from users is both a dream and a mission.

As project scale expands exponentially, we have to pile up a large number of human resources to increase productivity. In this​庞大​ industrial assembly line, every participant is alienated into a standardized part on a precision instrument, losing creative autonomy in the interlocking gears of processes, deeply trapped by requirement iterations and KPI assessments, and gradually reduced to a cold statistical unit in the digital torrent.

docs.title: C++ Reflection Compiler
docs.text: • GitHub Repository: https://github.com/Italink/XObject

docs.title: Build
docs.text: • Can be built directly using CMake (GUI)

docs.title: Brief Project Structure
docs.text:
• Core: Core module
  • 3rdParty: Third-party libraries
  • XHT: Code scanning tool
  • Test: Directory for module function test projects
  • XObject: Base class encapsulation

docs.title: Base Class XObject
docs.text: XObject serves as the base class for all objects, providing operations such as serialization and reflection.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
The library used for reflection is Rttr, an excellent C++ reflection library. It not only enables simple type information reflection but also provides a complete set of reflection processing interfaces:

  • rttr::variant: Similar to stl::any but more powerful, offering numerous type information and conversion interfaces (e.g., an int-type variant can be directly exported as double, which invokes the int-to-double conversion interface; custom variant type conversion functions can be defined in rttr).
  • Supports creating corresponding instances based on type names, with three creation modes (Type, Type*, std::shared_ptr\).
  • Metadata is used to append information, allowing many additional details to be added to properties via this feature.

XHT is used for code scanning (referencing QtMoc), completing automatic type registration through macro markers, which solves the problem of RTTR requiring manual registration function writing.

XHT may seem dispensable—writing registration functions manually is certainly possible—but there are better reasons to use it:

  • Not only RTTR requires registration functions; other features involving adding attachments to types (such as serialization) also need them. For the current XObject, an h-file containing two simple classes would generate nearly a hundred lines of additional code via XHT. This code requires a fixed format and is tedious to write manually.
  • XHT is less error-prone; only generation rules need to be defined.
  • When the original class is modified, XHT automatically synchronizes changes to the additional code without manual intervention.

docs.title: XHT Working Mode
docs.text:
• XObject.h: Defines macros whose markers will be captured by XHT
#define XENTRY(...) \
public: \
    static XMetaObject* staticMetaObject(); \
    virtual XMetaObject* metaObject() override; \
    virtual rttr::instance instance() override { return *this; } \
    using base_class_list = rttr::type_list<__VA_ARGS__>; \
  virtual void __intrusive_deserialize(Deserializer& deserializer) override; \
    virtual void __intrusive_serialize(Serializer& serializer) override; \
    virtual void __intrusive_to_json(nlohmann::json& json) const override; \
private:

#define XFUNCTION(...)
#define XPROPERTY(...)
#define XENUM(...)

XHT is a standalone command-line project with the following parameter format:

AxHeadeTool ${input_file} -o ${output_dir} 
Options:
-i include_dir: Include path for input files

This tool scans files, collects their symbol information, and generates new files. Refer to main.cpp for the processing flow.

docs.title: Define Keywords
docs.text:
XHT efficiently parses file content into symbol strings using a keyword lookup table. The table content is located in Keywords.inl, which is automatically generated by the KeywordsGen project. This project defines all keywords used in XHT.

static const Keyword pp_keywords[] = {...}   // Preprocessing keywords  
static const Keyword keywords[] = {
    { "<", "LANGLE" },
    { ">", "RANGLE" },
    ...

    { "XENTRY","XENTRY_TOKEN"},
    { "XFUNCTION","XFUNCTION_TOKEN"},
    { "XPROPERTY","XPROPERTY_TOKEN"},
    { "XENUM","XENUM_TOKEN"},
    ...
    };

Each keyword contains two parameters. Taking { "XENTRY","XENTRY_TOKEN"} as an example: XENTRY represents the exact symbol in the code file, and XENTRY_TOKEN corresponds to the enumeration used in XHT. The enumeration definition is located in XHT's Token.h file:

#define FOR_ALL_TOKENS(F) \
    F(NOTOKEN) \
    F(IDENTIFIER) \
    ...
    F(XENTRY_TOKEN) \
    F(XFUNCTION_TOKEN) \
    F(XPROPERTY_TOKEN) \
    F(XENUM_TOKEN) \
    ...

Therefore, defining a keyword requires the following steps:

  • Add a new keyword entry {symbol, enum_element} in the KeywordsGen project.
  • Run the KeywordsGen project to automatically generate Keywords.inl in XHT's code directory.
  • Define the enum_element in the Token.h file of the XHT project.

docs.title: Write Collectors
docs.text:
There's no need to concern yourself with the FileParser process unless you need to handle include and macro-related operations. The only thing to note is the bool parse(FileDataDef&, const Symbols&) function in SymbolParser.

The main hierarchical structure of the switch in the parser is as follows:

  • Top-level switch: Collects global file information
  • namespace: Collects namespace information
    • ...
  • class/struct: Collects class information
    • ...
  • ...

Checking the code reveals that the class contains case AX_INVOKABLE_TOKEN and case AX_PROPERTY_TOKEN.

Taking XPROPERTY_TOKEN as an example, its role is to mark variables in the following format:

XPROPERTY(GET getX SET setX)    // Where GET and SET specify the get and set functions for the variable 
int var;

Returning to SymbolParser, you can see that this case actually calls the function parseAxProperty():

case XPROPERTY_TOKEN:
    def.propertyList.push_back(parseXProperty());
break;

The function definition is as follows:

void SymbolParser::parseXProperty()
{
    PropertyDef axVarDef;               // Define the data structure for Property
    next(LPAREN);                       // Move to the next symbol and check if it's a left parenthesis
    while (test(IDENTIFIER)) {          // Check if it's an identifier (non-keyword)
        std::string type = lexem();     // Get the symbol string
        if (type == "GET") {            // Check if the obtained character is GET or SET
            next();                     // Move to the next symbol
            axVarDef.getter = lexem();  // Save the symbol
        }
        else if (type == "SET") {
            next(); 
            axVarDef.setter = lexem();
        }
    }
    next(RPAREN);                       // Move to the next symbol and check if it's a right parenthesis
    axVarDef.type = parseType();        // Parse the variable type
    next(IDENTIFIER);                   // Move to the next symbol and check if it's an identifier
    axVarDef.name = lexem();            // Get the variable name
    until(SEMIC);                       // Move backward until a semicolon is matched
    return axVarDef;
}

All data structures are defined in the DataDef.h file.

Therefore, to complete information collection, the general steps are as follows:

  • Define the data you want to collect in DataDef.h.
  • Add a case in the appropriate place in SymbolParser::parser.

  • Write a symbol parsing function, using the convenient methods provided by Parser to complete information collection.

  • Basic functions

    class ParserBase{
    inline bool hasNext() const { return (mIndex < mSymbols.size()); }
    inline Token next() { if (mIndex >= mSymbols.size()) return NOTOKEN; return mSymbols.at(mIndex++).token; }
    inline Token peek() { if (mIndex >= mSymbols.size()) return NOTOKEN; return mSymbols.at(mIndex).token; }
    bool test(Token);
    void next(Token);
    void next(Token, const char* msg);
    inline void prev() { --mIndex; }
    inline Token lookup(int k = 1);
    inline const Symbol& symbol_lookup(int k = 1) { return mSymbols.at(mIndex - 1 + k); }
    inline Token token() { return mSymbols.at(mIndex - 1).token; }
    inline std::string lexem() { return mSymbols.at(mIndex - 1).lexem(); }
    inline std::string unquotedLexem() { return mSymbols.at(mIndex - 1).unquotedLexem(); }
    inline const Symbol& symbol() { return mSymbols.at(mIndex - 1); }

    void error(int rollback);
    void error(const char* msg = nullptr);
    void warning(const char* = nullptr);
    void note(const char* = nullptr);
};

  • Utility functions

    class SymbolParser : public ParserBase{
    Type parseType();
    bool parseEnum(EnumDef* def);
    bool parseFunction(FunctionDef* def, bool inMacro = false);
    bool parseMaybeFunction(const ClassDef* cdef, FunctionDef* def);
    void parseFunctionArguments(FunctionDef* def);
    std::string lexemUntil(Token);
    bool until(Token);

docs.title: Generate Additional Code
docs.text:
Additional code generation is located in FileGenerator.

Opening FileGenerator.cpp, you will find that additional code generation simply writes data to a file using fprintf:

bool FileGenerator::generateSource()
{
    FILE* out;
    std::filesystem::path outputPath(fileData->outputPath);

    if (fopen_s(&out, outputPath.string().c_str(), "w") != 0) {
        return false;
    }
    std::string header_path = std::regex_replace(std::filesystem::relative(fileData->inputFilePath, outputPath.parent_path()).string(), std::regex("\\\\"), "/");
    fprintf(out, "#include \"%s\"\n", header_path.c_str());                 // Generate include code for the current cpp relative to the h directory
    fprintf(out, "#include <rttr/registration>\n");
    fprintf(out, "#include <XMetaObject.h>\n");
    fprintf(out, "#include <Serialization/SerializationBriefSyntax.h>\n");

    fputs("\n", out);                                                       

    for (auto classdef : fileData->classList) {
        generateAxonClass(out, classdef);
    }
    fputs("", out);

    generateGlobalData(out);                                            
    fclose(out);
    return true;
}

Therefore, this stage only requires writing code based on the collected information.

docs.title: Automatic Build
docs.text:
With XHT, files can only be processed manually via the command line. What if you want to automatically call XHT to process code files in a project?

This is implemented in the CMakeLists.txt of XObject:

function(target_xht_warp PROJECT_TARGET INPUT_FILE_PATH)            
    get_filename_component(INPUT_FILE_NAME ${INPUT_FILE_PATH} NAME_WE)               # Get the filename without extension
    set(OUTPUT_FILE_PATH ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR}/AutoGenFiles/XHT_${INPUT_FILE_NAME}.cpp)   
    add_custom_command(
        OUTPUT ${OUTPUT_FILE_PATH}                                                   # Specify the output file
        COMMAND XHT ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/${INPUT_FILE_PATH} -o ${OUTPUT_FILE_PATH}  # Command-line instruction
        MAIN_DEPENDENCY ${INPUT_FILE_PATH}                           # Specify dependencies; automatically invoke the instruction when the file changes
    )          
    set_property(TARGET ${PROJECT_TARGET} APPEND PROPERTY SOURCES ${OUTPUT_FILE_PATH})       # Add to the build target
    source_group("Generated Files" FILES ${OUTPUT_FILE_PATH})                                # File grouping
endfunction()

This function processes a single file, automatically generates additional code, and includes it in the project build.

Can we automatically call HeaderTool when certain symbols are detected in code files, similar to UE or Qt? The answer is yes. CMake provides the following function to check if code files contain certain symbols:

check_cxx_symbol_exists

However, this process is actually inefficient as it requires traversing the entire file. A better approach is to identify which files need HeaderTool processing via file extensions. The CMakeLists of XObject also provides the following function:

function(target_xht_auto PROJECT_TARGET)
    get_target_property(TARGET_SOURCES ${PROJECT_TARGET} SOURCES)
    message(WARNING "FILES ${TARGET_SOURCES}")
    foreach(FILE ${TARGET_SOURCES})
        get_filename_component(FILE_EXT ${FILE} EXT)     
        if(FILE_EXT STREQUAL ".hxx")
            target_xht_warp(${PROJECT_TARGET} ${FILE})
        endif()
    endforeach()
endfunction()

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
Rttr uses templates to register reflection types. Inheritance handling is implemented via template metaprogramming (when a subclass calls a parent class function, it retrieves the parent class based on using base_class_list = rttr::type_list<...> defined in the subclass). Therefore, this definition must be written in the header file to ensure visibility to subclasses. This requires manually specifying the parent class again during reflection marking, like this:

class Base : public XObject {
    XENTRY(XObject)                     // Must specify the parent class here; otherwise, Rttr cannot determine the inheritance relationship
}

docs.title: Pointer Decay
docs.text:
In Rttr, you cannot use a parent class pointer to call a subclass method. For example, the following code:

XObject* x = new Base;                  // Base contains the print method
rttr::invoke(x,"print");                // Call fails because Rttr cannot determine the real type of x

XObject adds the following definition in the XEntry() macro:

virtual rttr::instance instance() override { return *this; }

This provides a virtual function for XObject subclasses to obtain an rttr instance, avoiding the above pointer issue. The call looks like this:

XObject* x = new Base;
rttr::invoke(x->instance(),"print");    // Call succeeds

docs.title: Registration Timing
docs.text:
The official approach is static registration, whose principle can be simplified as follows:

// Located in CPP
struct Register{
    Register(){
        // Perform RTTR type registration here
    }
};
static Register register;

Explanation: RTTR creates a struct in CPP, writes the registration function in the struct's constructor, and then creates a static instance to complete type registration.

This approach has the following main issues:

  • Registration order is difficult to control.
  • Registering all reflection types at once can cause program startup lag.

To solve this problem, XObject adds the XMetaObject class, whose structure is similar to the above Register (i.e., Rttr registration code is located in its constructor). The difference is that we do not directly create a static instance of XMetaObject in cpp, but instead implement it as follows:

class XObject{
    static XMetaObject* staticMetaObject(){
        static XMetaObject instance;
        return &instance;
    }
}

The static instance inside is only created when the staticMetaObject() function is first accessed. Additionally, since XObject uses XMetaObject as the only entry for reflection data, Rttr registration is automatically performed when using the reflection interface of that type.

Here's another detail:

When using a subclass reflection interface to call a parent class interface, you need to ensure the parent class has been registered.

To achieve this, XObject calls the parent class's staticMetaObject once in the constructor of the subclass MetaObject to ensure the parent class is registered in advance.

docs.title: Meta Object
docs.text:
The above mentioned XMetaObject. Here's a brief explanation of how XObject uses it as the only reflection entry for a type.

Reflection is mainly used for the following purposes:

  • Read/write properties and obtain property information (type, metadata, etc.)
  • Call functions and obtain function information (parameter information, etc.)
  • Create instances based on type names

XMetaObject is type-related and instance-independent. It is only used to obtain reflection data. Part of its code is as follows:

struct XMetaObject {
public:
  XMetaObject();
  XObject* newInstance(std::vector<rttr::argument> args = {});    // Create instance
  rttr::property getProperty(std::string name);                   // Get the property named "name"
  rttr::array_range<rttr::property> getProperties();              // Get all properties of the type
  rttr::method getMethod(std::string name);                       // Get the method named "name"
  rttr::array_range<rttr::method> getMethods();                   // Get all methods of the type
};

Calling functions is instance-related. To call a function, you must provide an instance. This operation looks like this:

Base* base = new Base;
XMetaObject* meta = Base::staticMetaObject();         // Get the static meta object of Base
rttr::method method = meta->getMethod("print");           // Get information about Base's print function
method.invoke(base);                                      // Provide an instance when calling

As we all know, a weakened pointer type cannot call static functions of the actual type, i.e.:

XObejct *x = new Base;
x->staticMetaObject();        // This will call XObject::staticMetaObject() instead of Base::staticMetaObject()

To solve this problem, the XEntry() macro adds the following definition:

virtual XMetaObject* metaObject() override { return staticMetaObject(); }

Additionally, searching the type pool by type name in Rttr is expensive. To solve this problem, XMetaObject provides an additional virtual function for binding MetaObject to rttr::type:

virtual rttr::type getRttrType() { return rttr::type::get<void>(); };

When XHT generates the Rttr registration function, it also generates the definition of this function, which returns a determined rttr::type.

Based on the meta object interface, XObject also provides some instance-related reflection interfaces:

bool setProperty(std::string name, rttr::argument var);       // Set property
rttr::variant getProperty(std::string name);              // Get property
rttr::variant invoke(rttr::string_view name, std::vector<rttr::argument> args = {});      // Call function

docs.title: Serialization
docs.text:
Serialization is not difficult if you write the serialization functions manually, but if you want automatic serialization, you face the following challenges:

  • Serialization of custom types
  • Serialization of complex types (containers)
  • Deserialization of pointers
  • Runtime error checking for deserialization

Different serialization purposes require different handling methods:

  • Binary serialization has the best performance and memory efficiency, but its content is difficult to read.
  • Non-binary serialization (e.g., xml, json, cbor) has an elegant storage structure and strong readability, but with relatively higher performance and memory overhead.

docs.title: Binary
docs.text:
The library used for binary serialization is BitSery, which supports serialization of complex types (containers) through some template operations.

To make a type support BitSery serialization, you only need to provide the template function serialize(Serialize& s, type& o):

struct MyStruct {
    uint32_t i;
    std::vector<float> fs;
};

template <typename Serialize>
void serialize(Serialize& s, MyStruct& o) {  // This template function can be used as both a serialization and deserialization function
    s(o.i);
    s(o.fs);
}

To serialize this object, simply:

using SerializeBuffer = std::vector<uint8_t>;       // Define the buffer type
using OutputAdapter = bitsery::OutputBufferAdapter<SerializeBuffer>;
using InputAdapter = bitsery::InputBufferAdapter<SerializeBuffer>;
using Serializer = bitsery::Serializer<OutputAdapter>;
using Deserializer = bitsery::Deserializer<InputAdapter>;

void main(){
    MyStruct myStruct;
    SerializeBuffer buffer;

    // Serialize: output myStruct to buffer
    bitsery::quickSerialization(OutputAdapter(buffer), myStruct); 

    // Deserialize: read data from buffer into myStruct
    bitsery::quickDeserialization(InputAdapter(buffer), myStruct);      
}

docs.title: Bypassing Templates
docs.text:
To avoid templates, XObject splits the serialization and deserialization functions, adding the following definitions in the XENTRY() macro:

virtual void __intrusive_deserialize(Deserializer& deserializer) override; 
virtual void __intrusive_serialize(Serializer& serializer) override;

The function implementations are generated by XHT based on properties. Additionally, the parent class's serialization functions are called here.

Template adaptation of Bitsery API is used here. The problem is that the inheritance relationship of types cannot be determined through templates.

Fortunately, some definitions were added when implementing Rttr inheritance. These definitions can be used to easily determine whether a type is a subclass of XObject:

template<typename T, typename std::enable_if< std::is_class<T>::value&& rttr::detail::has_base_class_list<T>::value>::type* = nullptr>
void serialize(Serializer& serializer, T& ptr) {
  ptr.__intrusive_serialize(serializer);
}

template<typename T, typename std::enable_if<std::is_class<T>::value&& rttr::detail::has_base_class_list<T>::value>::type* = nullptr>
void serialize(Deserializer& deserializer, T& ptr) {
  ptr.__intrusive_deserialize(deserializer);
}

docs.title: Pointer Specialization
docs.text:
Since Bitsery does not support pointer serialization, specialized pointer serialization templates must be written.

Pointer types differ from original types in two ways:

  • Pointers can be null; nullptr cannot be serialized.
  • New instances may need to be created during pointer deserialization.

To solve these two problems, the following solutions are adopted:

  • Write the pointer's type during serialization; write an empty type for null pointers. During deserialization, the type is always read first. If the type is not empty, serialization continues.
  • Since the pointer type is written during serialization, new instances can be created via RTTR based on the type name. However, this requires ensuring the type has a registered parameterless constructor.

But for XObject, more work is needed—for x in XObject* x = new Base();, std::remove_pointer_t<T>::type cannot be simply used to obtain the original type. Therefore, for XObject types, the type needs to be obtained from the instance's metaObject. The core code is as follows:

template<typename T, typename std::enable_if<std::is_pointer<T>::value && !rttr::detail::has_base_class_list<rttr::detail::raw_type_t<T>>::value>::type* = nullptr>
void serialize(Serializer& writer, T& ptr) {
    std::string typeName;
    if (ptr != nullptr) {
        rttr::type type = rttr::type::get<rttr::detail::raw_type_t<T>::type>();     // Get the original type based on the pointer type
        typeName = type.get_raw_type().get_name().to_string();
    }
    writer(typeName);                   // Write the type
    if (ptr != nullptr) {
        writer(*ptr);                   // If the pointer is not null, write the data it points to
    }
}

template<typename T, typename std::enable_if<std::is_pointer<T>::value&& rttr::detail::has_base_class_list<rttr::detail::raw_type_t<T>>::value>::type* = nullptr>
void serialize(Serializer& writer, T& ptr) {
    std::string typeName;
    if (ptr != nullptr) {
        rttr::type type = ptr->metaObject()->getRttrType();                         // Get the type from metaObject
        typeName = type.get_raw_type().get_name().to_string();
    }
    writer(typeName);                   // Write the type
    if (ptr != nullptr) {
        writer(*ptr);                   // If the pointer is not null, write the data it points to
    }   
}

template<typename T, typename std::enable_if<std::is_pointer<T>::value>::type* = nullptr>
void serialize(Deserializer& reader, T& ptr) {
    std::string typeName;               
    reader(typeName);                   // Read the type
    if (typeName.empty())               // If the type is empty, return directly
        return;
    if (ptr != nullptr) {               // If the object pointed to during deserialization is not null, directly deserialize it
        reader(*ptr);
        return;
    }
    rttr::type type = rttr::type::get_by_name(typeName);        // Get the Rttr type
    if (!type.is_valid())
        return;
    rttr::variant var = type.create();                          // Create an instance using Rttr
    if (!var.can_convert<T>()) {                                
        return;
    }
    ptr = var.get_value<T>();                                   // If the instance is valid, deserialize it
    reader(*ptr);
}

docs.title: Include Optimization
docs.text: Bitsery is a Header-Only library. To avoid including all content in XObject.h, the core definitions are written in SerializationDefine.h, which XObject only includes. Other code is included in SerializationBriefSyntax.h, which XHT includes when generating additional code.

docs.title: Json And Cbor
docs.text:
The library used here is nlohmann json. The implementation here is somewhat hasty—it only completes serialization and not deserialization, and can only be used for debugging. The serialization functions are also generated via XHT. Naturally, new definitions are added in XENTRY():

virtual void __intrusive_to_json(nlohmann::json& json) const override;

The handling method is similar to binary serialization.

Json serialization was initially intended to be done via reflection, as I did with Qt before. But when I actually implemented it, I found it wasn't that simple:

Using rttr, I can read an rttr::variant data. How can I automatically convert it to json data? It seems I can only do this:

rttr::variant property;
if(var.isType<int>()){
    json[propertyName] = property.get_value<int>();
}
else if(var.isType<double>()){
    json[propertyName] = property.get_value<double>();
}
else if(...){
    ...
}

A roundabout way to solve the problem...?

I always thought that IO operations on QVariant in Qt would automatically redirect to the corresponding type's serialization function.

But rttr::variant does not support this. So I looked up how QVariant does it to fill this gap.

I found that its approach is actually the same, but it uses a Map to store functions:

rttr::variant property;
json[propertyName] = FuncMap[property.typeId()](property);

For custom types, Qt declares that they need to be modified using the macro Q_DECLARE_METATYPE:

struct CustomType{};
Q_DECLARE_METATYPE(CustomType)  // This macro registers the meta type. If the type has a serialization function, it binds the function pointer to the type id.

RTTR registration does not support such operations, so for now, XHT is still used to generate json serialization functions.

docs.title: Editor
docs.text:
The Core module does not depend on the Editor module at all, while the Editor module uses reflection data from Core to create the editor.

I have written many editors before and made many attempts, mainly going through the following stages:

  • Editor as Core

  • The early development goal was simple: I needed an editor of a certain type to achieve a certain effect, so I directly started designing the editor's UI and logic. The editor directly called methods of the effect class to edit effects, and sometimes even had to specifically ask the effect class to provide certain APIs for the editor. In the end, the original effect class was completely altered, editor and effect class code was scattered everywhere, coupling was very severe, and I had to be extremely careful when writing import/export interfaces.

  • Type Editor with Property as Core: There were many transitional stages before this, but they are not worth mentioning. You can understand it through the following features:

  • Property as the editing target, with logically consistent read/write interfaces

    When writing effect classes, editable properties should be reserved with corresponding read/write interfaces. When using these properties, their synchronization status should be ensured to correctly utilize data generated by editor serialization.

  • Editor widgets correspond one-to-one with data types

    That is:

    Int types have int editing widgets, curve classes have curve editing widgets, tree structures have tree editing widgets...

    These widgets are very fine-grained. Complete editors are assembled from these small widgets.

docs.title: Program Details
docs.text:
• Automatically adjusts the magnifier display position

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• First, cover the entire screen with a fully transparent borderless window (here I use the color (255, 255, 255) with transparency set to 1 (range [0, 255])).
  • Update the mouse position in real time via a timer or thread. Note: Do not use mouse move events, as color picking triggered by mouse movement cannot capture colors from dynamic videos.
  • Use a screenshot function to capture the entire window. Select a rectangle centered on the mouse position; I chose a size of 10*7, while the magnifier is 100*70, so the magnification factor is 10. Place this rectangular area in the magnifier and select the pixel color at the mouse position.
  • The selected pixel color will have deviations due to the transparent window, so the original color needs to be restored using a transparency algorithm.
  • Transparency principle: Assume B is the transparent color, a is the transparency, A is the underlying color, and C is the final displayed color. The formula is 255*C = a*B + (255-a)*A.
  • To restore the original color, simply solve for A using the formula.
  • When the mouse is clicked, close the transparent window and emit the color signal.
